This investigation focused on 18 peptides derived from cumin, and the essential findings from this analysis are summarized below:   ### 5.1 Anti-inflammatory Activity and Molecular Mechanisms The anti-inflammatory properties of the antimicrobial peptides SR11, FR19, CK19, LR18, CR17, and HR9 are facilitated through two distinct pathways, as reported by Chen, J., et al. (2020) and Liu, X., et al. (2019). Firstly, these peptides modulate signaling pathways by significantly impeding the phosphorylation of the p65 subunit in the NF-κB pathway, along with the activation of the MAPK pathway, specifically targeting ERK, JNK, and p38. This results in a remarkable reduction of 40-65% in the secretion levels of IL-1β and TNF-α, according to Liu, X., et al. (2019). Secondly, they regulate gut microbiota by enhancing the presence of Lactobacillus spp. by 2.3 times and inhibiting the formation of E. coli biofilms, consequently alleviating chronic inflammation. This mechanism bears resemblance to that of HR9, as discussed in the works of Haney, E.F., et al. (2015) and Hancock, R.E.W., et al. (2016).   ### 5.2 Antioxidant Function and Structural Basis The antioxidant potential observed in SR11, CR17, and DK34 can be attributed to several mechanisms: (1) Radical scavenging: The residues of tyrosine (Y) and tryptophan (W) played a crucial role in neutralizing DPPH radicals by donating hydrogen atoms, thus leading to a reduction in MDA production, as noted by Zhang, L., et al. in 2016; (2) Metal chelation: The thiol groups present in cysteine (C) demonstrated a strong capacity to bind with Fe²⁺/Cu²⁺ ions, effectively inhibiting the Fenton reaction, according to the findings of Fjell, C.D., et al. in 2011; (3) Structural stability: In CR17 and CK12, intramolecular disulfide bonds, specifically Cys3-Cys15 and Cys5-Cys12, contributed to the stabilization of β-sheet conformations, thereby prolonging the antioxidants' half-life as discussed in the study by Tossi, A., et al. from 2000.   ### 5.3 Hypoglycemic Potential and Metabolic Regulation Peptides such as IR8, FR19, IF8, LR19, and DK34 played a role in influencing glucose metabolism, as noted by Urry in 2015. This was achieved through several mechanisms: (1) Insulin signaling was impacted by the activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway, which resulted in a 3.2-fold increase in phosphorylation and facilitated GLUT4 translocation; (2) Enzyme inhibition was accomplished by acting as competitive inhibitors of α-glucosidase, thereby reducing the rate of carbohydrate hydrolysis, as observed by Lee and colleagues in 2019; (3) Regarding receptor interaction, the histidine residues, specifically H7 and H12, formed networks of hydrogen bonds with the insulin receptor (INSR), thereby enhancing insulin sensitivity, as described by Ramesh and his team in 2017.   ### 5.4 Anticancer Effects and Molecular Targets Anticancer peptides, namely FR19, LR19, GK18, DK34, and AR10, have been shown to effectively hinder tumor development, as noted in the studies by Wang, Y., et al. (2018) and Fjell, C.D., et al. (2011). These peptides accomplish this through several mechanisms: Firstly, they induce apoptosis by activating the Caspase-3/9 cascade, which results in a 4.7-fold increase in activity, thereby promoting programmed cell death in A549 cells. Secondly, they exhibit anti-angiogenic properties by downregulating VEGF, which subsequently prevents the formation of tubes by HUVEC cells. Lastly, they provide targeted therapy, as illustrated by peptides containing the RGD sequence, such as LR19, which have a particular affinity for integrin αvβ3. This binding effectively obstructs cancer cell invasion, as discussed by Harris, F., et al. (2014).   ### 5.5 Sequence-Activity Relationships Bioactivity has been found to correlate with certain sequence features, as demonstrated by Fjell, C.D., and colleagues in their 2011 study. These correlations can be broken down into three key features:   1. **Hydrophobicity**: The sequences LR18 and FR19 exhibit high content of hydrophobic amino acids, specifically phenylalanine (F, 18.4%), leucine (L, 15.2%), and tryptophan (W, 9.7%). These amino acids play a crucial role in disrupting membranes through the formation of hydrophobic cores.  2. **Cationicity**: In the sequences CK19 and GK18, lysine (K, 12.1%) and arginine (R, 10.3%) are prevalent. These cationic residues are effective at targeting pathogen membranes, demonstrated by a zeta potential of +15.2 mV, leading to subsequent membrane depolarization.  3. **Structural Flexibility**: The sequence SR16 is characterized by a significant presence of glycine (G, 41.2%) and serine (S, 23.5%) repeats. This composition contributes to enhanced plasma stability and is advantageous for targeting tumors, as indicated by the research of Arai, R., et al. (2016) and Urry, D.W. (2015).  These findings highlight the intricate relationship between sequence features and their bioactive functions.   ### 5.6 Multi-pathway Integration Mechanisms Some peptides, such as DK34, carry out their functions by synergistically manipulating multiple pathways, as noted by Lee, S.H., et al. in 2019. These include: (1) Regulation of metal ions: Histidine residues H15 and H22, together with aspartic acid residues D5 and D18, are involved in chelating Zn²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, which in turn influences the activity of hexokinase, increasing its Vmax by a significant 2.4-fold; (2) Interactions between inflammation and oxidative processes: This occurs by simultaneously preventing the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and suppressing ROS production, thereby disrupting the harmful "inflammation-oxidative stress" loop.   ### 5.7 Pleiotropic Functions and Application Prospects 1. The multi-target effects of cumin peptides, such as their antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant synergism, point to their potential utility in functional foods and pharmaceuticals. This potential manifests in several promising avenues: ① Precision Nutrition: Peptide complexes containing FR19/CR17 are candidates for development as gut microbiota modulators, with the aim of alleviating metabolic syndrome through a dual approach of "anti-inflammatory and microbiota balancing" pathways. ② Targeted Delivery: SR16-based nanoparticles, known for their flexibility, could be employed to deliver hydrophobic anticancer peptides like LR18, facilitating tumor microenvironment-responsive therapy. ③ Cross-species Activity: Furthermore, the similarity in sequence between CK12 and HIV-inhibitory peptides, such as Enfuvirtide, suggests a probable role in gp41-binding-mediated inhibition of viral fusion, although this requires further experimental validation.   ### 5.8 Limitations and Future Perspectives Despite making substantial discoveries, several critical issues still need to be addressed: ①Lack of Comprehensive In Vivo Validation: Existing research predominantly depends on in vitro assays; therefore, future investigations must confirm the anti-inflammatory effectiveness and safety within animal models, such as those induced by LPS to simulate sepsis in mice. ②Need for Structural Optimization: The extended sequence of DK34, which comprises 34 residues, could potentially hinder oral bioavailability with a predicted absorption rate of less than 5%. As such, it's pivotal to employ truncation strategies using alanine scanning to pinpoint core bioactive segments, notably the DHCLQYITA motif.   ### 6 Conclusion    ### 6.1 Innovation in Extraction Methods and Activity Screening In this research, bioactive peptide fractions designated as PD-30, PD-50, and PD-80 were effectively extracted from cumin seeds by employing a neutral phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution, aided by ammonium sulfate fractionation. When compared to the conventional method of organic solvent extraction, this approach presents several notable benefits. First, its simplicity stands out: using PBS as a natural medium for extraction eliminates the necessity for harmful chemicals, thus considerably lowering the expenses associated with the experimental process. Furthermore, its efficiency is noteworthy: by integrating fractionation with chromatography techniques, it allows for the meticulous separation of peptides, enhancing the yield of protein extraction to a remarkable 12.5%.   ### 6.2 Validation of Broad-Spectrum Bioactivities 1.2.1 Antimicrobial and Antifungal Activities   (1) Broad-spectrum inhibition: The compound PD-50 exhibited the most pronounced inhibitory effect against Escherichia coli, with an inhibition zone measuring an impressive 11.7 ± 0.5 mm. Meanwhile, PD-80 showed remarkable antifungal activity, particularly against Candida albicans, with its inhibition zone reaching 12.5 ± 0.5 mm. On the other hand, PD-30 displayed comparatively weaker activity.   (2) Mechanism: Cationic peptides employ electrostatic interactions to target membranes of pathogens, while hydrophobic residues like leucine and phenylalanine intensify membrane disruption, resulting in leakage of contents.  1.2.2 Antioxidant Capacity   (1) PD-80 excelled in DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging rates, achieving 72.4% and 62.1%, outperforming PD-50, which recorded 58.4% and 50.2%, and PD-30, with 47.4% and 37.1%.   (2) Activity source: The presence of tyrosine and tryptophan provides hydrogen-donating groups, whereas cysteine contributes to thiol redox activity, which is crucial for its functionality.  1.2.3 PTP1B Inhibition and Hypoglycemic Potential   (1) PD-80 exhibited the strongest inhibitory activity against PTP1B, with an IC₅₀ value of 18.39±1.12 μg/mL. This suggests its potential in boosting insulin sensitivity through the inhibition of negative insulin signaling regulation.   (2) PD-50 and PD-30 showed less effective inhibition, with IC₅₀ values of 29.43 ± 1.58 μg/mL and 45.6 ± 2.8 μg/mL, respectively. This implies that active peptides might interact with the enzyme through specific domains such as phosphotyrosine-mimicking sites.  1.3 Discovery of Novel Peptides and Functional Relevance   (1) Sequence identification: Mass spectrometry and database alignment have led to the identification of 414 peptides from cumin, including 18 novel monomeric peptides that have not been structurally characterized before.   (2) Functional diversity: Identified antimicrobial peptides (11), such as CK19 with a cationic-hydrophobic amphipathic structure, share mechanisms similar to LL-37; identified anticancer peptides (7), such as FR19, target integrin receptors via RGD sequences, significantly reducing the migration of cancer cells; identified hypoglycemic peptides (6), like IR8, mimic insulin A-chain conformation activating the PI3K/Akt pathway with a notable 2.1-fold increase in phosphorylation.   (3) Antiviral potential: CK12 presents 59% homology with HIV fusion inhibitors, including T20, indicating its capacity for gp41-mediated membrane fusion inhibition.  1.4 Research Significance and Future Directions   This research provides invaluable scientific evidence for modernizing traditional Chinese medicine by using cumin-derived peptides.   (1) Translational value: Owing to their low toxicity and immunogenicity, these peptides have a promising future as natural pharmaceuticals or functional food additives.   (2) Technical breakthroughs: Future development will require chemical synthesis and modification (for instance, Cys crosslinking and D-amino acid substitution) to optimize stability, validated through organoid models and preclinical trials.   (3) Multi-omics integration: Combining proteomics and metabolomics will clarify molecular targets related to inflammation and metabolism networks, propelling forward precision medicine applications. This study systematically uncovers the multifunctionality and structural foundations of cumin peptides, establishing an innovative framework for discovering bioactive peptides from natural sources. Moving forward, research should target industrial-scale production and interdisciplinary applications, like combating drug-resistant bacteria and providing adjunct therapy for diabetes, thus opening new avenues for the high-value application of traditional Chinese medicine resources.  Key Mechanistic Insights:   (1) Electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions: Positively charged residues, for example, Arg in FR17 and Lys in AK18, play a crucial role in disrupting bacterial membranes, while hydrophobic cores like Trp13 in AK18 penetrate lipid bilayers similarly to LL-37. summary: Cerebral perfusion plays a crucial role in maintaining brain function and is tightly coupled with neuronal activity. While previous studies have examined cerebral perfusion trajectories across development and aging, precise characterization of its lifespan dynamics has been limited by small sample sizes and methodological inconsistencies. In this study, we construct the first comprehensive normative model of cerebral perfusion across the human lifespan (birth to 85 years) using a large multi-site dataset of over 12,000 high-quality arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI scans. Leveraging generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), we mapped nonlinear growth trajectories of cerebral perfusion at global, network, and regional levels. We observed a rapid postnatal increase in cerebral perfusion, peaking at approximately 7.1 years, followed by a gradual decline into adulthood. Sex differences were evident, with distinct regional maturation patterns rather than uniform differences across all brain regions. Beyond normative modeling, we quantified individual deviations from expected CBF patterns in neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions, identifying disease-specific perfusion abnormalities across four brain disorders. Using longitudinal data, we established typical and atypical cerebral perfusion trajectories, highlighting the prognostic value of perfusion-based biomarkers for detecting disease progression. Our findings provide a robust normative framework for cerebral perfusion, facilitating precise characterization of brain health across the lifespan and enhancing the early identification of neurovascular dysfunction in clinical populations.

contents: ### 1 Normative Cerebral Perfusion Across the Lifespan Xinglin Zeng¹, Yiran Li¹, Lin Hua², Ruoxi Lu¹, Lucas Lemos Franco¹, Peter Kochunov³, Shuo Chen⁴, John A Detre⁵, and Ze Wang¹ are affiliated with the following institutions: ¹Department of Diagnostic Radiology and Nuclear Medicine at the University of Maryland School of Medicine, located in Baltimore, Maryland, United States; ²Department of Radiology at the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, United States; ³Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Science at the University of Texas Health Science in San Antonio, Texas, USA; ⁴Department of Psychiatry at the University of Maryland School of Medicine, situated in Baltimore, Maryland, United States; and finally, ⁵Department of Radiology at the University of Pennsylvania, based in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States.  For any correspondence, please contact Ze Wang, the corresponding author, at the Department of Diagnostic Radiology and Nuclear Medicine, University of Maryland School of Medicine. The address is 670 W Baltimore St, HSF III, Baltimore, MD 21202, United States. You can also reach out via phone and fax at Tel: +1 410-706-2797 or through email at ze.wang@som.umaryland.edu.   ### 2 Abstract Cerebral perfusion is fundamentally significant for maintaining brain function, intricately linked to neuronal activity. Although previous research has explored the developmental and aging trajectories of cerebral perfusion, detailed characterization of its dynamics over the lifespan has been restricted by limited sample sizes and varying methodologies. In this research, we created the initial comprehensive normative model of cerebral perfusion spanning the entire human lifespan—from birth up to 85 years—using an extensive dataset from multiple sites, comprising over 12,000 high-quality arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI scans. By employing generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), we illustrated nonlinear growth trajectories of cerebral perfusion at global, network, and regional scales. We detected a swift increase in cerebral perfusion after birth, which reaches its zenith at around 7.1 years of age, followed by a steady decline into adulthood. We also noted sexual dimorphism, with distinct maturation patterns manifesting in specific regions rather than showing uniform differences across all areas of the brain. Aside from developing normative models, we measured individual deviations from anticipated cerebral blood flow (CBF) patterns in neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders, pinpointing disease-specific perfusion anomalies across four particular brain disorders. Utilizing longitudinal data, we delineated both typical and atypical cerebral perfusion patterns, underscoring the prognostic potential of perfusion-based biomarkers for tracking disease progression. Our discoveries offer a reliable normative structure for cerebral perfusion, enabling precise characterization of brain health throughout the human lifespan and improving the early identification of neurovascular impairment within clinical groups.   ### 3 Introduction Cerebral perfusion, synonymous with cerebral blood flow (CBF), denotes the supply of oxygen and essential nutrients to the brain tissue via the capillary network, a process critical for maintaining typical brain operations and brain health (Churchill et al., 2023; Fantini et al., 2016). This perfusion is intricately linked with neuronal activity through neurovascular coupling. In this process, regions of the brain that become active send signals to the neurovascular unit, prompting an escalation in blood flow to ensure sufficient oxygen and nutrients are supplied to meet the increased metabolic demands (Kaplan et al., 2020; Kastrup et al., 2002; Kisler et al., 2017; Logothetis & Wandell, 2004; Schaeffer & Iadecola, 2021). Besides its pivotal role in brain function, the dynamics of CBF are profoundly tied to the brain's structural integrity, emphasizing the importance of vascular health in preserving brain structure and cognitive prowess (Chen et al., 2013; Li et al., 2023; Ngo et al., 2024). Interruptions in CBF have been linked to a variety of neurological and psychiatric conditions, such as stroke (Hernandez et al., 2012), Alzheimer’s disease (AD) (Alsop et al., 2008; Alsop et al., 2010; Alsop et al., 2000; Camargo et al., 2021; Camargo et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2017; van Dinther et al., 2024; Wang, 2014; Wang et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2010), frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (Hu et al., 2010b; Mutsaerts et al., 2019), and major depressive disorder (MDD) (Chiappelli et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2018). Past research has endeavored to map cerebral perfusion trajectories throughout development and aging, consistently showing a notable rise in early childhood, stabilization during preschool ages, and a gradual descend with age (Biagi et al., 2007; Carsin-Vu et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2016; Ouyang et al., 2024; Paniukov et al., 2020; Wang, Fernandez-Seara, et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2018). Pinpointing the exact timing of peak CBF, however, remains elusive due to two main challenges. Firstly, numerous studies have focused on narrow developmental phases with limited age ranges, resulting in findings that depict either a consistent positive or negative age-related correlation of CBF (Biagi et al., 2007; Leung et al., 4 2016; Paniukov et al., 2020). Secondly, although some studies explore broader age spans from childhood to late adulthood, inconsistencies in findings and restrictive sample sizes hinder comprehensive conclusions (Carsin-Vu et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 1999; Wu et al., 2016). Thus, a holistic comprehension of the ongoing lifespan dynamics in CBF, encompassing gestation through to old age, remains fragmented. To bridge these gaps, developing normative models that systematically chart brain maturation through life could be crucial. Bethlehem et al. (2022) developed a normative brain morphometry model using the largest cumulative multi-site structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) dataset to date, which offers a repeatable and comprehensive framework for brain growth charts. This model employed generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), a versatile statistical framework approved by the World Health Organization for modeling non-linear growth trajectories (Borghi et al., 2006; Stasinopoulos & Rigby, 2008). Extending such an approach to establishing a cerebral perfusion chart could offer invaluable insights into CBF dynamics and their relevance to brain health and disorders. Beyond lifespan depiction, normative models significantly inform individual-level insights, allowing for the identification of aberrations from mean CBF values. These models could serve as biomarkers for brain growth and for neurological and psychiatric disorders, improving diagnostic accuracy for these conditions (Holz et al., 2023; Marquand et al., 2019; Segal et al., 2023). Considering the broad heterogeneity of these conditions (Segal et al., 2023; Verdi et al., 2024; Wolfers et al., 2018), normative modeling acts as a potent tool to link group-level biomarkers with individual metrics. By enabling statistical inferences regarding individual deviations, these models foster more personalized diagnoses and targeted treatments (Bethlehem et al., 2022; Marquand et al., 2019; Rutherford et al., 2023; Rutherford et al., 2022). While normative deviation scores have been applied to structural MRI and resting-state 5 functional MRI data (Bethlehem et al., 2022; Segal et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Verdi et al., 2023; Verdi et al., 2024), their potential in CBF research has remained relatively untapped, despite CBF's essential role in brain function and pathology. To tackle this gap, we compiled a broad, multi-site neuroimaging dataset with rigorous quality control measures, integrating both cross-sectional and longitudinal resting-state arterial spin labeling (ASL) perfusion MRI data. ASL MRI stands out as the only non-invasive means to quantify regional CBF (Detre et al., 2012; Tsujikawa et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2014). Because it doesn't require any exogenous contrast or radioactive tracers and can be conducted repeatedly as needed, ASL MRI holds significant appeal for lifespan research, offering detailed insights into cerebral perfusion dynamics and their implications for brain health and disease throughout human life (Detre et al., 2012; Detre et al., 2009; Z. Wang, 2022). Initially, we utilized cross-sectional ASL data to develop comprehensive normative models capturing the non-linear trajectory of cerebral perfusion across global, network, and regional scales. By integrating these models with structural MRI data, we set benchmarks for pivotal developmental milestones. Additionally, we evaluated the clinical utility of CBF-based normative models by calculating individual deviation scores related to the 50th percentile, employed to characterize disease heterogeneity among patients with AD, FTD, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and MDD. Through longitudinal ASL data integration, we pinpointed typical and atypical disease progression patterns in MCI and AD. Our results underline the clinical potential of cerebral perfusion-based normative models in detecting atypical brain development, monitoring disease processes, stratifying patient subtypes, and appraising therapeutic responses, potentially leading to precise and personalized diagnosis and treatment options. As the pioneering study to establish cerebral perfusion normative models, this work delivers a solid framework for individualized evaluations, providing a set of open science resources to advance standardized, quantitative CBF evaluations. This approach encourages novel 6 investigative directions on the role of vascular health in brain function and pathology. Results Mapping the normative growth of the global cerebral perfusion across the lifespan We gathered multi-modal MRI data from 12,633 participants, including structural MRI and resting-state ASL MRI. Following application of strict quality control informed by the quality evaluation index (QEI) and narrowing the age range from childbirth to 85 years, the final dataset consisted of 9,363 participants boasting high-quality imaging data. This cohort comprised 8,460 healthy individuals and 903 patients pooled from 20 datasets. Detailed demographics and acquisition parameters for each dataset are documented in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2. We explored the developmental and aging trends of global cerebral perfusion by mapping out the normative growth patterns of its mean and variability (assessed via bootstrapping) over the lifespan (Figure 1, Panels A–D). Both shared and area-specific patterns emerged across cortical, white matter, and subcortical regions. Global CBF showed a sharp postnatal surge, peaking around 7.1 years (95% CI: 6.5–7.5), followed by a gradual, near-linear decline into adulthood and later life. Cortical CBF reached its highest during early childhood, with significant between-subject variability that leveled in adulthood (Figure 1, Panels A and D). White matter CBF, however, took a more level trajectory, peaking earlier at 5.5 years (95% CI: 4.5–6.2) and declining at a slower pace (Panel B). In contrast, subcortical perfusion exhibited an intermediate pattern, peaking late in childhood to early adolescence at 6.7 years (95% CI: 6.1–7.2) and declining at a pace comparable to cortical CBF (Figure 1, Panels B and C). Growth rate assessments (Figure 1, Panel C) further accentuated region-specific dynamics, with the sharpest perfusion upsurges seen in early childhood. These findings 7 underpin the differential timing of peak perfusion and subsequent declines across brain regions, offering crucial insights into lifespan trajectories of cerebral perfusion and their potential ramifications for neurodevelopmental and aging-related processes. A significant influence of sex on cerebral perfusion was observed. Utilizing GAMLSS modeling, we incorporated sex as a covariate to form normative growth curves across the lifespan. The analysis unveiled that females exhibited significantly higher global cerebral perfusion, encompassing cortical, white matter, and subcortical areas, compared to males (p < 0.0001). A notable sex difference in variance was detected solely in white matter (pFDR = 0.002), whereas no significant variance differences were seen in cortical or subcortical regions. Detailed sex-specific patterns of cerebral perfusion at the network and regional levels are included in Supplementary Tables 3. 8 Figure 1. Normative Cerebral Perfusion Chart. Panel A, Raw CBF values across the cortex, white matter, and sub-cortical areas, normalized to the maximum cortical CBF. Panel B, Normative CBF Trajectories for men and women, modeled using a generalized additive model. Solid lines denote mean CBF, while dashed lines signify the 95% confidence intervals (CI). Panel C, CBF Growth Rate Across Age: showing a steep decrease in early childhood, stabilization during adulthood, followed by a gradual decline in later stages. The horizontal line (y = 0) signifies the turning point where CBF transitions from increasing to decreasing, whereas the vertical line indicates the age of peak CBF growth. Panel D, Inter-Subject Variability in CBF: Trajectories of median CBF variability and corresponding 95% CI, estimated using sex-stratified bootstrapping. Developmental milestones Important neuroimaging milestones were identified by noticing inflection points in brain trajectories (Figure 2). Global cortical cerebral perfusion peaked around approximately 7.1 years (95% CI: 6.5–7.5), aligning closely with the peak age for global gray matter volume (GMV) at 7.8 years (95% CI: 7.3–8.3). Conversely, white matter volume (WMV) peaked considerably later, near 32.5 years, reflecting its prolonged maturation path. Meanwhile, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume showed a continuous increase throughout life, indicating progressive ventricular enlargement and brain atrophy with aging. To extend brain charts beyond global cerebral perfusion, we applied the GAMLSS modeling approach to estimate normative regional cerebral perfusion trajectories. Analysis results revealed a distinctive maturation gradient across brain regions, mirroring the hierarchical cortical gradient noted in earlier neurodevelopmental studies. This maturation took a structured sequence, beginning in sensorimotor zones, advancing through the limbic system, posterior temporal cortex, parietal cortex, finally reaching the prefrontal cortex, with peak ages ranging from 6.2 to 8.6 years (highlighted in the gray circle in Figure 2). Moreover, relative perfusion retention was examined 9 at crucial lifespan benchmarks—18, 50, and 80 years—exemplifying distinct age- related declines in metabolic and vascular demands (shown in the bottom section of Figure 2). Figure 2. Neurodevelopmental milestones. A visual summary of the normative trajectories of the median (50th percentile) for cerebral perfusion, gray matter volume, white matter volume, and cerebrospinal fluid volume over the lifespan. Triangles mark the peak age for each phenotype, defined as the maximum of the median trajectories. The peak ages for regional cerebral perfusion are color-coded, with warmer colors indicating regions that mature later. Below the graph, regional perfusion maps display the relative retention of cerebral perfusion at diverse life stages (for instance, early childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and old age), with warmer colors signifying regions retaining a greater portion of their peak perfusion. Characterizing individual CBF heterogeneity in brain disorders using cerebral perfusion normative models We explore the clinical relevance of normative CBF modeling by evaluating individual 10 deviation scores derived from CBF data covering four neurological and psychiatric disorders —AD, MCI, FTD, and MDD (Figure 3). These deviation scores assessed the atypicality in cerebral perfusion patterns, revealing disorder-specific deviations. At the global cerebral perfusion level (Figure 3, Panel A-B), a substantial portion of patients exhibited extreme negative deviations in cortical perfusion, with 14.1% of AD (Z = -1.57 ± 0.745), 13.6% of FTD (Z = -1.65 ± 0.734), 9.7% of MCI (Z = -1.09 ± 0.909), and 6.5% of MDD (Z = -1.15 ± 0.811) cases falling under normative thresholds. A kindred pattern was evident in white matter perfusion, where 3.5% of AD (Z = -1.05 ± 0.856), 2.3% of FTD (Z = -0.93 ± 0.738), 5.2% of MCI (Z = -0.80 ± 0.936), and 3.8% of MDD patients (Z = -0.826 ± 0.818) showing extreme deviations. Subcortical perfusion demonstrated significant deficits in 10.6% of AD (Z = -1.43 ± 0.732), 9.1% of FTD (Z = -1.445 ± 0.783), 10.8% of MCI (Z = -1.04 ± 0.914), and 5.3% of MDD patients (Z = -1.12 ± 0.832). At the network level (Figure 3, Panel A-B), disorder-specific patterns of perfusion deficits became apparent. AD patients displayed noteworthy perfusion reductions in the dorsal attention network (DAN, Z = -1.69 ± 0.771, 25.6% extreme negative deviation), frontoparietal network (FPN, Z = -1.74 ± 0.766, 24.7%), and default mode network (DMN, Z = -1.70 ± 0.793, 25%). FTD patients showcased even greater deficits in: ventral attention network (VAN) (Z = -1.62 ± 0.844, 20.5%), FPN (Z = -1.83 ± 0.804, 25%), and DMN (Z = -1.85 ± 0.837, 34.1%). MCI patients demonstrated more diverse deficits across several networks, with higher variability in network-specific Z-scores. In contrast, less than 10% of MDD patients exhibited extreme perfusion reductions across networks, indicating relative stability in perfusion patterns within this group. Regional differences (Figure 3, Panel C-D) are detailed in Supplementary Tables 4. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in cerebral perfusion profiles across brain disorders, underscoring the utility of normative models in identifying individual deviations from usual perfusion patterns. Such deviations provide insights into 11 disorder-specific pathophysiology and hold promise for clinical applications, including subtype identification, classification, and forecast of clinical outcomes. Employing individual deviation scores, we identified two MCI subtypes and delved into their prognostic value for disease progression using cognitive score and diagnostic data (Figure 3, Panel E): MCI-N (MCI normal cerebral perfusion) and MCI-A (MCI AD-like cerebral perfusion). Baseline (within 90 days to first ASL scan) Mini-mental state examination (MMSE) scores (Estimate = 0.766, t = 1.768, p = 0.078) and clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores (Estimate = -0.47625, t = 1.631, p = 0.103) did not differ significantly between the two clusters. However, individuals in the MCI-A group exhibited a steeper decline in MMSE scores (Estimate = -0.335, t = 4.156, p < 0.001) and a steeper increase in CDR scores (Estimate = 0.175, t = -3.133, p = 0.0018) over time, indicating faster cognitive decline. Logistic regression further revealed that individuals in the MCI-N group had significantly lower odds of converting to AD compared to the MCI-A group (OR = 0.45, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.94], p = 0.031), highlighting the clinical relevance of identifying these subtypes. We evaluated the classification performance of each disorder based on the area under the curve (AUC) derived from individual deviation scores following 1,000 permutation tests (Figure 3, Panel F). The classification model demonstrated high accuracy for FTD (mean AUC = 87.67, p < 0.001) and AD (mean AUC = 80.24, p < 0.001). For MCI, the classification performance was significant but lesser in accuracy (mean AUC = 70.90, p = 0.001). In contrast, the model's performance for MDD was not significant (mean AUC = 54.88, p = 0.272), likely stemming from the imbalanced sample size between MDD and healthy controls. Beyond classification, we examined the predictive worth of perfusion deviations for clinical outcomes (Figure 3, Panel G). Perfusion deviations significantly predicted CDR scores in AD (R² = 0.117, p = 0.022) and MCI (R² = 0.046, p = 0.004). However, 12 no significant association was found in FTD (R² = 0.003, p = 0.420). In MDD, perfusion deviations displayed a modest but significant connection with Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) scores (R² = 0.012, p = 0.045). Figure 3. Clinical Relevance of Perfusion Deviation Patterns in Brain Disorders. A) Violin plots depicting deviation scores across global and network levels for AD, 13 FTD, MCI, and MDD. B) Proportion of extreme deviations (z < -2.3) at global and network levels across the four disorders. C) Regional deviation score maps showcasing spatial patterns of perfusion deviations in AD, FTD, MCI, and MDD. D) Regional maps highlighting extreme negative deviations (Z < -2.3) across the four disorders. E) Identification of MCI subtypes (MCI-A and MCI-N) using Euclidean distances of regional deviation scores. Subtypes showcase distinct clinical trajectories for CDR, MMSE, and conversion rates to AD over time. F) Classification effectiveness of brain disorders (AD, FTD, MCI, and MDD) compared to controls using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves based on deviation scores. G) Predictive value of perfusion deviation scores for clinical outcomes, including CDR in AD, CDR Box in FTD, CDR in MCI, and HDRS in MDD. Longitudinal Cerebral Perfusion in brain disorders We established new normative modeling of the longitudinal cerebral perfusion alterations in neurodegenerative diseases, including AD, MCI, and CN (Figure 4). Changes in deviation scores over time supplied valuable insights into the typicality or atypicality of aging-related perfusion patterns, unveiling disorder-specific progression trajectories (Figure 4A-B). At the start, the total extreme negative proportion (TNP) of cerebral perfusion deviations (Z < -2.3) was significantly higher in AD (Estimate = 4.234, t = 2.773, p = 0.006) and MCI (Estimate = 2.053, t = 2.072, p = 0.039) compared to CN. Over time, TNP increased significantly in AD compared to CN (Estimate = 2.752, t = 2.260, p = 0.009), indicating a quicker advancement of perfusion abnormalities in AD. However, the rate of TNP increase was not significantly different between MCI and CN. Regionally, MCI and AD displayed distinct progression trajectories in perfusion deviation scores (Figure 4C, left and right), and detailed statistical differences between the groups are presented in Supporting Table S5. We further delved into longitudinal changes in TNP between stable MCI and progressive MCI. Though no significant difference in TNP was noted at baseline (p = 0.47), 14 progressive MCI exhibited a notably faster increase in TNP over time compared to stable MCI (Estimate = 1.629, t = 3.643, p = 0.0003), highlighting divergent trajectories within the MCI group (Figure 4D, left). Progressive and stable MCI subgroups also demonstrated different regional patterns in deviation score trajectories over time (Figure 4D, right). Statistical differences between the groups at the regional level are presented in Supporting Table S6. Finally, we assessed progression trajectories in MCI-A (AD like perfusion changes) and MCI-N (perfusion akin to NC) subtypes. Initial TNP was significantly higher in MCI-A compared to MCI-N (Estimate = 6.41, t = 4.527, p < 0.001). However, the rate of TNP increase over time was not significantly different between the subtypes (p = 0.527). Both subtypes showed significant increases in TNP over time (MCI-A: β = 0.611 [0.293, 0.929], p = 0.0002; MCI-N: β = 0.773 [-0.0125, 1.56], p = 0.05; Figure 4E, left). Distinct regional progression patterns in deviation scores were also discerned between the subtypes (Figure 4E, right). Regional progression statistics are detailed in Supporting Table S7. 15 Figure 4. Longitudinal perfusion progression in Brain Disorders. Panel A, longitudinal perfusion deviation score maps at the regional level in CN, MCI, and AD 16 groups at baseline and follow-up. Panel B, longitudinal extreme negative perfusion deviation maps (Z < -2.3) at the regional level in CN, MCI, and AD groups at baseline and subsequent periods. Panel C: Perfusion change rates in CN, MCI, and AD groups. The left panel shows changes in total extreme negative proportion (TNP) over two years, while the right panel depicts regional variability in perfusion change rates. Panel D: Perfusion change rates in progressive vs. stable MCI. The left panel displays changes in TNP between the two subgroups, while the right panel shows regional differences in perfusion change rates. Panel E: Perfusion change rates in MCI-A vs. MCI-N subtypes. The left panel illustrates changes in TNP over time for the two subtypes, while the right panel portrays regional variability in perfusion change rates. Sensitivity analyses The lifespan growth patterns of cerebral perfusion were validated at global, network, and regional levels utilizing multiple rigorous analysis strategies. Each validation approach exhibited strong alignment with the principal results, affirming the robustness of the findings: 1. Data Quality Validation: Analyses were reiterated with a stricter quality control threshold (QEI > 0.15) to evaluate the influence of data quality. 2. Balanced Sampling: A balanced sampling strategy was deployed to tackle potential biases from uneven sample and site distributions over ages. Participants and site numbers were uniformly matched by resampling 1,000 times. 3. Reproducibility Testing: A split-half approach was utilized to validate the reproducibility of the results by splitting the dataset into two equal halves and comparing the outcomes. 4. Bootstrap Resampling: A bootstrap resampling analysis (1,000 iterations) was executed to study the influence of data sample variability. 5. Site-Specific Effects: A leave-one-site-out (LOSO) analysis was conducted to evaluate the potential impact of specific sites on the observed patterns. 17 The outputs of these validation strategies were quantitatively compared to the main findings, demonstrating consistent growth patterns across all analyses. Detailed results are provided in Supplementary Tables 8–13. Discussion This study marks the first comprehensive characterization of cerebral perfusion growth patterns spanning the lifespan (birth to 85 years) using large multisite datasets. By merging structural MRI and ASL MRI data, we drew nonlinear growth trajectories at global, network, and regional levels, unveiling pivotal milestones of perfusion maturation and age-related decline. Our normative models lay down typical cerebral perfusion ranges, enabling precise individual deviation detection and offering insights into both healthy aging and disorder-specific patterns. The longitudinal analysis grasped dynamic perfusion changes over time, providing a framework for comprehending disorder progression and transitions among clinical stages. These findings underscore the value of cerebral perfusion-based normative models as vital tools for studying brain development, aging, and the pathology of neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. At the global level, our study ratified a swift postnatal surge in cerebral perfusion, succeeded by a gradual age-related decline, with peak age slated through precise confidence intervals derived from bootstrap and balanced resampling analyses. This early upswing in cerebral perfusion is vital for catering to the heightened metabolic demands of the developing brain, supporting pivotal processes like synaptogenesis, dendritic arborization, myelination, and glial proliferation (A et al., 2021; Ouyang et al., 2024; Silbereis et al., 2016). During childhood, the brain accounts for up to 44% of the body’s overall energy use (A et al., 2021; Blüml et al., 2013), surpassing adult metabolic demands substantially. This elevated perfusion secures the supply of oxygen and nutrients essential for dynamic plasticity underpinning sensory, cognitive, and motor development (Hijman et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2024). At the 18 network level, the clawing maturity of the DMN is facilitated by increased perfusion in DMN regions, epitomizing the growing connectivity and functional specialization of this network (Yu et al., 2023). The structural development of cerebral vasculature, among which include increased intracranial arterial diameters observed in early life, further supports these metabolic needs (Taylor et al., 2022). Disruptions in global and regional cerebral perfusion are associated with neurodevelopmental delays and several infant disorders, underscoring the importance of balanced perfusion for typical brain development (Hijman et al., 2024; Mahdi et al., 2018; Nagaraj et al., 2015). Following cerebral perfusion's rapid increase in infancy, it peaks around age 7 and steadily decreases into later life. This trajectory reflects previous findings indicating the peak GMV arises in early childhood, closely paralleling peak cerebral perfusion (Bethlehem et al., 2022). Preserving brain volume during this interval necessitates considerable energy since daily brain glucose consumption reaches its highest levels around this age (Kuzawa et al., 2014). Remarkably, brain glucose demand inversely relates to body growth from infancy to puberty, signifying that the substantial metabolic expenses of neurodevelopment may come partly at the cost of slowing somatic growth (Aronoff et al., 2022; Kuzawa et al., 2014; Vandekar et al., 2017). During adolescence, as GMV diminishes and WMV expands, the associated cerebral perfusion reduction reflects a transition towards greater neural efficiency (Satterthwaite et al., 2014). This transition mirrors increasing neurovascular coupling during childhood, suggesting improved synchronization between neural activity and vascular responses (Schmithorst et al., 2015). After a phase of synaptic overproduction, synaptic pruning selectively removes redundant synapses to achieve optimal network efficiency (Nikiruy et al., 2024; Tierney & Nelson, 2009). Crucially, this process adheres to a regionally specific timeline, with auditory regions completing pruning by roughly age 6, whereas higher cognitive areas, such as the frontal cortex, continue pruning into adolescence (Dow-Edwards et al., 2019; Tierney & Nelson, 2009). These spatially inhomogeneous developmental patterns align with our findings of later cerebral perfusion peaks in frontal areas, 19 reflecting the extended development of higher-order cognitive and executive functions. Multiple studies consistently report significant sex differences in cerebral perfusion (Alisch et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2016; Satterthwaite et al., 2014; Vandekar et al., 2017), highlighting the vital influence of biological, hormonal, structural, and cardiovascular elements on the brain's vascular and metabolic processes. Anatomically, sex-based variations in brain size, gray matter volume, and cortical thickness contribute to differing perfusion patterns (Bethlehem et al., 2022; Dukart et al., 2018). Hormonal influences, notably estrogen and progesterone, play a central role in modulating cerebral blood flow, with estrogen’s vasodilatory effects contributing to the typically higher perfusion levels seen in females (Cote et al., 2021; Krause et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2016). Cardiovascular factors further shape these differences, with sex-related variations in systemic blood pressure, heart rate, and vascular compliance influencing cerebral perfusion regulation (Barnes & Charkoudian, 2021). Cerebral perfusion normative modeling provides a robust tool for grasping individual differences, mapping disease-specific patterns, and characterizing variability in disorders like AD, FTD, MCI, and MDD. While previous research extensively examined group-level differences in cerebral perfusion between these disorders and healthy controls (Alsop et al., 2000; Hu et al., 2010a; Liao et al., 2017; van Dinther et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2007; Wei et al., 2018; Ze Wang, 2017), this study is the first employing a normative modeling framework, offering several key benefits and new insights. First, normative modeling enables individualized inferences, revealing disease heterogeneity beyond group averages. By leveraging substantial multisite datasets, this approach provides more precise estimates of individual deviations from the median. For instance, in FTD, while the mean deviation z-score was similar between the FPN and the DMN, the proportion of extreme negative deviations was significantly higher in the DMN (34%) compared to the FPN (25%), suggesting greater consistency of alterations in the FPN but higher heterogeneity in the DMN. Second, 20 age- and sex-normalized cerebral perfusion facilitates transdiagnostic comparisons and disorder-specific analyses. Segal et al. Segal et al. (2023) previously demonstrated the utility of such methods in identifying shared and distinct brain abnormalities across psychiatric disorders. In our study, distinct patterns of cerebral perfusion alterations were observed across neurodegenerative diseases and psychiatric conditions. Neurodegenerative diseases, such as AD, FTD, and MCI, showed greater perfusion alterations, marked by higher proportions of extreme deviations and lower mean z scores compared to MDD. These findings align with evidence suggesting that neurodegenerative diseases are prominently linked with neurovascular dysfunction (Solis et al., 2020). Third, the normative model enhances sensitivity to subtle perfusion changes, boosting statistical power and improving discrimination between disease-related and non-disease-related variability (Rutherford et al., 2022). This benefit is crucial for early diagnosis, as illustrated in our MCI analysis. We identified two subgroups: MCI-A, characterized by decreased cerebral perfusion similar to AD, and MCI-N, with perfusion patterns resembling normal controls. While baseline cognitive impairment didn't differ significantly between the subgroups, their trajectories diverged considerably over time. MCI-A showed more considerable cognitive and cerebral perfusion declines and a higher likelihood of converting to AD, highlighting the predictive worth of cerebral perfusion deviations for disease progression (Duan et al., 2021; Solis et al., 2020; Wolters et al., 2017). Lastly, we demonstrated the practical applications of deviation scores in disease classification and prediction. These findings underscore the significance of individualized cerebral perfusion assessments for understanding disease heterogeneity, anticipating progression, and guiding early interventions. The longitudinal analysis of cerebral perfusion using normative modeling provides critical insights into the progression paths of neurodegenerative diseases, chiefly in AD and MCI, compared to CN individuals. Over time, the vastly quicker fall in cerebral perfusion and rise in TNP (total negative perfusion) in AD compared to 21 CN highlights the progressive nature of perfusion abnormalities in AD. This pattern reflects accelerated neurovascular and metabolic dysfunction, consistent with earlier findings of increasing brain atrophy in AD using normative models (Verdi et al., 2024). Given that accelerated disease progression is a signature of AD (Leung et al., 2013), these findings highlight the value of normative modeling for early diagnosis and intervention. Alternatively, MCI showed notable variability, with distinct trajectories noted in stable and progressive MCI subgroups. Progressive MCI recorded a faster TNP rise over time, while no baseline differences were evident between stable and progressive MCI, suggesting longitudinal modeling can uncover subtle progression patterns that may be overlooked in cross-sectional analyses. Furthermore, the longitudinal trajectories of cerebral perfusion in stable and progressive MCI, along with the MCI-A and MCI-N subgroups, suggest mutual associations between cerebral perfusion decline and the probability of AD conversion. This aligns with former studies linking increasing brain atrophy to an elevated AD conversion risk (Verdi et al., 2023; Verdi et al., 2024). Collectively, these findings illustrate the utility of merging cross-sectional and longitudinal normative modeling to capture disease progression dynamics, inter-individual variability, and region-specific patterns in neurodegeneration. Several challenges and implications should be considered in the context of this study. First, CBF estimations can be swayed by various ASL sequence factors, such as employing PASL versus PCASL, single versus multiple PLDs, specifically acquiring an M0 image or generating one from control images, and using background suppression (Luis Hernandez-Garcia, 2022; Ze Wang, 2022). Although sequence effects were accounted for by incorporating them as fixed factors in the normative modeling, enhancing generalizability, it doesn't fully surmount the inherent primary study design limitations. Further development of a more standardized and quantitative pipeline for cerebral perfusion evaluation across multicenter studies is required to assure robust and comparable outcomes. Second, akin to previous normative 22 modeling studies utilizing structural MRI (Bethlehem et al., 2022), the current neuroimaging datasets disproportionately represent populations from Europe and North America. Future research should prioritize the inclusion of more diverse neuroimaging cohorts, ensuring balanced representation across ethnic groups and decreasing geographic bias. Third, ASL data included in this study had low resolution. Some had limited brain coverage to include the full visual cortex and cerebellum. As more research sites adopt cutting-edge ASL MRI sequences developed by us (Chang et al., 2017; Vidorreta et al., 2014; Vidorreta et al., 2017; Vidorreta et al., 2012) and others (Alsop et al., 2014), high-resolution ASL CBF maps may become more accessible, permitting exploration of finer-grained cerebral perfusion atlases. Fourth, participant age distribution in datasets was uneven, with certain ages, like 0–5 years and 30–40 years, being underrepresented. Including data from fetal and neonatal stages would foster a more thorough understanding of cerebral perfusion across the lifespan (Wang, Fernandez-Seara, et al., 2008). Fifth, the focus, in this study, was exclusively on CBF, although ASL MRI can provide several other neurovascular measurements in addition to CBF, including arterial transit time, blood-brain-barrier water exchange time or rate, and vascular health (Li et al., 2022; Li & Wang, 2023). However, these parameters rely on lengthy ASL MRI scans with varied PLDs and TEs or pre-conditions like diffusion-weighted vasculature water saturations, which were unavailable in most datasets used in this paper. With future data availability, expanding models to incorporate these metrics could offer a more comprehensive grasp of brain physiology. Sixth, while the potential of regional deviation scores in subgroup identification, classification, and prediction was illustrated, the reliability and utility of these applications could be immensely enhanced with progressions in artificial intelligence algorithms and superior-quality cerebral perfusion data. These advancements may ultimately facilitate translating these tools into clinical settings. Finally, the cerebral perfusion-based growth charts established in this study are intended to serve as a dynamic resource. As more high-quality datasets on brain metabolism become available, these lifespan normative growth models can be 23 refined and updated, further enhancing their utility for research and clinical applications. Conclusion This study establishes normative cerebral perfusion charts over the lifespan, offering a solid framework to quantify individual variability and identify deviations associated with neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative pathways. By integrating cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses, these models provide insights into brain development, aging, and disorder progression, enabling accurate heterogeneity characterization and clinical trajectory predictions. These findings highlight the potential of perfusion-based models as invaluable tools for research and clinical applications. Method Datasets and Participants To outline the normative growth of cerebral perfusion in the human brain, we collected multisite neuroimaging datasets, each containing both 3T structural MRI and resting-state ASL data. For participants with repeated test-retest scans or longitudinal data, only the session with the highest quality score was included. Written informed consent was obtained from participants or their legal guardians, and all recruitment procedures were approved by the local ethics committees overseeing each dataset. Image quality control process To secure the reliability of imaging data, all T1-weighted structural MRI and ASL scans exhibiting severe artifacts or partial brain coverage were independently reviewed and excluded by X.Z. and Y.L. Furthermore, data quality was additionally assessed using the cerebral blood flow quality evaluation index (QEI) (Dolui et al., 2024), a metric ranging from 0 to 1, with elevated values denoting better quality. The QEI captures three crucial aspects of valid CBF maps: 1) Structural similarity: The correlation degree between brain structure and CBF, as structure and function are generally aligned; 2) 24 Spatial variability: CBF value variability across voxels within each tissue type. High variability suggests data noise or insufficient post-labeling delay. All participants with QEI less than 0.1 were excluded from further analysis, and several thresholds were used for validation. Image preprocessing Structural data preprocessing Publicly available, containerized HCP structural preprocessing pipeline was employed (Glasser et al., 2013). Briefly, this pipeline incorporates two stages: (1) The PreFreeSurfer stage: This stage normalizes anatomical MRI data and comprises preprocessing steps such as brain extraction, denoising, and bias field correction of T1-weighted images. (2) The FreeSurfer stage: This stage generates cortical surfaces from the normalized anatomical data. Key steps include anatomical segmentation, construction of pial, white, and mid-thickness surfaces, and surface registration to the standard atlas. The preprocessed T1 data was utilized for further ASL CBF assessing, registration, and providing brain volume information. ASL data preprocessing ASLtbx (Li et al., 2018; Wang, 2012; Wang, Aguirre, et al., 2008) was used to process the ASL MRI data using standard processing pipelines. The ASL label and control images were motion-corrected, temporal confound filtered, and spatially smoothed. Quantitative CBF maps were calculated in physiological units (mL/100 g/min) using the general kinetic model: 𝐶𝐵𝐹= ∆𝑀 2 ∗𝑀0 ∗𝜆∗ 𝛼∗ 𝛽∗ 𝑒−𝜎/𝑇 (1) , where ∆𝑀 is the difference between control and label images, 𝑀0 is the equilibrium magnetization of arterial blood, 𝜆 is the brain-blood partition coefficient, 𝛼 is the labeling efficiency, 𝛽 is the bolus duration, 𝜎 is the post-labeling delay (PLD), and 𝑇 is the longitudinal relaxation time of blood (1.65 s at 3T). M0 images were explicitly acquired in the 3D background suppressed ASL data, and the pulsed ASL (PASL) data. 25 For the 2D background unsuppressed pseudo continuous Arterial Spin Labeling (pCASL) data, the mean of the control images from the ASL time series was used as the M0 image. Partial volume correction was performed using tissue segmentation results based on the structural T1-weighted images. Functional-to-standard image registration was performed to align processed CBF maps to MNI152 space for region-specific analysis. First, the CBF map was linear registered to the subject’s T1-weighted structural image. The T1-weighted image was then non-linearly aligned to the MNI152 standard space. The CBF image was subsequently transformed to standard space by combining the functional-to-structural affine matrix and the nonlinear warp. All registration outputs were visually inspected to ensure accuracy. Regional CBF values were measured using the Harvard-Oxford brain atlas, encompassing 48 cortical and 8 subcortical regions (Desikan et al., 2006). Additionally, network-level CBF values were explored using Yeo’s atlas, focusing on networks like the DMN, FPN, affective network (AN), VAN, DAN, and somatosensory network (SSN) (Yeo et al., 2011). Due to potential sequence issues, the visual network was excluded from the analysis. Modeling normative growth curves across the lifespan To estimate normative growth patterns for cerebral perfusion metrics in healthy individuals across cohorts, we applied GAMLSS to the cross-sectional data using the gamlss package (version 5.0-6) in R 4.2.0 (Borghi et al., 2006; Stasinopoulos & Rigby, 2008). The GAMLSS procedure consisted of two steps: identifying the optimal data distribution and determining the best-fitting model parameters for each global cerebral perfusion metric (Sun et al., 2024). Using these metric-specific GAMLSS models, we obtained nonlinear normative growth curves and their first derivatives. Furthermore, the sex-stratified growth patterns were assessed. Nonlinear normative growth curves and their first derivatives were generated, with sex-stratified growth patterns also examined. The robustness of these growth curves was validated using bootstrap 26 resampling, leave-one-study-out analysis, balanced resampling, and split-half replication (Bishop, 2006). (i). Model data distributions We assessed 28 continuous distribution families for their fit to the data using global cortical CBF as the reference metric. Model fits were evaluated using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) (Neath & Cavanaugh, 2012), where lower BIC values indicate superior model performance. Among the evaluated distributions, the Generalized Beta 2 (GB2) distribution consistently provided the best fit across all models (see Supplementary Figure). (ii). The GAMLSS framework. The GAMLSS framework was applied with CBF values as the dependent variable, age as a smoothing term (using B-spline basis functions), and sex as a fixed effect. To account for variability introduced by ASL sequences, the ASL sequence type was also included as a fixed effect, while dataset site was treated as a random effect (Sun et al., 2024). The GB2 distribution, which has four parameters: median (μ), coefficient of variation (σ), skewness (ν), and kurtosis (τ), was chosen to fit the data distribution. Each CBF values, denoted by y, was modeled as: 𝛾= 𝐺𝐵2 (𝜇, 𝜎, 𝜈, 𝜏) (2) 𝜇= 𝑓𝜇 (𝑎𝑔𝑒) + 𝛽𝜇 1 (𝑠𝑒𝑥) + 𝛽𝜇 2 (𝑠𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒) + 𝑍𝜇 (𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑒) (3) 𝜎= 𝑓𝜎 (𝑎𝑔𝑒) + 𝛽𝜎 (𝑠𝑒𝑥) (4) 𝜈= 𝛽𝜈 (5) 𝜏= 𝛽𝜏 (6) To explore the age-related trends in global and network-level CBF values, three GAMLSS models with different degrees of freedom (df = 5–9) were tested for the B- spline basis functions in the μ(location) and σ (scale) parameters. The optimal model was selected based on the lowest BIC value. Across all analyses, a consistent df = 8 was 27 identified as optimal. Regional CBF models also used df = 8 to maintain consistency in identifying potential peak ages. Following prior studies, only intercept terms were included for the ν and τ parameters (Di Biase et al., 2023). For model estimation, we used a default convergence criterion of log-likelihood < 0.001 between iterations, with a maximum of 500 iteration cycles. (iii). Sex differences across the lifespan. To assess the influence of sex on CBF across the lifespan, we included sex as a fixed effect in the GAMLSS model. Adjusted mean (μ) and variance (σ) coefficients, along with their standard errors, T-values, and P-values, were computed for the sex variable (see Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 for global and network-level CBF, respectively). The T-value, calculated as the coefficient divided by its standard error, was used to test the null hypothesis that the sex has no significant effect on CBF. To ensure robust estimates of sex-specific effects on CBF growth trajectories, we adjusted for key covariates, including age, ASL sequence type, and scanner site as a random effect. Sensitivity analysis of normative models To validate the lifespan normative growth patterns at global, network, and regional levels, we conducted multiple sensitivity analyses. These analyses addressed critical methodological concerns, including data quality, sample size imbalance, site distributions variability, model replication, model stability, and the influence of specific sites. By systematically testing these factors, we ensured the robustness and generalizability of our normative models across diverse datasets and methodological conditions. (i). CBF data quality assurance using QEI > 0.15. To ensure the robustness of our findings against variations in ASL data quality, a stricter quality control threshold was applied, excluding participants with a QEI below 0.15. This stricter threshold was selected based on previous research emphasizing the critical 28 role of ASL data quality in brain imaging studies (Li & Wang, 2023). Normative model analyses were then re-run to verify consistency with the original results, ensuring the reliability of our findings. (ii). Balanced resampling analysis. To mitigate potential biases from uneven sample sizes and site distributions across age groups, a balanced sampling strategy was employed. The lifespan was segmented into 17 five-year age bins spanning birth to 85 years, with the smallest group containing 64 participants (ages 35–40). To achieve balanced representation across age groups, random sampling was used to equalize all age group to 64 participants. This procedure was repeated at ratios of 1×, 1.5×, and 2× the size of the smallest group size (64 here) to assess the robustness of the findings. For global and network CBF values, sampling was repeated 1,000 times on a pool of 9,800 participants. Each iteration included a random subset of 1,300 participants, and GAMLSS models were refitted to generate 1,000 growth curves per metric. Confidence intervals were calculated for the growth curves, the peak of the 50th centile, and the correlations between the resampled median centile curves and the original cohort’s median centile curve. (iii). Split-half replication analysis. We conducted a split-half validation to evaluate the model's reproducibility and performance. The dataset was randomly divided into two equal halves, stratified by site. One half was used to train the GAMLSS model, and the other half was used to evaluate the model’s goodness of fit. This process was repeated with the roles of training and testing sets reversed. Model fit was assessed using R-squared (R2) for central tendency and quantile randomized residuals (randomized z-scores) for calibration. The Shapiro-Wilk test evaluated the normality of residuals, with W values close to 1 indicating good fit. Higher-order moments, including skewness (values near 0 indicate symmetry) and 29 kurtosis (values near 0 indicate light tails), offered further insights into model fit. This procedure was repeated 1,000 times, generating median and 95% CI values for R2, W, skewness, and kurtosis. (iv). Bootstrap resampling analysis. To assess the robustness of lifespan growth curves, we conducted 1,000 bootstrap repetitions with replacement sampling. The sampling preserved the age and sex proportionality of the original cohort by stratifying the lifespan into nine intervals. For each functional metric, 1,000 growth curves were generated, and 95% CIs were computed for the median (50th) centile curve and inflection points. The CIs were derived from the mean and standard deviation of the bootstrap growth curves and growth rates. (v). Leave-one-study-out (LOSO) analysis. To evaluate the influence of individual sites on the growth curves, LOSO analysis was performed. Samples from one site were omitted in each iteration, and the GAMLSS models were refitted. Growth curves and rates were then re-calculated, with mean and standard deviation values used to compute 95% CIs for both the growth curves and rates. The narrow CIs indicated that the models remained robust and consistent, even when data from specific sites were removed. Clinical relevance of CBF-based normative models in brain disorders To evaluate the clinical utility of lifespan perfusion models, this study analyzed quality- controlled structural MRI and ASL data from individuals with four brain disorders: MDD, MCI, AD, and FTD. Data were drawn from the EMBARC (MDD), ALLFTD (FTD; 5 sites), ADNI (AD and MCI), and UMB (MCI) datasets, including 28 CNs and 186 patients with MDD, 56 CNs and 44 patients with FTD, 213 CNs and 64 patients with AD, and 251 patients with MCI. 30 (i). Individual deviation z scores. The standard protocol for normative modeling emphasizes the importance of including control samples from the same imaging sites as the patient data in the testing set to account for site effects. To ensure robust modeling, a stratified approach was adopted, incorporating site-specific CNs in the testing set. This approach enabled the identification and mitigation of site effects, minimizing confounding in case-control comparisons. All CNs from disease-specific datasets were randomly split into training and testing subsets, stratified by sex and site. Lifespan normative models of cerebral perfusion were constructed using the training set, which included half of the CNs and data from other large datasets. The testing set, comprising the remaining CNs and all patient cases, served as an independent validation set for calculating deviation scores. Quantile scores relative to the normative model curves were calculated for each individual, followed by the computation of deviation z-scores. These z-scores were derived by transforming the fitted generalized beta distribution (GB2) quantiles into standard Gaussian z-scores using quantile randomized residuals. Extreme negative deviations were defined as z < -2.3, consistent with prior studies. Percentage maps of extreme deviations revealed substantial heterogeneity in deviation patterns among individuals within each disease group. To ensure reliability, this process was repeated 100 times, generating 100 independent models and corresponding sets of deviation scores for both patients and testing CNs. The normality of the z-score distributions was evaluated using two-tailed Kolmogorov- Smirnov tests, which consistently yielded p<0.05 across all models and iterations. Subsequent analyses were based on these independently derived deviation scores for testing HCs and patient cohorts. The stability of individual deviation estimates was assessed by calculating pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients and mean squared errors (MSE) across the 100 independent models. Results demonstrated highly stable deviation scores within specific disease cohorts, with mean correlations exceeding 0.95 and mean MSE values below 0.2 for all metrics. Case-control comparisons and disease 31 classification analyses were repeated across the 100 models to confirm robustness. (ii). Identification of MCI Subtypes Using individual perfusion deviations. Given the substantial individual heterogeneity in cerebral perfusion patterns and the limited number of patients, we employed a data-driven k-means clustering algorithm to identify subtypes of MCI. Deviation features for each patient included both regional and network-level CBF metrics. The Euclidean distance was used to calculate the similarity matrix across patients. The optimal number of clusters was determined to be between 2 and 8. To identify the final cluster count, we utilized the NbClust package, which computes 30 different clustering indices. The most frequently identified optimal cluster number was selected as the final solution. The clustering analysis revealed two distinct MCI subtypes. One subtype exhibited deviation patterns closer to those of AD, which we labeled MCI-A, while the other showed deviations more similar to CNs, labeled MCI-N. We then explored disease progression trajectories within these subtypes. A logistic regression analysis was conducted to assess the association between baseline subtype and the risk of conversion from MCI to AD during the follow-up period. The outcome variable was binary, indicating whether participants converted to AD (Converted = 1) or stayed MCI (Converted = 0). Age and gender were included as covariates to account for potential confounding factors. The logistic regression model was fitted using a generalized linear model (GLM) with a binomial distribution (logit link function). The odds ratio (OR) and corresponding 95% CIs were calculated to quantify the effect of each predictor on conversion risk. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. To further evaluate the longitudinal cognitive changes in the identified subtypes, we applied a linear mixed model (LMM) to examine the interaction between MCI subtype and time on the MMSE scores and CDR scores. Age and gender were included as covariates in the model. The fixed effects included MCI subtype, time (defined as year), and their interaction to capture group differences in longitudinal changes. Time points were defined as whole-year intervals, with measurements within ±3 months assigned to the closest year (e.g., 11 months as Year 1, 26 months as Year 32 2). Different participants were as a random effect to account for repeated measures over time. (iii). Disease classification and prediction based on connectome-based deviations. We applied support vector machine (SVM; www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvm/) analysis to assess the discriminative power of perfusion-based deviations in distinguishing patients from healthy controls (HCs). The model was repeated 1000 times utilizing a 2-fold cross-validation framework, with training and testing sets alternated in each fold. Classification performance was assessed by plotting receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and calculating the area AUC. The statistical significance of AUC values was determined using a nonparametric permutation test (1,000 iterations), in which labels were randomly shuffled prior to implementing SVM and cross-validation. This procedure generated a null distribution of AUC values, and corresponding p-values were computed. Mean ROC curves and mean AUC values were derived by averaging results across the 1000 repetitions. We employed support vector regression (SVR) with a linear kernel to predict clinical scores based on connectome-based deviations. A 2-fold cross-validation framework was used to estimate prediction accuracy. Each fold alternated as the training and test set. Similar to SVM, features were normalized in the training set, with the same parameters applied to the testing set. Predictive performance was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation coefficients between predicted and observed clinical scores. Statistical significance was assessed via a nonparametric permutation test (1,000 iterations), with target scores shuffled before implementing SVR and cross-validation. This process yielded a null distribution of correlation coefficients, and p-values were computed. All analyses were conducted using the libsvm software. Longitudinal cerebral perfusion changes in brain disorders To investigate longitudinal changes in cerebral perfusion in brain disorders, this study utilized quality-controlled structural MRI and ASL data (visual inspection and QEI 33 values) from individuals with at least one year of longitudinal neuroimaging follow-up. Prevent AD and Dalas lifespan were set as reference health control datasets, which include 506 participants with 1430 scans; the ADNI was set as a disease dataset, included 649 health controls with 213 scans, 256 MCI with 911 scans, 64 AD with 189 scans. (i). Deviation z scores at each scan. Deviation z-scores for each scan were calculated using a procedure similar to the previously described normative model. The reference healthy control dataset, combined with a randomly sampled 50% of healthy controls from the disease dataset, served as the training dataset. The remaining 50% of healthy controls and all patients were included in the testing dataset. This process was repeated 100 times, and the final deviation z-scores for each scan were averaged across the 100 iterations. The TNP was defined as the proportion of extreme negative deviations (z < −2.3) across all brain regions (58 cortical and 8 subcortical regions) (Verdi et al., 2024). (ii). Cerebral perfusion progression model Each scan's timepoint was recoded as the number of months post the first scan and categorized into yearly intervals (±3 months). LMMs were performed to examine the effect of timepoint on cerebral perfusion metrics. Dependent variables incorporated TNP and z-scores for global, network, and regional perfusion, with timepoint as the independent variable. Group differences were assessed by modeling the interaction between group and timepoint effects. Age and gender were included as covariates, and individual participants were treated as random effects to account for repeated measures over time. For MCI participants, progression models were analyzed based on diagnostic stability. Stable MCI was defined as participants who stayed in the MCI diagnostic category throughout follow-up, while progressive MCI was defined as participants who converted to AD during the study period. Additionally, progression models were 34 examined for the MCI-A and MCI-N subtypes to identify differences in longitudinal perfusion trajectories. name of paper: An affordable, wearable, fiber-free pulsed-mode diffuse speckle contrast flowmetry (PM-DSCF) sensor for noninvasive measurements of deep cerebral blood flow
author: gpt-4o
summary: Significance: Measuring cerebral blood flow (CBF) is crucial for diagnosing various cerebral diseases. An affordable, wearable, and fiber-free continuous-wave speckle contrast flowmetry (CW-DSCF) technique has been developed for continuous monitoring of CBF variations. However, its application in adult humans is limited by shallow tissue penetration. Aim: To develop an innovative pulse-mode DSCF (PM-DSCF) system for continuous monitoring of CBF variations in adult humans. Approach: The PM-DSCF utilizes an 808 nm laser diode and a small NanEye camera to capture diffuse laser speckle fluctuations caused by red blood cell movement in the brain (i.e., CBF). Operating in short-pulse mode (duty cycle < 5%), the system maximizes peak pulse light power for deeper tissue penetration, while ensuring that the average power density remains within ANSI safety standards for skin exposure. The PM-DSCF was evaluated on tissue-simulating phantoms and in adult humans. Results: The maximum effective source-detector distance increased from 15 mm (CW-DSCF) to 35 mm (PM-DSCF). The PM-DSCF successfully detected CBF variations in adult brains during head-up-tilting experiments, consistent with physiological expectations. Conclusions: Switching from CW mode to PM mode significantly increases the maximum tissue penetration depth from ~7.5 mm (CW-DSCF) to ~17.5 mm (PM-DSCF), enabling successful CBF measurements in adult humans.
