contents: ### 1 Introduction Continuous and thorough monitoring of deep tissue hemodynamics is essential for the diagnostic and therapeutic evaluation of various ailments that manifest within large or deep tissue volumes, such as tumors, burns or wounds, and brain injuries. A prime example of such a volume is the human brain, positioned beneath layers of scalp and skull. In adults, the average thickness of these layers ranges from 10 to 15 millimeters. For an accurate assessment of cerebral blood flow (CBF) beneath these layers, a minimum penetration depth of 10 millimeters from the head's surface is required.   By integrating CBF measurements with wearable technology, it becomes possible to continually and longitudinally monitor deep brain hemodynamics in conscious individuals who are free to move, thus shedding light on cognitive processes and adaptive behaviors. Various near-infrared (NIR) diffuse optical methodologies have been developed for assessing CBF in the human brain. A notable approach among these is diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS), which employs point, continuous-wave (CW), coherent NIR light, and single-photon-counting avalanche photodiodes (APDs) to observe temporal fluctuations of diffuse laser speckles caused by red blood cell movements in the brain, thus indicating CBF.   Traditional DCS systems feature source-detector (S-D) distances that can extend up to approximately 25 millimeters, achieving a penetration depth of around 12.5 millimeters, which is half the S-D distance. This depth facilitates CBF measurements in the cerebral cortex, though it is subject to significant partial volume effects from the overlying scalp and skull tissues. Recent improvements in DCS performance include longer wavelength illumination, interferometric detection, and time-resolved methods, which have extended tissue penetration depths and increased sampling rates.   Despite these advances, most DCS systems are equipped with bulky and costly discrete long-coherence lasers and APDs, which are typically connected to fiber-optic probes to detect variations in CBF, resulting in large and expensive devices that can cost over $50,000 for a 16-channel unit. Additionally, the rigid fiber bundles used in DCS probes are prone to motion artifacts and restrict the subject's movement. Recent innovations focus on using point, coherent NIR illumination for deep tissue penetration in combination with cost-effective CCD/CMOS cameras to detect spatial fluctuations of diffuse laser speckles for CBF measurement. Techniques such as diffuse speckle contrast analysis (DSCA), speckle contrast optical spectroscopy (SCOS), and our own diffuse speckle contrast flowmetry (DSCF) have replaced expensive discrete APDs with 2D cameras, enhancing sampling density and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) through spatial averaging across numerous pixels, while simultaneously reducing device costs.  More recently, pulsing techniques have been explored to increase tissue penetration depths. However, many systems continue to depend on fiber optics to connect lasers and/or cameras to probes, making them vulnerable to motion artifacts and limiting subject mobility. The fiber coupling also requires additional optical components, which adds complexity, increases the cost and size, and leads to light loss and possible nonuniform detection.   To overcome these issues, we have developed a novel, low-cost, and fiber-free DSCF system, protected by U.S. Patent #10/842,422, 2020 (priority July 21, 2017), featuring a variety of wearable probe sizes that enable continuous and longitudinal monitoring of CBF variations in animals and human neonates. The continuous-wave (CW) DSCF system integrates affordably priced, compact laser diodes as focused point sources for deep tissue penetration, alongside low-cost, small, compact CMOS cameras as 2D detector arrays for CBF detection.   A defining feature of the CW-DSCF is its fiber-free design, with wearable probes containing the laser diodes and compact cameras connected to a portable electronic device via four flexible electrical wires, allowing for uninterrupted monitoring in subjects without fiber motion artifacts. The utilization of inexpensive, rapid, and compact 2D cameras for detection enhances the sampling rate and SNR through spatial sampling, expands head coverage, and reduces both the device's overall size and cost. Additionally, a dual-wavelength continuous-wave diffuse speckle contrast flow-oximetry (CW-DSCFO) system employing time-multiplexed laser-diode illumination was developed for simultaneous CBF and cerebral oxygenation measurements.   The CW-DSCF and CW-DSCFO systems have been validated against traditional near-infrared spectroscopy and DCS on tissue-simulating phantoms, freely behaving rodents, neonatal piglets, and human premature infants. Nonetheless, they lack the capability to frequently detect deep tissue hemodynamics within adult human brains due to their limited penetration depth of approximately 7.5 millimeters. Consequently, the focus of this study is to develop and validate an accessible, wearable, and fiber-free pulse-mode DSCF (PM-DSCF) system designed for deeper tissue penetrations to enable continuous monitoring of CBF variations in human adults.   Briefly, the laser diode in the PM-DSCF operates in short pulse mode (with a duty cycle of less than 5%) instead of the CW mode previously utilized. This adjustment maximizes the peak pulse power for deep tissue penetration and high SNR while managing the average power density to avoid thermal damage to the skin. The PM-DSCF system was carefully optimized and characterized using tissue-simulating phantoms with known optical properties, and its performance was compared with our existing CW-DSCF system. The maximum effective S-D distance for valid signals notably increased from 15 millimeters (CW-DSCF) to 35 millimeters (PM-DSCF). Consequently, the tissue penetration depth rose from about 7.5 millimeters to 17.5 millimeters, making CBF measurements in adult humans feasible.  The optimized PM-DSCF system was then employed alongside a conventional DCS system to observe CBF variations concurrently and continuously in five healthy adult volunteers during head-up-tilting (HUT) experiments at a 70-degree angle. Impressively, both the PM-DSCF, with an S-D distance of 35 millimeters, and the DCS, with an S-D distance of 25 millimeters, detected similar CBF changes in the adult brain during these experiments.   ### 2 Materials and Methods    ### 2.1 PM-DSCF System    ### 2.1.1 PM-DSCF Device Figure 1 illustrates the cost-effective and wearable, fiber-free PM-DSCF system, which has been designed using the principles from our published CW-DSCF30. The PM-DSCF system features a wearable probe composed of a compact laser diode that acts as a point source, alongside a minuscule NanEye 2D camera serving as the 2D detection array (see Fig. 1a). Integral to the setup is a small collimator (A230TM-B), which has an effective focal length of 4.51 mm, a numerical aperture of 0.55, an outer diameter of 9.24 mm, and a working distance of 2.53 mm. It possesses an anti-reflection coating effective between 650 and 1050 nm, manufactured by Thorlabs, and is positioned in front of the laser diode (L808P1000MM, with a diameter of 9 mm, 1 W, 808 nm, from Thorlabs) to project a collimated light spot (4.45 mm in diameter) onto the target tissue surface. To guarantee skin safety, a diffuser is situated between the collimator and the scalp.   Figure 1 presents: an affordable, wearable, fiber-free PM-DSCF system that facilitates measurements of deep tissue blood flow. (a) A PM-DSCF headband is placed on a participant's forehead. The PM-DSCF device integrates several components: a user interface ①, an Arduino controller ②, a custom laser diode driver ③, a laser diode ④, a camera board (NanEye USB 2.2, Awaiba) ⑤, and a NanEye camera ⑥. (b) It includes a schematic diagram detailing the PM-DSCF device structure. (c) There is synchronization seen between the pulsed laser and the NanEye 2D camera within the PM-DSCF.  A very small CMOS camera (NanEye 2D Black and White, Awaiba; measuring 1 × 1 mm², with a resolution of 250 × 250 pixels, and pixel size of 3 × 3 µm², 10-bit depth, electronic amplification gain of 2, and consuming power at 4 mW) was employed to detect diffuse speckle contrasts. The drive of the NanEye camera includes an auto-scaling feature for transforming the 10-bit data captured by the camera to 16-bit through interpolation. Although this does not expand the dynamic range of detection, it does improve precision by making use of the 16-bit format. A tiny lens, with an effective focal length of 0.66 mm, has been incorporated into the camera, facilitating a suitable field of view (FOV) of 4 × 4 mm² at a working distance of 3.5 mm. Both the laser diode probe and the NanEye 2D camera are encased in a malleable foam pad and affixed to a subject's forehead using a wearable headband. The built-in dials on the headband can be adjusted to firmly secure these source and detector components onto the participant's forehead. The distance between the laser diode and the camera sensor, referred to as the S-D distance, can be modified to vary the depth of tissue penetration.   The laser diode and the camera are linked to a portable DSCF device through flexible electrical wires, ensuring a fiber-free connection. As previously documented in references 6, 26, 30, 31, 34, and 38, the operation of DSCF is managed via a custom graphical user interface (GUI) coded in C# and a LabVIEW™ (National Instruments) control panel set up on a computer (as seen in Fig. 1a). The C# GUI is the primary interface, managing camera exposure and displaying real-time outcomes (depicted in Fig. 1b). A LINX module together with application logic in LabVIEW™ enables communication between the computer and an Arduino board, which is responsible for controlling the laser diode driver (LDC240C, with ±4 A, from Thorlabs). This setup generates pulsed light at a predetermined intensity and pulse width. Synchronization between the camera and the laser control module is accomplished through TCP/IP communication linking C# and LabVIEW™ by leveraging the computer’s loopback address (refer to Fig. 1b). An optimal delay, determined through experimental processes, is established between C# and LabVIEW™ controls to perfectly sync the camera exposure with the laser pulses. Additionally, any conspicuous noise caused by misalignment is excluded from subsequent data analyses. For experiments involving varying camera exposure times, the laser’s pulse width is adjusted accordingly to ensure full overlap, effectively minimizing any potential light wastage (as per Fig. 1c).   ### 2.1.2 Pulse-mode Strategy The primary aim of this research is to enhance the penetration depth of DSCF in tissues so that continuous monitoring of cerebral blood flow (CBF) variations in adult humans can be achieved. By increasing the source-detector (S-D) distance, deeper tissue penetration is possible; however, this also leads to a decreased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) due to heightened light attenuation, as noted in prior studies30, 34. SNR is defined as the ratio between the detected light intensity and the dark noise. To bolster the measurement SNR, one might consider either elevating the intensity of the laser light or extending the camera's exposure duration. However, using a laser at high intensity risks causing thermal damage to the skin. On the other hand, lengthening the exposure times could weaken the laser speckle contrast, thereby diminishing the measurement's sensitivity in capturing rapid changes in CBF39, 40. Measurement sensitivity is the capability of the DSCF device to identify minor changes in CBF. In our study, we incorporated a pulse-mode strategy within the DSCF system, which employed high-intensity illumination for brief pulse durations while ensuring that the average power density remained below the levels prescribed by the ANSI standard (ANSI Z136.1). According to this standard, for an 808 nm wavelength, the power density on the tissue surface should not exceed 0.32 W/cm². Thus, the laser diode within the PM-DSCF was operated in a short pulse mode, featuring a duty cycle of less than 5% and maintaining an average power density of less than or equal to 0.28 W/cm². Additionally, the instantaneous peak power was kept constant during varied exposure time experiments. Although the NanEye camera is capable of a maximum sampling rate of 50 Hz, the sampling rate for PM-DSCF was adjusted to 1.65 Hz. This adjustment ensured that adequate SNRs30, 34 were achieved while preserving laser safety with pulse illumination.   ### 2.1.3 Data Processing In our continuous wave diffusing speckle contrast flowmetry (CW-DSCF) approach, we quantified laser speckle contrast within the spatial domain, denoted as 𝐾𝑠, by analyzing a pixel window measuring 7 × 7 pixels6, 26, 30, 31, 34. The calculation of 𝐾𝑠 was accomplished by taking the ratio of the standard deviation (𝜎) to the mean value (𝜇) across the light intensities (𝐼) of a total of 49 pixels, formalized as 𝐾𝑠 = 𝜎(𝐼) ⁄ 𝜇(𝐼). This calculation involved employing a sliding window over selected pixels within the predefined region-of-interest (ROI) to create a two-dimensional map of 𝐾𝑠. Subsequently, these 𝐾𝑠 values were averaged, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We then defined a blood flow index (𝐵𝐹𝐼) according to the formula (1 ⁄ 𝐾𝑠^2)41, 42. The computation of relative changes in 𝐵𝐹𝐼, referred to as 𝑟𝐵𝐹𝐼 or rCBF, hinged on normalizing the 𝐵𝐹𝐼 values against their baseline prior to any physiological changes. Upon examining the raw intensity images gathered, we selected a region-of-interest consisting of 6,400 pixels (80 × 80) positioned centrally on the NanEye camera sensor, which comprises 250 × 250 pixels, for the purpose of PM-DSCF data analysis, thus eliminating potential shadowing artifacts created by the probe wall within the camera’s field of view (FOV). In previous research, a single-window method has been employed to ascertain a single 9 𝐾𝑠 value, leveraging a range of larger pixel window sizes, including 5,00027, 2,50043, 2,40144, 1,00045, and 44146 pixels. Our comparative results from human studies (data not presented here) revealed that the single-window approach exhibited a more pronounced rCBF response to head-up tilt (HUT) than the sliding-window averaging method. Moreover, rCBF responses measured utilizing the single-window approach were found to be consistent with diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS) measurements. Therefore, in this study, we adopted a single window encompassing 6,400 pixels for the calculation of 𝐾𝑠.   ### 2.2 Measurement Protocols on Tissue-simulating Phantoms Figure 2a illustrates the experimental arrangement designed to assess the performance of PM-DSCF on liquid phantoms that simulate tissue. This approach, utilizing phantoms with established optical properties, is a well-regarded method for calibrating and validating NIR instruments, as highlighted in references 41 and 42. The liquid phantom was prepared using Intralipid particles (Fresenius Kabi, Sweden), India ink, and water. The concentration of India ink in the phantoms was used to control the absorption coefficient, denoted as μa, while the concentration of Intralipid served to adjust the reduced scattering coefficient, μs ′. Furthermore, the Intralipid particles within the liquid phantom provide Brownian motion, which mimics the movement of red blood cells in the brain, as noted in references 47 and 48. For this investigation, the optical properties of the liquid phantom were configured with μa = 0.03 cm−1 and μs ′ = 9 cm−1. It is important to note that the absorption coefficient μa is lower in the phantom compared to typical values for real tissue, and this will be optimized in future work to enhance both accuracy and relevance. To ensure a fair comparison, the average power density of the laser illumination on the phantom was maintained at approximately 0.28 Watt/cm² for both CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements. Additionally, ambient lighting was minimized in the room during the experiments to reduce its impact. The CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF readings were taken independently under each condition for a duration of 15 seconds at a sampling rate of 1.65 Hz, with the mean value over this period being reported. The initial experiment was performed on the tissue-simulating phantom at an ambient temperature of 23 ℃, corresponding to a constant BFI, to compare the sensitivities, SNRs, and levels of dark noise between CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements, as varied by S-D distances and camera exposure times. The S-D distance ranged from 10 mm to 40 mm in increments of 5 mm by adjusting the camera location. Meanwhile, the camera exposure time was adjusted from 1 ms to 15 ms in increments of 5 ms. The subsequent experiment used the same tissue-simulating phantom but with variable temperatures to assess how effectively CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF could detect dynamic changes in the flow of Intralipid particles. As indicated in references 47 and 48, the Brownian motion of these particles increases with rising phantom temperatures. A heating plate (PC-620D, Corning) situated beneath the liquid tank was employed to alter the liquid temperature from 10 ℃ to 40 ℃ in 5 ℃ increments. A thermometer sensor from Physitemp was placed inside the liquid phantom to continuously monitor changes in temperature. To compare measurement sensitivities under various conditions, the S-D distance was set between 30 mm and 40 mm, increasing by 5 mm intervals, while camera exposure times spanned from 1 ms to 15 ms in 5 ms intervals. Figure 2 provides a visual of the experimental setup for evaluating how PM-DSCF performs in both tissue-simulating phantoms and human adults. In part (a), a PM-DSCF probe is positioned on the surface of an Intralipid liquid phantom, whose optical properties are well-known, to test and compare measurement sensitivities and SNRs in detecting the flow of Intralipid particles. Additionally, the liquid temperature, which affects Intralipid particle flow, is adjusted using the heating plate underneath the liquid tank. Part (b), at the top, shows a hybrid probe placed on a subject's forehead for simultaneous PM-DSCF and DCS measurements of changes in cerebral blood flow (CBF) in human adults. At the bottom, it is shown that CBF is continuously monitored by PM-DSCF and DCS devices during a 70° HUT experiment.   ### 2.3 Measurement Protocols in Human Adults In an investigation involving six healthy adult participants (comprising two males and four females, with an average age of 30.33 ± 2.88 years), simultaneous PM-DSCF and DCS measurements were carried out. These measurements aimed to evaluate the potential of wearable PM-DSCF technology in determining changes in deep cerebral blood flow (CBF) during 70° head-up tilt (HUT) experiments (as shown in Fig. 2b). The University of Kentucky Institutional Review Board granted approval for the study protocol (IRB #44104). Throughout the experiments, the room temperature was controlled at 23 ℃, and the lighting was dimmed to create a conducive environment. Participants were instructed to lie supine on a tilting table manufactured by Hausmann Inc., USA. A headband embedded with PM-DSCF and DCS probes was then positioned on each subject's forehead to measure CBF in the right and left hemispheres, respectively. The study primarily focused on examining the use of extended source-detector (S-D) distances in PM-DSCF to examine deeper CBF in the adult brain. Following methodologies from previous research49, we ensured that the headband was tightly secured (as illustrated in Fig. 1a and Fig. 2b) to facilitate optimal light coupling between the DSCF probe and the head by displacing blood from the scalp away from the probe area. This technique effectively reduces the influence of scalp blood flow on the obtained measurements. The DCS measurements utilized a customized setup, incorporating a coherent 785 nm laser source (DL785-100, CrystaLaser) connected to a multi-mode fiber (with a diameter of 200 μm) and an avalanche photodiode module (SPCM-AQ4C, PerkinElmer) linked to a single-mode detector fiber (5 μm in diameter). Autocorrelation functions were computed from the APD output using an autocorrelation board (available at www.correlator.com) for BFI reconstruction. Additional details on DCS instrumentation and data analysis are available in previous publications14, 15, 22, 24, 25. Initially, a case study was conducted with one participant (Subject #4) to evaluate the devices' performance, using a camera exposure time of 10 ms for PM-DSCF and varied S-D distances of 12, 25, 30, and 35 mm for both DCS and PM-DSCF. Results from this case study led to the decision to use a camera exposure time of 10 ms with a 35 mm S-D distance for PM-DSCF when assessing CBF variations during the HUT in all six participants. Nevertheless, the DCS S-D distance was maintained at 25 mm due to poor signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) with longer distances. During the HUT, CBF was monitored continuously with PM-DSCF at a sampling rate of 1.65 Hz and DCS at 1 Hz over a 15-minute span, encompassing three phases: a 5-minute baseline at 0°, a 5-minute tilt at 70°, and a 5-minute recovery at 0°. DCS data was interpolated to 1.65 Hz using MATLAB's 1D-data interpolation function (Interp1) to ensure alignment with PM-DSCF data for comparative purposes. Regression correlation analyses were conducted to determine the correlations between measurements from PM-DSCF and DCS.   ### 3 Results    ### 3.1 PM-DSCF Demonstrates Better Performance than CW-DSCF on Tissue-simulating Phantoms The laser diode's steadiness was evaluated by consistently keeping track of the intensity detected by the camera (in digital counts) and the calculated relative Blood Flow Index (rBFI) values in Intralipid liquid phantoms, all under conditions where room temperature was kept stable for a period of ten minutes. The results from three separate trials demonstrated coefficients of variation of no more than 2.3% and no more than 10.2% for the camera intensity, and no more than 0.6% and no more than 7.6% for the calculated rBFI at 5% and 10% duty cycles, respectively. These outcomes verify that employing shorter duty cycles yields more consistently stable outputs. Furthermore, the laser diode is noted to need a warm-up time of around five minutes before any experimentation to achieve a steady power output. In Figure 3, a comparison of Continuous Wave Diffuse Speckle Contrast Flowmetry (CW-DSCF) and Pulsed Mode Diffuse Speckle Contrast Flowmetry (PM-DSCF) measurements in phantoms that simulate tissue is depicted under controlled room temperature conditions, highlighting the sensitivities and signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) as they vary with source-detector (S-D) distance and camera exposure duration. As anticipated, the digital counts measured with the laser switched on were notably higher than the dark counts logged when the laser was turned off (refer to Fig. 3a and Fig. 3b). A detailed look into the dark noise region shows a linear relationship between dark counts and exposure time (though this data is not shown). There was a reduction in detected light intensities as the S-D distance increased and the camera exposure time decreased for both CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF evaluations. In comparing CW-DSCF (Fig. 3a) with PM-DSCF (Fig. 3b), the intensity decay graphs noticeably shifted from the left (indicating shorter S-D distances) to the right (indicating longer S-D distances), which suggests enhanced penetration depth into the tissue. As illustrated in Fig. 3c, SNRs diminished as the S-D distance increased and the camera exposure time decreased for both CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements. The effective S-D ranges providing SNRs of at least 6 dB and intensities below the camera's saturation point (where the digital count is under 60,000) were found to be 15–25 mm (with camera exposure times of at least 5 ms) for CW-DSCF measurements, and 20–35 mm (with camera exposure times of 5 ms and 10 ms) for PM-DSCF measurements. Fig. 3 showcases the sensitivity and SNR comparison for CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements on phantoms that simulate tissue, with varied S-D distances and camera exposure times: (a) displays the average light intensity in digital counts and dark-noise counts as detected by the CW-DSCF, (b) shows the same metrics for the PM-DSCF, and (c) illustrates a comparison of SNRs achieved by the CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF. The two dashed lines demarcate the valid SNR range (6–12 dB), confirming that the detected intensities stayed well above noise levels (i.e., dark counts) and below the saturation threshold of the camera (digital count < 60,000).   ### 3.2 PM-DSCF Captures Dynamic Flow Changes with Large Penetration Depths on Tissue Simulating Phantoms Figure 4 presents a comparison of the outcomes from CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements, which assess dynamic flow alterations in tissue-simulating phantoms caused by adjustments in the phantom temperature. The top section of Figure 4 (Figs. 4a-4c) highlights that CW-DSCF, when using source-detector (S-D) distances of 30 mm or greater, falls short in sensitivity for detecting changes in blood flow index (BFI). Notably, sensitivity was achieved with S-D distances of 15 mm or less, data not presented here, which corroborates our previously published findings30, 34. The source-detector (S-D) distances utilized were 25, 30, and 35 mm, respectively. The PM-DSCF measurements were conducted with a camera exposure time of 10 ms. To ensure accuracy between each set of measurements, the subject was given ample rest exceeding one hour. As the S-D distances increased, PM-DSCF identified higher cerebral blood flow (CBF) responses to the HUT. Furthermore, PM-DSCF recordings showed more consistent right-sided rCBF responses to the tilt, with lower noise levels, in contrast to the DCS measurements observed in the left hemisphere. Interestingly, with a shorter S-D distance of 25 mm, DCS mirrored the rCBF changes captured by PM-DSCF under the same conditions (refer to Fig. 5a). Yet, when employing longer S-D distances of 30 mm and 35 mm, the DCS measurements showed a marked decline in detection sensitivity coupled with heightened noise levels (illustrated in Fig. 5b and Fig. 5c). Figure 6, on the other hand, delves into the group average results of rCBF changes during the 70° HUT gathered from a cohort of six subjects. In these measurements, the PM-DSCF assessed right-rCBF with an S-D distance of 35 mm, while the DCS evaluated left-rCBF using an S-D distance of 25 mm. It was observed that PM-DSCF measurements consistently displayed a greater rCBF response to the tilt when compared to DCS readings (see Fig. 6a).   An analysis based on mean percent differences from baseline (set as 100%) during both the HUT and recovery phases, drawn from PM-DSCF data, showed mean values ± standard errors of 45.23 ± 9.17% and 20.99 ± 35.20%, respectively. Correspondingly, data from DCS indicated values of 44.13 ± 15.14% and 0.59 ± 23.86%, respectively. A notable observation was the strong linear regression correlation between the two measurement techniques, with an R² value of 0.75 and a p-value of less than 10⁻⁵ (as displayed in Fig. 6b). The regression slope, calculated as 1.25, suggests that PM-DSCF demonstrates a higher sensitivity in comparison to DCS measurements.  During the recovery stage of the HUT test, an overshoot in CBF was observed, reminiscent of post-occlusive reactive hyperemia—a phenomenon characterized by ischemia of tissues followed by reperfusion. This increase in blood flow during recovery aids in reinstating typical perfusion to the brain regions that faced diminished flow during the head-up tilt. The process is mainly facilitated by a brief decrease in sympathetic tone and the activation of local vasodilatory processes, culminating in a transient overshoot in CBF. Previous research using DCS had also recorded this CBF overshoot. Notably, the hyperemic responses identified by DCS were less pronounced than those detected by PM-DSCF (refer to Fig. 6a). This discrepancy primarily arises due to the lower sensitivity of DCS in reaching deeper brain regions, particularly when a headband tightens and displaces scalp blood away from the probe. Portable near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) devices have been developed to continuously track variations in CBF deep within the brain7-13, 15, 26, 28, 29, 32, 37, 38, 50, 51. However, the majority of these systems make use of rigid fiber-optic probes for light delivery and detection, which significantly restricts the movement of subjects7-15, 22, 28, 29, 32, 37, 38, 45, 50, 51. With the support of the National Institute of Health, we have engineered an innovative wearable, fiber-free CW-DSCF probe available in multiple sizes to continuously monitor CBF variations in conscious animals as well as human neonates6, 26, 30, 31, 34, 38. Notably, we have published findings from a comparative study involving simultaneous DCS and CW-DSCF measurements in neonatal piglets, which revealed that motion artifacts were distinctly present only in the DCS measurements26. Despite this advancement, significant challenges with the CW-DSCF persist, including low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) and limited penetration depths in tissues (up to roughly 7.5 mm). This paper introduces an affordable and wearable, fiber-free PM-DSCF with enhanced SNR and tissue penetration depth for CBF measurement in adult humans (Fig. 1). The PM-DSCF is similar in many ways to the CW-DSCF, featuring a wearable, fiber-free sensor and a cost-effective portable device. Unlike the CW-DSCF, however, the PM-DSCF operates in a short pulse mode (duty cycle < 5%), optimizing peak pulse light power while maintaining average power density within the safety standards of the ANSI Z136.1 for skin protection. Consequently, PM-DSCF facilitates measurements at greater source-detector (S-D) distances with adequate SNR, allowing for the detection of CBF variations in adult humans who have thicker scalp and skull layers. We executed a thorough comparison of CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements using tissue-simulating phantoms (see Fig. 3, Fig. 4, and Table 1). The first experiment 19 was performed using an Intralipid phantom solution with a constant blood flow index (BFI) to compare the sensitivity, SNR, and dark noise levels between CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF measurements across varied S-D distances and camera exposure times (Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 3a, the findings are in line with our previous reports, indicating that CW-DSCF achieves a maximum penetration depth of approximately 7.5 mm at an S-D distance of 15 mm28,30,31. In contrast, the Fig. 3b results show that, with optimized exposure times, PM-DSCF attains a maximum penetration depth of approximately 17.5 mm at an S-D distance of 35 mm. The second experiment involved altering the temperature of the same phantom to assess CW-DSCF and PM-DSCF's capability in discerning dynamic changes in the flow of Intralipid particles. The outcomes depicted in Fig. 4a-4c illustrate that CW-DSCF with significant S-D distances of 30-40 mm cannot detect shifts in BFI. However, Fig. 4d-4f shows that PM-DSCF with optimized exposure and large S-D distances of 30-40 mm can successfully detect dynamic BFI changes that correspond to temperature variations within the phantom. Notably, PM-DSCF readings with optimized exposure at S-D distances of 30 mm and 35 mm were found to be remarkably consistent (Fig. 4d and Fig. 4e). These results showcase the sensitivity of the PM-DSCF in detecting dynamic flow changes in deep tissue layers (up to ~17.5 mm). We then carried out concurrent PM-DSCF and DCS measurements on six healthy adult subjects to evaluate and compare the PM-DSCF's ability to measure deep CBF variations during 70° head-up tilt (HUT) experiments (Fig. 2b). PM-DSCF readings at S-D distances of 25-35 mm demonstrated more consistent relative CBF responses to HUT with less noise compared to DCS readings at a 25 mm S-D distance (Fig. 5a and Fig. 6a). Conversely, DCS readings at larger S-D distances (30 mm and 35 mm) displayed noticeably reduced detection sensitivities with increased noise (Fig. 5a and Fig. 5c). These observations suggest that PM-DSCF offers superior sensitivity and SNR over DCS. Furthermore, no temperature changes were observed on the scalp during the HUT experiment, and no complaints were expressed by the participants, indicating that both PM-DSCF and DCS measurements are safe and comfortable. Nonetheless, some challenges and limitations of the current study have been identified. The statistics of speckle patterns depend largely on the spatial and temporal coherence of the light source, as well as the surface or medium roughness. A highly coherent laser source (such as a monochromatic laser) tends to produce speckle patterns with high contrast that are largely independent of surface properties. These are often referred to as normal speckle patterns. However, multimode lasers with partial coherence, such as those employed in our study, can also produce speckle patterns, albeit with reduced contrast and greater dependence on the specific structure of the surface or tissue31, 52. Pulse broadening often occurs in time-domain systems during propagation through a diffusive medium, affecting speckle contrast when the coherence length of light is insufficient. In our PM-DSCF approach, pulse durations range from 1 to 15 milliseconds, corresponding to the camera exposure times (1-15 ms). These durations are considerably longer than those typically utilized in time-domain systems, which usually range from picoseconds to nanoseconds. Similar millisecond-level pulse durations have been adopted in NIRS systems, including continuous wave49, 53-55, and frequency-domain56-58 strategies, to facilitate rapid sampling across multiple S-D channels. Recent developments in DCS technology, which employ shorter light exposure durations of 10-100 ms, have enabled rapid measures of pulsatile CBF related to the cardiac cycle, though this has often come at the cost of lowering the SNR59-64. In a separate study, we investigated the impact of laser coherence lengths on CBF measurements using diffuse optical techniques65. In contrast to DCS, DSCF does not necessitate a laser with a particularly long coherence length. Overall, the effects of pulse broadening and the shortening of coherence length are not significant concerns for our PM-DSCF approach utilizing pulse durations at the millisecond level. Within this study, we chose a region of interest (ROI) of 6400 pixels (80 × 80 pixels) centered in the NanEye camera sensor (with a total resolution of 250 × 250 pixels) for the purpose of data analysis, aiming to enhance the SNR through spatial averaging across the ROI's pixels. The constraint of using just a portion of the total resolution can be alleviated by optimizing the design of the PM-DSCF probe in order to minimize shadowing artifacts caused by the probe walls. Additionally, the SNR can be further enhanced by utilizing compact cameras with a higher pixel count, as improvements from spatial averaging scale with the square root of the total number of averaged pixels. As recent studies have underscored32, 66, low photon flux levels near the noise threshold are a frequent occurrence in human CBF measurements. Under these conditions, camera noise and imperfections can significantly impact fiber-based SCOS measurements. The authors of that research systematically assessed various noise sources, including shot noise, read noise, and spatial inhomogeneity noise, and effectively mitigated these elements to facilitate accurate BFI calculation. However, this study utilized the traditional method for analyzing speckle contrasts (Section 2.1.3). Subsequent studies will address this limitation by identifying specific noise sources pertinent to the NanEye camera and, if deemed necessary, implementing noise reduction strategies to further refine the accuracy of CBF measurements. In summation, the findings from the tissue-simulating phantoms and human adult heads (Fig. 3-6 and Table 1) indicate that transitioning from CW mode to PM mode with optimized exposure time notably increases the maximum effective S-D distances from 15 mm to 35 mm. As a result, the maximum penetration depth of PM-DSCF approaches roughly 17.5 mm (half of 35 mm). This substantial improvement in tissue penetration depth greatly aids in CBF measurements in adult humans. Future research will focus on refining the system to develop and commercialize a cost-effective, user-friendly, wireless, wearable, and fiber-free PM-DSCF setup for continuous monitoring and instant reporting of cerebral hemodynamic variations in both comatose and conscious individuals. The ultimate aim is real-time diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring of various cerebral vascular conditions and neurological disorders. summary: We introduce a simple framework for predicting the behavior of an agent in multi-agent settings. In contrast to autoregressive (AR) tasks, such as language processing, our focus is on scenarios with multiple agents whose interactions are shaped by physical constraints and internal motivations. To this end, we propose Poly-Autoregressive (PAR) modeling, which forecasts an ego agent's future behavior by reasoning about the ego agent's state history and the past and current states of other interacting agents. At its core, PAR represents the behavior of all agents as a sequence of tokens, each representing an agent's state at a specific timestep. With minimal data pre-processing changes, we show that PAR can be applied to three different problems: human action forecasting in social situations, trajectory prediction for autonomous vehicles, and object pose forecasting during hand-object interaction. Using a small proof-of-concept transformer backbone, PAR outperforms AR across these three scenarios. The project website can be found at this https URL.

contents: ### Abstract We introduce a straightforward framework aimed at predicting the behaviors of agents operating in multi-agent environments. Unlike autoregressive (AR) models commonly used in language processing, our focus lies in multi-agent scenarios where interactions are influenced by physical constraints and internal motivations of the agents involved. To address this, we have developed a method known as Poly-Autoregressive (PAR) modeling. PAR is designed to predict the future behavior of an ego agent by analyzing the agent's historical state information as well as the past and current states of other agents in the environment. Central to PAR is the representation of all agents' behaviors through a sequence of tokens, with each token indicating the state of an agent at a specific point in time. With only minimal changes to data preprocessing, our approach has proven applicable to three distinct problems: forecasting human actions in social contexts, predicting the trajectories of autonomous vehicles, and forecasting the poses of objects during interactions involving hands and objects. Leveraging a concise proof-of-concept transformer architecture, PAR demonstrates superior performance when compared to AR models across these varied scenarios.   ### 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant success in tackling natural language processing (NLP) tasks that require intricate reasoning to understand the relationships between words within a text. At the heart of LLMs is autoregressive (AR) modeling, which involves predicting each word token by considering the sequence of preceding word tokens. Drawing inspiration from AR modeling's success in the NLP community, this research pivots towards exploring the dynamic relationships among agents and entities in everyday interactions that occur within the physical world. Such interactions include social exchanges, driving, and hand-object interactions. In contrast to language that is governed by grammar and semantics, interactions in the physical realm are largely dictated by the laws of physics—such as how a hand grips an object—and the internal state of each agent, exemplified by the path an agent selects to move an object it holds, a latent variable shrouded in mystery. Furthermore, unlike text where words follow one after another in a straightforward linear sequence, the states of multiple agents evolve simultaneously. For instance, in social settings, the historical states of a single person aren't enough to predict their future states in isolation; one must also consider the states of those around them. Hence, we assert that AR modeling alone falls short. In this paper, we present poly-autoregressive (PAR) modeling, a seamless and unifying approach for capturing the influence exerted by other agents and entities on individual behavior. We conceptualize behavior as a chronological sequence of states, aiming to predict an ego agent's future actions based on its past behavior, along with the historical behavior of other agents. By integrating the behaviors of additional agents, our approach significantly enhances the solution to the seemingly impossible problem laid out in single-agent prediction scenarios within interactive environments. The PAR framework leverages a transformer-based model for next-token prediction. Known for their impressive efficacy in language modeling, transformers are naturally suited for forecasting behavior over time. In a setting involving N agents, our model anticipates the future actions of an ego (Nth) agent based on both its past behaviors and those of the other N-1 non-ego agents (refer to Figure 1b). Each prediction task can focus on different behavior modalities, such as action prediction in social contexts or forecasting 6DoF poses in hand-object interactions. We apply PAR to three distinct real-world interaction scenarios: 1. Social action prediction. We evaluate our method using the AVA benchmark [19] for action forecasting. By factoring in both the ego agent and another agent using PAR, we achieve a total gain of +1.9 absolute mAP over AR, which only models the ego agent for predicting its future actions, and an absolute gain of +3.5 mAP on 2-person interaction classes. 2. Trajectory prediction for autonomous vehicles. For forecasting future xy coordinates of an ego vehicle, incorporating the positional data of neighboring vehicles through PAR surpasses AR, which merely utilizes the ego vehicle's previous trajectory. On the nuScenes dataset [5], PAR achieves 6.3% and 6.4% relative improvements in ADE and FDE, respectively. 3. 6DoF object pose forecasting during hand-object interaction. Utilizing the DexYCB dataset [8], we treat the object as the ego agent while the hand serves as the interacting agent. Whereas PAR incorporates the hand’s 3D location alongside the historical object pose, AR relies solely on the object's prior pose to predict its 6DoF position. PAR achieves relative improvements of 8.9% and 41.0% for rotation and translation predictions, respectively. Across all these scenarios, including the behavior of other agents within the scene results in better predictions of the ego agent’s behavior. All these challenges are addressed through the same PAR framework, implemented using a 4-million-parameter transformer, without altering the core framework or architecture, only adjusting data preprocessing and tokenization strategies. We offer an example of an additional application of our architecture with a location positional encoding, as detailed in Sec. 5. Our primary contribution is a highly adaptable framework, applicable across a wide variety of contexts with only modifications for domain-specific data processing. Our findings indicate that PAR can offer a straightforward formulation, capable of advancing multi-agent interaction prediction using a more sophisticated transformer backbone and larger datasets. To spur further investigation and innovation, we have made our code publicly available, providing the essential components needed to apply PAR to other types of multi-agent interactions.   ### 2. Related Work Autoregressive models have a longstanding and profound influence in the realms of information theory and deep learning. This influence traces back to pioneering contributions such as Shannon’s seminal paper on language prediction [45] and Attneave’s research into visual perception [2]. These early works laid a crucial foundation for contemporary applications in deep learning. For instance, [25] revisits neural autoregressive models and [18, 50] delve into modeling with continuous values. Another significant development in this field was the creation of PixelRNN and PixelCNN by [53], which use RNN and CNN architectures to autoregressively generate images pixel-by-pixel. The advent of the transformer model [54] gave a significant boost to computer vision, resulting in innovations like the image transformer [36] and the vision transformer [14]. In the domain of natural language processing, autoregressive models [9, 41] have notably advanced, particularly with the GPT family of models [4, 37, 38], showcasing the remarkable potential of large-scale unsupervised autoregressive pre-training. Further developments in research are delving into multimodal learning. Examples include the Flamingo [1] and LlaVa [28] models, which merge capabilities in both vision and language processing, underscoring the adaptability of autoregressive models across different sectors of artificial intelligence. While these methodologies involve image patches and word tokens, our work focuses on symbolic representations derived from videos capturing natural interactions. An innovative approach [39] conceptualizes humanoid locomotion as an autoregressive next-token prediction task that works with two kinds of continuous tokens: observations and actions. This methodology projects continuous tokens into a hidden dimension and applies a shifted loss, akin to the next-timestep prediction strategy outlined in our framework.   When it comes to multi-agent regressive models, there have been several earlier studies that tackled specific multi-agent challenges via regressive models as isolated case studies. However, here we introduce the PAR framework designed to bring all these efforts together into one comprehensive framework. Numerous behavior prediction research papers focus on scenarios where two agents are engaged in social interaction, such as dyadic communication [32–34] or social dancing [30, 46]. These investigations mainly address predicting the state of one interaction partner (Person B) given the input about Person A’s state, with occasional extensions into forecasting future states [20, 30]. While initial approaches employed architectures like variational RNNs [3], the latest studies have largely shifted towards leveraging transformer architectures for modeling social interactions [10, 20, 32, 33, 46]. There are also explorations into methodologies like diffusion [27], or diffusion enhanced with attention mechanisms [17]. Our PAR framework is primarily centered on transformer models. The research encompassed within the PAR framework extends beyond just human social interactions. Numerous multi-agent human or car trajectory prediction techniques employ autoregressive prediction. As an illustration, MotionLM [44] incorporates a transformer decoder to process multi-agent tokens, which includes a learned agent ID embedding. This technique is fundamental to our approach across the entirety of our case studies. Importantly, contrary to all previous multi-agent regressive projects that were tailored to specific applications, we exhibit the possibility of integrating a broad range of multi-agent regressive issues within a singular PAR framework. For details focused on specific case studies, see Appendix Section 9.   ### 3. Poly-Autoregressive Modeling Our objective is to simulate the behavior of an agent or entity while considering any interactions it may have with other agents. To assess how effectively our model captures the dynamics of these interactions, we attempt to forecast the future behavior of the agent and juxtapose this prediction with empirical ground-truth data. We outline the following task: within an interaction involving N agents, given the recorded past states of the N−1 interacting agents, as well as the observed or previously predicted past states of the Nth ego agent, our aim is to predict the forthcoming states of this Nth ego agent. We introduce a transformer-based poly-autoregressive (PAR) predictor, denoted as P, which is designed to learn and model interactions over extended periods within the input sequence. The inputs for this predictor consist of the historical states of all N interacting agents, and its output forecasts the future state of the Nth ego agent.   ### 3.1. Problem Definition Consider a temporal sequence of agent states, denoted as S = {si}T i=1. In this sequence, we use SN to signify the temporal sequence of states for the Nth agent, while S1:N−1 refers to the sequences for the other N−1 agents. At each specific time step t within the interval [tπ, T]—where tπ is the initial point from which we begin our predictions, lying between 1 and T—we take as inputs the historical state sequences of all the other N−1 agents, observed up to time t−1, written as S1:N−1 1:t−1. Additionally, we include the Nth agent’s observed states up to tπ, denoted as SN 1:tπ, as well as any previously predicted past states of the Nth agent, ˆSN tπ+1:t−1, if those are available (refer to Figure 1 for clarification).   The function of our predictor, P, is to forecast the future states of the Nth agent in a poly-autoregressive manner, by progressing one time step at a time: ˆsN t = P(S1:N−1 1:t−1, SN 1:tπ, ˆSN tπ+1:t−1). P is designed to learn how to model the distribution of the subsequent state of the Nth agent based on all other agents’ states: p(ˆsN t |S1:N−1 1:t−1, SN 1:t−1). During the inference phase, we provide the actual observed states of the other agents. However, when training, the process involves maximizing the likelihood for all N agents by evaluating losses on their future state projections. Our aim in training the predictor is to maximize the likelihood of the target state, y, at time t, expressed mathematically as LP = Ey∼p(y)[−log(p(sN t ))], with the target state y at time t extracted from the ground truth future state of the Nth agent.   ### 3.2. The Poly-Autoregressive Framework We tackle the challenge of predicting the future states of an agent from a starting time t to a future time T using a data-driven approach, based on a temporal sequence of its past states ranging from time 1 to t −1. We operate under the assumption that the agent possesses certain features or a set of features of interest that can be tokenized from a video, such as a 3D pose, for example. Our task is to forecast the agent's forthcoming states in terms of this tokenized feature set, applying one token or a set of tokens per time step. The tokens we predict may either be discrete, functioning as an index within a feature codebook, or they may be continuous, representing a vector composed of one or more continuous values. The loss ℓ we encounter depends heavily on the specific details of the problem and the type of token applied. To train our prediction model, we utilize all interaction dynamics of a specified length T found in our training dataset as the ground truth examples. As a point of comparison, we first examine the single-agent autoregressive (AR) model, where a transformer is trained to predict the next token using teacher forcing. During inference, AR employs greedy sampling to generate sequences, forecasting one subsequent token at each step (see Fig. 1(a)). On the other hand, our multi-agent poly-autoregressive (PAR) framework takes into account the presence of the other N −1 agents within the scene as it predicts the future state of the Nth agent. In this scenario, we tokenize the features of interest for all N agents, thus producing N tokens at every timestep, aggregating up to a total of N ∗T tokens. Practically, we work with a flattened sequence comprising N ∗T tokens. Rather than applying the AR training strategy in this multi-agent context, as shown in Fig. 3a, we jointly represent the states of the N agents at each timestep by incorporating the following features into our PAR approach. Regarding next-timestep prediction, while a standard AR model forecasts the next token, given the flattened sequence of N ∗T tokens we use, next-token prediction would entail inputting the state of agent k at timestep t to predict the state of agent k + 1 at the same timestep t, in line with Fig. 3a. However, our target is to predict the future state of the input agent k at time t+1. Thus, we engage in same-agent next-timestep prediction rather than next-token prediction (refer to Fig. 3b for an example of same-agent next-timestep during training). Additionally, we implement learned agent identity embeddings. When a model deals with information from multiple agents, it can gain significantly from discernibly knowing which token is associated with which agent, achieved here through a learned agent ID embedding. For joint training, we train the model to collectively predict the future states of all agents by calculating a loss based on the predicted tokens for every agent (see Fig. 3b). For more details on our inference approach, please consult Section 3.1.   ### 3.3. Task-Specific Considerations Our straightforward PAR methodology seamlessly integrates diverse issues within a unified framework and structure, eliminating the need for any alterations. The process begins with data collection, entity extraction, PAR training, and inference evaluation, encapsulating activities such as talking, standing, watching, and listening with near-perfection percentages—100% across the board for the majority of activities, although there's a notable exception with "watch," which dips to an 85% prediction accuracy. There’s also data regarding the specific actions of walking (scored at 1.0), listening (also at 1.0), and more complex consistencies like hugging at 0.13 or talking at 0.01. These tasks also involve action prediction, object pose estimation, and token decode, with discrete tokens bearing a regression loss while continuous tokens encounter cross-entropy loss. Specific values include a Tx of -0.636 and Ty and Tz valued at 0.143 and 0.938, respectively. Figure 2 illustrates the PAR Framework: initially, we acquire a video dataset, such as AVA for the top section or DexYCB for the bottom. With either dataset labels or computer vision techniques, we extract a predictive trajectory specific to each agent's modality, such as action class labels or object pose combined with 3D hand translation. The next step involves tokenizing the data either through discretization or continuously, as our framework is adaptable to both modes. Appropriately, the loss function for PAR's training is selected according to whether tokenization and prediction tasks were involved. Following PAR training, we then decode the predicted tokens back into data space for evaluation using pertinent metrics.   Looking at the Transformer Predictor—two approaches are presented: (a) illustrates AR which involves multiple agents for next-token training, whereas (b) refers to PAR which focuses on the same agent over the next timestep for training. In Figure 3, training is portrayed with teacher forcing for both multi-agent next-token prediction in autoregressive models (AR) and poly-autoregressive models (PAR), with solid colors representing ground-truth tokens and striped ones indicating predicted tokens, where different colors denote distinct agent identities. AR concentrates on next-token predictions, and PAR attends to the next timestep prediction for the same agent. The visualization is simplified to portray three agents, but the PAR approach supports any number of agents as needed. To tailor a problem into an interaction-conditioned prediction, special task-specific elements have to be contemplated. Figure 2 provides a look at how the PAR framework disentangles multi-agent learning from specific problem modeling.   Regarding the Data, video collections act as our input source across various task examples. From these videos, we draw numerous modalities pertinent to each task, ranging from high-level features like action class labels to granular features such as 3D poses, elucidated in the first two columns of Figure 2. It's presumed that every dataset agent is identified per frame, paired with an agent ID. Our framework offers support for both discrete, quantized tokens and continuous vector tokens. The choice between discrete and continuous formats is contingent upon the task's nature. If discrete tokens are utilized, they are projected to the hidden dimension via a standard embedding layer, while continuous tokens are managed by a specialized projection layer designed to transpose tokens into the transformer’s hidden dimension. For instance, with a 3D vector token having (x, y, z) coordinates being projected to a hidden 128-dimension space, the subsequent un-projection layer reverses the transformation back to the token's original dimensionality.   Loss functions are dictated both by the token type and task-specific requirements during training. With discrete tokens, classification loss becomes apt, while continuous tokens are paired with regression loss mapped to the token’s original dimension. Baseline comparisons include options like selecting a random token from the optimal token space or randomly choosing a trajectory from training data to propose as the prediction. The NN approach involves finding the trajectory closest to a given agent A’s historical trajectory within the training data and using agent AT’s trajectory future as the forecast. Multiagent NN operates similarly but includes an additional agent B, with ego-agent B’s future intended for prediction. There’s also a Mirror approach where agent B’s actual future gets utilized as forecasted for agent A.  Section 3.4 revolves around Framework Implementation Details, noting constant implementation practices for all case studies (elucidated further in Section 10). This includes the formulation of a learned agent ID embedding, where idempotent agent IDs are translated into a hidden dimensional vector and combined into the token embedment. From an architectural perspective, every case study deploys a Llama transformer decoder structure, consisting of eight layers, eight attention heads, and dimensional factors of 128 for both hidden and intermediate layers. The decoder embodies around 4.4 million learned parameters, not factoring in the supplementary few thousand parameters present in learned embedding layers. Additionally employed is a rotary positional encoding in conjunction with agent ID and locational encodings explained in Section 5. Throughout the training process, we utilize teacher forcing. Furthermore, the learning rate emerges as the sole hyperparameter that varies across different case studies.   ### 4. Case Study 1: Social Action Forecasting Our initial case study delves into predicting human actions. At their core, human behaviors are inherently social; people often move in groups and switch between speaking and listening roles during conversations. Some actions, such as hugging or shaking hands, are inherently designed for multiple participants. Consequently, by effectively modeling human interactions, we can enhance the accuracy of action forecasting, particularly when it comes to actions involving more than one person, a point that we demonstrate in this case study.   ### 4.1. Experimental Setup Dataset. The Atomic Visual Actions (AVA) dataset [19] encompasses 235 training videos and 64 validation videos, each lasting 15 minutes, sourced from films. Annotations occur at a frequency of 1Hz, specifying bounding boxes and tracks for individuals within the frame, and detail each person's actions within a span of one second. Individuals can partake in several simultaneous actions from a set of 60 diverse action categories (e.g., one may sit while simultaneously talking). For our analysis, we focus on clips that exhibit a continuous sequence of actions from an agent lasting at least 4 seconds, dividing any sequences longer than 12 seconds. We utilize the first portion of each clip as historical context to predict the latter half. For any ego agent's trajectory, we choose a secondary agent by selecting the individual who remains in the scene for the longest duration during the ego agent’s trajectory. Results In Table 1, we present the performance results of a single-agent autoregressive (AR) model, establishing a baseline for comparison. Notably, this AR model surpasses our initial baselines, as shown in Table 2, with the single-agent neural network (NN) representing the strongest alternative among these. Our comparisons extend to a two-agent predictive autoregressive (PAR) model, as found in the table's final row, alongside several model variants where we either omit the agent ID embedding or shift to predicting the next token rather than the next timestep for the same agent. The table's second row illustrates results from a multi-agent next-token prediction strategy, depicted in Fig. 3a. This method appears to mislead the model, yielding considerably weaker performance compared to training that focuses solely on a single agent's data. In Fig. 4, we provide an example of action forecasting. The graph highlights, in white, the actual distribution of actions against our red predictions. Using a 6-second history of actions sampled at 1 Hz, we predict 6 seconds into the future. In the scenario presented, there's an interchange between a man and woman where each alternates between speaking and listening. At the outset, the man is the speaker. The single-agent AR model anticipates he will remain speaking, whereas the 2-agent PAR model, understanding the nuances of interaction, accurately anticipates the woman's turn to speak. Our predictions for interactions such as singing to, watching, talking to, listening to, fighting/hitting, hugging, kissing, grabbing, handshaking, lifting, giving, and pushing or taking actions are quantified with mean Average Precision (mAP) values illustrated in Figure 5. The data reveal enhanced performance across most two-person action classes in the AVA dataset, indicated by significant mAP improvements: listening actions saw a +7.0 increase, kissing actions increased by +8.3, fighting/hitting received a +5.7 boost, talking actions improved by +4.4, hugging showed a +5.7 gain, and handshaking went up by +4.0. Incrementally adding elements of our PAR approach leads to performance refinements, with the complete model, inclusive of next timestep prediction combined with agent ID embedding, achieving a +1.9 mAP increase. Focusing on two-person action classifications, as outlined in Fig. 5, we note that the single-agent PAR model attains a mAP of 36.3, whereas the two-agent PAR model rises to 39.8, marking a +3.5 mAP enhancement. Figure 4's action forecasting episode further demonstrates the two-agent PAR model's capacity to interpret complementary speaking and listening actions, an association that eludes the AR model. This is further substantiated in Fig. 5, where the multi-agent model enhances the "talk to" class by +4.4 mAP and the "listen to" class by +7.0 mAP, alongside substantial improvements in other classes relevant to personal interactions, such as a +8.3 mAP in kissing and +5.7 in fighting/hitting, with further insights reflected in single-person actions analyzed in Fig. 11.   ### 5. Case Study 2: Multiagent Car Trajectory Prediction Our second case study delves into the prediction of car trajectories. Successfully predicting these pathways necessitates a vehicle's awareness of other cars on the roadway to avoid collisions and encourage cooperative behavior among them. This particular study exemplifies how our framework facilitates the joint modeling of the movements of multiple vehicles engaging on the road.   ### 5.1. Experimental Setup Dataset. In this study, we leverage the nuScenes dataset [5], where we incorporate 2 seconds worth of position data to project vehicle positions 6 seconds into the future. Our specific aim is to accurately forecast the xy coordinates of each agent, with a particular focus on vehicles as the exclusive agents. To load and visualize this data, we employ the trajdata interface [23]. Task-specific considerations. Contrary to discretizing the xy position space, our approach involves discretizing the agents' motion, which yields discrete tokens pertaining to their velocity or acceleration. These integer tokens are then mapped to the transformer's hidden dimension through the Llama token embedding layer. By using solely these tokens, our PAR model gains insight into the speeds at which other agents are traveling, but it lacks information about their specific locations. To address this critical shortcoming, and ensure that our model is capable of determining potential collisions between agents, it is imperative that location information is incorporated. We achieve this by inputting the relative locations of the agents being predicted into a sinusoidal-cosine positional embedding (described in full in Sec. 12.1), which we refer to as location positional encoding (LPE). This LPE is added to our token embeddings. We employ a cross-entropy classification loss on our discrete tokens: L = Ey∼p(y)[−log(p(sT tπ)]. Our model’s predicted trajectories are evaluated using the standard average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) metrics. Regarding our baseline methods (Sec. 3.3), we opt for the closest agent at the present timestep for both Multiagent NN and Mirror. Case Study 3: Predicting Object Pose Amid Hand-Object Interactions   In our concluding case study, we examine how interactions between hands and objects can be exploited for predicting object poses. Case Study 3: Object Pose Forecasting During Hand-Object Interaction Dataset. Our research utilizes the DexYCB dataset, which consists of a substantial 1000 videos featuring 10 different subjects engaging in tasks that involve manipulating objects. This involves 20 distinct items from the YCB-Video dataset. The dataset is strategically divided into 800 videos dedicated to training, 40 set aside for validation, and 160 for testing purposes. In our study, we employ one of the eight available camera angles. During each trial, participants are tasked with picking up and lifting the objects under randomly varied conditions. The provided labels specify the object's SO(3) rotation and its 3D translation, as well as the 3D translation of the participant’s hand. Our primary focus is on accurately predicting either the object's rotation or its translation. Task-specific considerations. In experiments involving only objects, we tokenize the information pertaining to objects. Conversely, in experiments dealing with both hand and object information, we tokenize both. The object is represented as a 4D token for scenarios focusing on rotation prediction (quaternion derived from SO(3) rotation) or a 3D token when the focus is on predicting translation (Euclidean coordinates). For experiments that involve both hand and object, we include a hand token, which is defined by a 3D translation vector, and use agent ID embeddings to differentiate between hand and object tokens. Normalization techniques are applied to all 3D translation vectors across both AR and PAR experiments. Meanwhile, quaternions, by their nature, are inherently normalized and need no further processing. Tokens are projected into the transformer's hidden dimension through an embedding layer, and another layer subsequently projects them back for prediction purposes. For rotation-only forecasting, the loss function is designated as Lrot = 1 − |ˆq · q|, where ˆq represents the predicted quaternion and q is the actual ground-truth quaternion. In the case of translation-only forecasting, the loss Lt is computed as the mean squared error (MSE) between the predicted and ground-truth translations. In PAR scenarios, the focus shifts to predicting relative object-to-hand translations at each frame, taking the current position of the hand as the reference point. For AR, forecasts concern absolute object translations and exclude consideration of the interacting agent. For PAR models, we introduce an additional loss term Lh, calculated as the MSE on hand translations. The object-only AR rotation model is optimized using Lrot, while the PAR rotation model employs a combined Lrot + Lh; similarly, the object-only translation model is refined using Lt, and the hand-object translation model leverages Lt + Lh. During inference, the first half of each video serves as input, and objects’ predictions for the latter half are generated in an autoregressive manner. We assess translation using MSE and measure rotation with geodesic distance (GEO) on SO(3).   ### 6.1. Results This study unveiled the Poly-Autoregressive (PAR) framework, which serves as a comprehensive method for predicting outcomes in multi-agent interactions. By utilizing the identical transformer architecture and maintaining the same hyperparameters across a variety of scenarios—including predicting actions in social environments, forecasting the trajectory of autonomous vehicles, and anticipating object pose during hand-object interactions—we have showcased the adaptability and strength of our framework. Our results highlight the crucial role of considering the impact of multiple agents within a scene to improve prediction tasks. By effectively capturing these interactions, we notably enhanced prediction accuracy compared to single-agent models for all the issues we explored. Although we obtained promising results with our straightforward architecture, this work is only an initial step that invites further development. Expanding this research could involve integrating environmental context or tokenizing pixel patches, particularly to alleviate the assumption of needing high-quality tracking. It would be intriguing to experiment with larger datasets and more complex models. We have not yet focused on the relative importance of neighboring agents, which presents an exciting area for future investigation, for example, through dynamic attention mechanisms. The framework we present with PAR serves as a straightforward and adaptable foundation comprised of universal building blocks, primed for enhancement or adaptation in subsequent tasks. The potential of the PAR framework could significantly drive progress in AI systems, boosting prediction precision and facilitating more accurate navigation and functioning in dynamic, real-world, multi-agent contexts.   ### 7. In the realm of autonomous driving, predicting the future movement of vehicles has emerged as a pivotal challenge [11, 22], owing to a surge in the availability of relevant datasets over recent years [5, 7, 49]. Related Work: Case Studies    ### 10. Additional PAR Framework Details Token embeddings and loss. When dealing with discrete tokens, we implement a conventional learned embedding layer that transforms the tokens into the model’s hidden dimension denoted as \(d_h\). To determine the loss in this scenario, we employ a classification loss, comparing the predicted distribution, or output logits, with the input ground truth tokens. For cases involving continuous inputs with dimension \(d\), a linear layer is trained to project from \(d\) to \(d_h\). Additionally, an un-projection layer is designed to translate the model from \(d_h\) to \(d\). In order to compute the loss here, we extract the model’s last hidden state, un-project it to dimension \(d\), and subsequently compute a regression loss in the original token space.  Next-timestep prediction. In typical autoregressive models, like the single-agent model mentioned in Section 3.2, the next token prediction objective is enforced by calculating the loss on both the input and the predicted target, after both are shifted by one step. In our approach, however, we shift both by \(N\), facilitating the model, with its flattened sequence of \(N \times T\) tokens, to predict a token that signifies the subsequent timestep yet pertains to the same agent.  Inference. In a single-agent model context, we start by providing the model with an initial sequence history of \(h\) tokens. These tokens are fed into the model to generate the subsequent token, and this token is then added to our sequence, forming a new sequence of \(h + 1\) tokens. This process is repeated, allowing the generation of sequences of any length. For our multi-agent model, we begin with a ground-truth history encompassing \(h\) timesteps, equivalent to \(h \times N\) tokens, which include the ego agent known as agent \(N\). Inputting this data into the model produces the last output token as our ego agent at timestep \(h + 1\). To predict the next timestep, \(h + 2\), we append the ground truth of agents 1 through \(N-1\) at timestep \(h + 1\) alongside our prediction of the ego agent at the same step to the ground truth history of \(h \times N\) tokens, and repeat the procedure.  For a multi-agent next-token prediction ablation, the process involves inputting the ground truth of agents 1 to \(N-1\) at timestep \(h + 1\) into the model to predict our ego agent, designated as agent \(N\), at that timestep. This sequence continues by providing the model with the ground truth tokens of agents 1 to \(N-1\) so as to predict agent \(N\) at every timestep. Consequently, this ablation inherently offers more information during inference.  In the architecture depicted, particularly Figure 9, at the top, PAR training is shown with teacher forcing. Initially, tokens are introduced to the model and projected into a token embedding dimension of size \(d_h = 128\), where embeddings such as the agent ID embedding are summed up. Following projection, the transformer outputs are either sampled (in the case of discrete tokens to the left) or deprojected (in continuous tokens to the right) to yield a predicted token. During inference, a similar approach is used where embeddings are summed, and the same conversion operation from transformer output to token space ensues.  The bottom left of the diagram illustrates PAR on discrete tokens. Here, the specified token is represented as an integer index in a codebook, utilizing a standard transformer embedding layer for projection to \(d_h\). Demonstrated here is the summation of our agent ID embedding alongside our location positional encoding to the embedded token. Once this is processed through the transformer, the output is a distribution of logits from which a token is sampled, with our experimentation utilizing the argmax function. In this discrete scenario, the token undergoes conversion back to its actual modality through a detokenization step.  In the bottom right, PAR is applied to continuous tokens. This involves projecting the token to \(d_h\) using a dedicated learned projection layer. The subsequent transformer output retains the dimension \(d_h\). A trained deprojection layer then serves to reproject back from \(d_h\) to the token dimension. Post-deprojection, no additional constraints are imposed on predicted token values, ensuring the absence of operations that might otherwise limit these values. Overall, this ablation configuration inevitably has more contextual information available during inference stages.   ### 10.1.
