Additional Results on Car Trajectory Prediction Rather than breaking down the xy coordinate space into discrete units, we focus on discretizing motion, thereby obtaining discrete tokens for velocity or acceleration. These tokens are created as follows. We begin by taking the ground truth trajectory for each agent, including both past and future segments, and shift it so that the starting point aligns with the origin at x, y = 0, 0. Next, we rotate the entire path to ensure that the initial heading at time t = 0 aligns with 0 radians. Velocity space is then divided into 128 uniform bins ranging from [−18, 18] meters. Refer to AR 2-Agent PAR in Figure 12, where Rotation Prediction Progression is sampled every 5 frames. The qualitative results show predictions from two videos. The 3D model in blue depicts the ground-truth translation for visualization purposes beside our predicted rotation. In the top panel (AR), the focus is solely on the object of interest, whereas the bottom panel (2-agent PAR) showcases improved performance when the human hand is incorporated as a second agent in the grasping interaction. For each trajectory, we identify the difference between consecutive coordinates separately for x and y to obtain a sequence of deltas of length T −1. Each delta is then assigned to a bin index. Our initial experiments utilized velocity tokens by taking the Cartesian product of the bin space which results in a singular index for each xy-delta, ranging between 1 and 128∗128 = 16,384. To form acceleration tokens, we calculate differences between each x delta and y delta, and place these differences into 13 bins each. By taking the Cartesian product of these bins, we create a token vocabulary ranging from 1 to 13 ∗ 13 = 169 possible indices.   For Location Positional Encoding (LPE), we employ the following approach. Initially, we determine relative positions in relation to the 'ego' agent at the first timestep of the history. The ego agent's path is recentered to begin at location (0, 0) at time t = 0, with all other agent paths adjusted accordingly to reflect their relative positions to this reference point. These paths are additionally rotated such that the ego agent has a heading of 0, coordinating the rotation of all other paths relative to the ego agent’s orientation. These relative positions are normalized into a range from 0 to 1. Subsequently, we quantize the normalized positions to integer values between 0 and 100 and apply a sin-cos positional encoding separately to x and y. The encoding operates on these quantized positions rather than sequence position indices. Separate positional encodings are computed for both axes, combining by concatenating these to match half the hidden dimension. We sum this encoding with the model inputs during training to encompass the entire trajectory (including both history and future). During inference, this encoding is computed for all agents (from 1 to N-1) on the full trajectory (history and future). However, for our ego agent, validation relies solely on the historical location's ground truth, while future locations are predicted incrementally. At each sampling stage, velocity or acceleration tokens are integrated to update these predictions step-by-step, and the resulting location is encoded accordingly. Further reference to translation prediction can be seen in Figure 13. The results highlight translations from two video sequences, with a blue 3D model illustrating ground-truth rotation and our predicted translation. In the top panel (AR), the object stands alone, whereas the 2-agent PAR row below shows enhanced performance by involving human hand movement in grasping tasks. For evaluation purposes, given that the nuScenes test set requires leaderboard submission, our demonstration of PAR’s efficacy compared to AR takes place using the nuScenes validation set.   ### 11.4. Results with more than Three Agents In the primary text, it was noted that we employ relative translations concerning the hand's position to calculate the PAR results. For translation prediction, the relative translation is defined in relation to the hand's position at the specific current timestep. This implies that the hand's token is consistently considered the origin—a zero vector—at each timestep, and the translation of the object is determined by the displacement between the current locations of the hand and the object. When it comes to predicting rotation, the situation is different; we cannot determine the object's rotation relative to the hand because our dataset lacks information about the hand's rotation. Instead, for the hand token, we compute the relative translation in relation to the hand’s position during the initial frame of the sequence. This approach ensures that the hand’s position is regarded as the origin only at the first timestep, allowing the hand’s movement to have an impact on the rotation prediction throughout the entire sequence. To train both prediction tasks effectively, we stabilize the learning process by utilizing Exponential Moving Average (EMA); for rotation prediction, a decay rate of 0.999 is applied, while translation prediction makes use of a decay rate of 0.99. Both tasks are trained using the AdamW optimizer, which operates with a learning rate set to 10⁻⁴.   ### 12. Additional Case Study Implementation Details Included in our supplementary video is the complete footage of all the qualitative results presented in this paper, along with some additional qualitative outcomes. It is important to note that no temporal smoothing techniques have been applied to the results, nor have any other alterations been made to the outputs displayed in the videos.

summary: Real-world data collection for robotics is costly and resource-intensive, requiring skilled operators and expensive hardware. Simulations offer a scalable alternative but often fail to achieve sim-to-real generalization due to geometric and visual gaps. To address these challenges, we propose a 3D-photorealistic real-to-sim system, namely, RE$^3$SIM, addressing geometric and visual sim-to-real gaps. RE$^3$SIM employs advanced 3D reconstruction and neural rendering techniques to faithfully recreate real-world scenarios, enabling real-time rendering of simulated cross-view cameras within a physics-based simulator. By utilizing privileged information to collect expert demonstrations efficiently in simulation, and train robot policies with imitation learning, we validate the effectiveness of the real-to-sim-to-real pipeline across various manipulation task scenarios. Notably, with only simulated data, we can achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with an average success rate exceeding 58%. To push the limit of real-to-sim, we further generate a large-scale simulation dataset, demonstrating how a robust policy can be built from simulation data that generalizes across various objects. contents: ### Abstract Collecting data in the real world for robotics purposes can be both expensive and labor-intensive, often demanding skilled operators in addition to costly hardware. Simulations present a more scalable alternative, yet they frequently struggle to generalize effectively from simulation to reality due to discrepancies in geometry and visuals. To confront these hurdles, we introduce RE3SIM, a 3D-photorealistic real-to-sim system designed specifically to bridge the geometric and visual gaps that often hinder sim-to-real transitions. RE3SIM leverages cutting-edge 3D reconstruction as well as neural rendering technologies to accurately replicate real-world conditions, supporting real-time rendering of simulated cross-view cameras in a physics-driven simulator environment. By taking advantage of privileged insights to gather expert demonstrations efficiently in a simulated setting and employing imitation learning to train robotic policies, we validate the robustness of our real-to-sim-to-real pipeline across a diverse range of manipulation tasks. Remarkably, utilizing solely simulated data, we achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with a notable average success rate surpassing 58%. To further extend the bounds of real-to-sim capabilities, we also develop a large-scale simulation dataset, showcasing the creation of a resilient policy that effectively generalizes diverse objects. Those interested can find codes and demonstrations at: http://xshenhan.github.io/Re3Sim/. Collaboration for this project involves institutions such as Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai AI Lab, and The University of Hong Kong. For any queries, please contact Yilun Chen at <chenyilun@pjlab.org.cn> or Jiangmiao Pang at <pangjiang-miao@pjlab.org.cn>. This is a preprint version of the paper.   ### 1. Introduction We've observed notable generalization capabilities exhibited by robotic models (Brohan et al., 2023; Cheang et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; 2024b; Tian et al., 2024) within specific tabletop or kitchen settings, largely facilitated by the acquisition of high-quality teleoperation data. Yet, gathering real-world expert data (Black et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2022) continues to be a process that is both labor-intensive and expensive. Despite improvements in teleoperation systems (Cheng et al., 2024; Aldaco et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024), the amount of manual work remains substantial, underscoring a significant challenge in the field of robotics research. Recent initiatives (O’Neill et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024) have considered inter-institutional collaborations to tackle this issue. Comparatively, simulation data provides the advantage of virtually limitless scalability through computational resources, making it an attractive and renewable option for training robotic policies. Increasing research in sim-to-real transfer (Mandlekar et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024; Nasiriany et al., 2024) has concentrated on creating high-quality simulated or synthetic data to inform the development of real-world robotic policies. However, one of the persistent challenges with simulation data is the significant sim-to-real gaps, which necessitate the collection of target domain data for fine-tuning policies. Among these gaps, two of the most pronounced are the geometric gap and the visual gap. The geometric gap stems from discrepancies in object shapes, often due to the constraint of relying on a finite set of pre-formulated CAD models in simulations that presume perfect structures. On the flip side, the visual gap is the result of flawless but unrealistic rendering, creating hurdles for tasks that are highly dependent on appearance cues, such as picking fresh fruits, pressing colorful buttons, and sorting products by packaging, among others. To effectively bridge the divide between real and simulated environments, we introduce a system known as 3D-photorealistic real-to-sim-to-real, or RE3SIM, which stands for reconstruction-rendering-based real-to-sim. RE3SIM aims to accurately replicate real-world scenarios by merging realistic 3D geometry reconstruction with visual RGB rendering. The 3D geometry is reconstructed using multi-view stereo (MVS) methodologies (Schönberger & Frahm, 2016; Cernea, 2020), while the visual rendering is performed through Gaussian rasterization (Kerbl et al., 2023). This harmonized approach allows for efficient and high-precision reconstruction, where simulated dynamics are calculated using physics engine backends (Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020; Todorov et al., 2012), and real-time rendering is managed by a specialized hybrid rendering engine. RE3SIM employs a sequential real-to-sim pipeline that involves three critical stages: (a) mesh recovery for reconstructing both scene and object geometry; (b) hybrid visual rendering to blend foreground and background elements; and (c) real-world alignment to match world coordinates between real and simulated realms. Human intervention in the real-to-sim procedure is minimal and limited to: (a) Positioning ArUco markers within the target scenario for real-world alignment, and (b) Capturing photos or videos of the scene and objects, including an extra step to align the robot base. Once all assets and robots are imported into the simulator, RE3SIM employs a privileged policy to generate expert data of high fidelity. It integrates several key features to boost sim-to-real transfer: • Superior geometry and vision fidelity: Achieves exceptional reconstruction and rendering quality, diminishing the sim-to-real gap in terms of both geometry and vision. • Quick scene reconstruction: Allows for the creation of new scene reconstructions in less than three minutes with manual setup. • Efficient rendering: Delivers 24 FPS rendering for 480p images from two separate camera perspectives. To confirm the pipeline's effectiveness, we devised a range of tabletop tasks to demonstrate the generality and applicability of the real-to-sim-to-real process, as depicted in Fig. 1. The zero-shot sim-to-real policies reach an average success rate of 58% with merely approximately 10 minutes of data collection in simulation, underscoring the efficacy of our approach. We anticipate that these experiments will underscore the potential of the real-to-sim-to-real pipeline in reducing sim-to-real discrepancies, thus paving the way for future improvements in scalable, efficient, and broadly applicable robotic policy.   ### 2. Background    ### 2.1. 3D Reconstruction The objective of 3D reconstruction is to recreate the geometry of three-dimensional scenes using various signals, such as images and point clouds. Achieving this goal typically begins with structure-from-motion techniques, like Colmap, that are used to determine camera poses and generate sparse point clouds (Schönberger & Frahm, 2016). Once the positions of the cameras have been established, dense point clouds can be produced through multi-view stereo (MVS) methods. This includes both traditional techniques (Schönberger et al., 2016) and methods that utilize network-based approaches (Yao et al., 2018). This procedure successfully reconstructs geometry from images. Furthermore, commercial software solutions such as ARCode and PolyCam employ RGB-D SLAM methods, which simultaneously determine camera poses and capture depth information, thereby aiding in the creation of 3D models. These software options frequently integrate post-processing methods, like smoothing and inpainting, and come with user-friendly graphical interfaces, which enhance both the user experience and the quality of the 3D models generated.   ### 2.2. Rendering Rendering involves the creation of photorealistic images based on specific camera angles using either explicit or implicit representations of 3D spaces. Implicit techniques, like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) (Mildenhall et al., 2021), model the 3D environment by utilizing a density field encoded within a neural network, and they render these images through techniques related to volumetric rendering. On the other hand, explicit representations such as meshes and point clouds employ texture mapping (Blinn & Newell, 1976) for the purpose of rendering images and generating new viewpoints. A notable advancement in explicit representation is the use of Gaussian primitives, which take advantage of Gaussian rasterization to achieve high-fidelity rendering, a process referred to as 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023). Compared to other techniques, 3DGS stands out by producing more lifelike rendering outcomes while also providing greater efficiency in rendering processes. Each Gaussian primitive is intricately modeled as an ellipse with a comprehensive 3D covariance matrix Σ that is defined in the global space, centered at a point µ, and expressed as: G(x) = e−1/2 xT Σ−1x. The covariance matrix Σ of a Gaussian primitive is derived by combining its rotational component R and scaling factor S, described by: Σ = RSST RT. Additionally, each Gaussian is given a color ci and sorted by depth using the Z-buffer technique. Using the formula for alpha blending, the color C rendered for a particular view is computed as: C = N Σ i=1 Π j<i αj(1−αi)ci.   ### 3. RE3SIM Robot simulators grounded in physics, such as Isaac Sim (NVIDIA, 2021a) incorporating PhysX (NVIDIA, 2021b), PyBullet (Bullet) by Coumans & Bai (2016–2021), Mujoco crafted by Todorov et al. (2012), and Gazebo by Koenig & Howard (2004), which involves physics engines like Bullet, ODE (Smith, 2001), DART (Lee et al., 2018), and Simbody (Sherman et al., 2011), provide highly accurate simulations thanks to sophisticated physics engines. Despite this, creating an accurate 3D model of a real-world scene directly is quite challenging with these tools, and they fall short in rendering high-resolution images that closely match those found in real-life scenarios. This discrepancy results in a significant gap between simulated and real-world images. The field has witnessed recent advances in 3D reconstruction techniques (Mildenhall et al., 2021; Kerbl et al., 2023; Cernea, 2020; Yu et al., 2024; Guédon & Lepetit, 2024) which offer high-quality rendering outcomes and detailed 3D geometric models, promising to close this gap. In response, we present RE3SIM, a system based on 3D reconstruction designed to narrow the visual divide and recover realistic 3D meshes for transferring simulations to real-world applications. One simple method is to reconstruct the objects and their background simultaneously. Yet, employing Multi-View Stereo (MVS) methods for reconstructing backgrounds often results in visuals of subpar quality, while techniques such as SuGaR (Guédon & Lepetit, 2024) face difficulties in precisely reconstructing flat surfaces, leading to unwanted protrusions and indentations that degrade the realism in object movement. Moreover, segmenting foreground objects for manipulation tasks is notably labor-intensive. To tackle these challenges, our strategy involves separately reconstructing background meshes for estimating collisions and making use of 3DGS to enhance rendering realism. This helps to better align the two elements. Given that object rendering comprises only a small fraction of the robot’s visual observations, we decide not to apply 3DGS for rendering the objects themselves.   ### 3.1. System Overview RE3SIM is a sophisticated pipeline that bridges real-world scenarios to simulation and back to reality. It accomplishes this by reconstructing meshes to estimate collisions, using 3D Gaussian scene representations for rendering purposes, and producing simulated data within a physics-based simulator. One important aspect to highlight is that our focus is strictly on reconstructing both the background and the foreground objects. Robots are excluded from our system because their precise 3D models are generally readily available and accessible. In addition, we approach this work as an exploratory study of RE3SIM, demonstrating and validating it through experiments involving a table-top robot arm designed for tasks involving rigid bodies. As illustrated in Figure 2, the RE3SIM framework is built upon four essential components: first, it includes mesh recovery aimed at calculating potential object collisions; second, it performs hybrid visual rendering that merges 3D Gaussian scene representations for background elements with mesh-based rendering techniques for foreground elements. Furthermore, the system ensures that the reconstructed scene aligns perfectly with real-world configurations of scenes and robot positions. Finally, it facilitates large-scale data generation that is crucial for tasks involving manipulation.   ### 3.2. Mesh Recovery This phase is crucial for rebuilding realistic objects and background geometries to enhance the precision of collision detection and simulation. When it comes to mesh reconstruction, we handle the meshes of backgrounds and objects separately, allowing for greater flexibility. We represent these in USD format for improved extensibility. For the background, we initially use Structure from Motion (SfM) techniques, specifically COLMAP, to determine the pose for each image and obtain a sparse point cloud from a series of images. To achieve detailed mesh reconstruction, we then employ OpenMVS (Cernea, 2020). While PolyCam (Polycam, 2020) is another tool capable of reconstructing the background mesh, our empirical observations indicate that the geometric reconstruction results from OpenMVS typically feature fewer minor protrusions and depressions compared to those generated by PolyCam. After obtaining the initial mesh, we simplify it to form collision bodies. This methodology captures intricate details while preserving precise planar reconstruction. For the reconstruction of foreground objects, we utilize AR-Code (Code, 2022); this tool can automatically segment objects, maintaining a balance between usability and quality.   In the post-processing stage, the reconstructed collision bodies often exhibit voids or sharp edges due to suboptimal image quality, which can lead to unpredictable behavior during simulation. For instance, objects might not rest properly on surfaces. To address this, we employ void filling and surface smoothing techniques to enhance stability and realism in the simulation. Since deriving physical parameters like mass and friction is complex when relying solely on initial static visual data, we opt to use default values to simplify the process, ensuring there is no loss in performance. This approach is effective for a multitude of manipulation tasks. By default, we utilize Isaac Sim (NVIDIA, 2021a) for this purpose, although other ray tracing options can be explored.   In the section “Generating High-Fidelity Simulation Data via 3D-Photorealistic Real-to-Sim for Robotic Manipulation,” we elaborate on the steps involved: beginning with input mesh recovery, refining through ICP, ensuring smoothness, and simplifying data generation for simulators. The process involves rule-based policy rollouts, reject sampling, and datasets optimized for real-world deployment and imitation learning. The system is designed to handle aspects like foreground elements, zero-shot Sim2Real integration, hybrid visual rendering, and textured mesh creation. In the 3DGS-rendering process, real-world alignment is achieved using cameras (Cam 1, Cam 2, Cam 3, Cam 4) aligned through ArUco markers. Our proposed RE3SIM system is illustrated in Figure 2. This real-to-sim-to-real approach leverages both 3D reconstruction and physics-based simulation, bridging small 3D gaps to facilitate large-scale simulation data generation, crucial for learning manipulation skills through Sim2Real transfer.   ### 3.3. Hybrid Visual Rendering Color images, as a fundamental form of perception signals, frequently create a significant visual difference between simulations and the real world. In an effort to bridge this notable disparity, we utilize hybrid real-to-sim rendering techniques to render both the foreground objects and the backgrounds. For foreground objects, we employ object renderings based on mesh data, which are enhanced with ray tracing support to improve realism. The reconstruction of the background—which encompasses the majority of the scene—incorporates more photorealistic rendering methods by utilizing 3DGS. To combine objects according to the true depth of the scene, we apply Z-buffer rendering. Importantly, this hybrid visual rendering process allows for multi-view rendering, accommodating various perspective views. An in-depth analysis of the rendering time needed for each component is presented in Table 5.   ### 3.4. Real-World Alignment While previous steps have focused on aligning rendering with meshes, another essential task is ensuring alignment with real-world scenarios. This involves considering the positions of background and foreground elements in relation to the robots. For objects in the foreground, we establish a set of potential placements within the simulated environment. As for the background, we utilize an ArUco marker located on the table to synchronize the coordinates of the 3D Graphics System (3DGS) with those of the marker. Following this, the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm, as detailed by Schenker in 1992, Censi in 2008, and Low in 2004, is used in post-processing to fine-tune any discrepancies in coordinate alignment. Specifically, the ICP method refines the transformation between the partial point cloud captured by the depth camera and the full point cloud derived from the reconstructed mesh.   ### 3.5. Expert Data Collection To assess the real-to-sim-to-real system's performance, particularly in carrying out tasks like pick-and-place, we amass extensive demonstrations by employing a scripted policy. Each iteration involves the incorporation of domain randomizations, such as divergences in source or target objects and variations in the robot arm's base location. Furthermore, an expert policy, denoted as πpriv(at|opriv,t), is delineated based on privileged information opriv,t, which includes precise details about target objects' poses. Using πpriv, interactions with the simulator allow us to compile observation-action pairs (ot, at). The term ot refers to observations obtainable from the real world, encapsulating visual and proprioceptive data. At specific pivotal steps, we ascertain the gripper's 6D pose, employing a motion planner grounded in the RRTConnect algorithm (presented by Kuffner & LaValle in 2000) to chart paths between these keypoints within joint space. While generating data, reject sampling is strategically used to discard any unsuccessful rollouts, thus elevating the dataset's quality and securing its reliability. This method enables continuous generation of data to match our requirements, resulting in the creation of simulated datasets D. 4 Generating High-Fidelity Simulation Data via 3D-Photorealistic Real-to-Sim for Robotic Manipulation.   ### 4. Experiment Our research primarily focuses on exploring four key questions pertaining to the RE3SIM system we have developed. The first question (Q1) examines whether the RE3SIM system is capable of delivering high-quality reconstructions that are well-aligned. The second question (Q2) seeks to determine if RE3SIM can create highly accurate simulation data characterized by minimal 3D sim-to-real discrepancies, ultimately aiding in addressing real-world manipulation challenges. In tackling the third question (Q3), we aim to understand the role of extensive simulation data in enhancing the capability to undertake more complex tasks within real-world environments. Lastly, the fourth question (Q4) explores whether RE3SIM can efficiently construct entire scenes in simulation and generate data cost-effectively and within a reasonable timeframe.   ### 4.1. Experimental Setups Hardware platform. In this study, we conduct an evaluation of RE3SIM using a Franka Research 3 robot that is equipped with a parallel gripper. To gather visual observations, we utilize two Realsense D435i depth cameras: one is attached directly onto the end-effector while the other is strategically placed beside the robot to provide a third-person perspective. Policy model and training details. For our sim-to-real experiments, we employ a policy structured by ACT, as outlined in the study by Zhao et al. (2023), along with DINOV2 from Oquab et al. (2023). The dataset comprises images compressed using the JPEG format. Throughout training, we apply visual augmentations and, during the evaluation phase, we employ the temporal ensemble technique, as described by Zhao et al. (2023).   ### 4.2. Rendering in Robot Task B offers additional information for a more comprehensive understanding.   ### 4.3. Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Table 1 presents a comparison of background rendering methods. The table provides quantitative results related to reconstruction outcomes measured by PSNR and SSIM values. The data come from assessments conducted at 8 different robot arm positions viewed either from the wrist or a third-person perspective. For background rendering, Polycam yielded a PSNR of 11.57 ±1.25 and an SSIM of 0.30 ±0.08, while 3DGS produced a PSNR of 14.02 ±1.50 and an SSIM of 0.34 ±0.05. Achieving high-quality visual outcomes requires not just superior reconstruction but also precise alignment. In order to respond to Q1, we assess both the quality and alignment of reconstructed results by choosing a trajectory from the simulation dataset tasks detailed in Section 4.3. This selected trajectory is replayed in the physical world to collect ground truth (GT) images using calibrated cameras. We make comparisons regarding visual similarity from both perspectives: the wrist view and a third-person outlook, presenting quality rendering outcomes in Figure 3. Additional rendering outcomes from the simulation can be found in Subsection E. The strong resemblance to real-world images convincingly underscores the precision of our alignment. Additionally, Table 1 elucidates the PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) and SSIM (structural similarity index measure) metrics, which assess the quantitative vision gap of the background rendering approach employed in RE3SIM versus the reconstruction and rendering method adopted by Torne et al. (2024). The latter reconstructs the background using Polycam and renders the mesh to acquire visual observations. These findings highlight the benefit of the rendering component design choice in RE3SIM, facilitating minimized vision gaps.   ### 4.4. Large-Scale Sim-to-Real The core question, denoted as Q2, is the driving force behind the development of RE3SIM, prompting us to design three table-top manipulation tasks to explore the system's capabilities. These tasks are as follows:   1. The first task involves picking up a bottle and placing it into a basket. The challenge here is for the robot to identify and pick an orange bottle that is randomly situated within a designated area measuring 25 cm by 35 cm on a table and then successfully deposit it into a basket.  2. The second task requires placing a vegetable onto a cutting board. In this scenario, a model of a cucumber will be placed within an area of 35 cm by 50 cm on the table, while the location of the cutting board is adjusted within a variable space of 35 cm by 80 cm. The robot's objective is to grasp the cucumber and place it accurately onto the cutting board.   3. The third task involves block stacking. Here, the robot must stack three black cubes placed on the table, with each cube positioned randomly within its own separate area of 30 cm by 10 cm. The robot needs to effectively pick up and stack these cubes.  These tasks have been recreated in a simulated environment using the RE3SIM framework, where we gathered 100 trajectory samples and developed independent training policies. Detailed explanations regarding the rule-based policy implementations and the methods used for evaluation within simulators can be found in Subsection A.  We conducted an evaluation of the policies' performance by measuring their success rates in real-world scenarios. The comparison was drawn among policies trained with simulated data from RE3SIM, those implemented via a real-to-simulation baseline method known as RialTo (as cited in Torne et al., 2024), and policies trained on 50 actual real-world trajectories. The findings reveal that doubling the simulation data yields a performance level comparable to that achieved with real-world data. This parity in results can be attributed to a minimal gap between simulation and reality, as well as differences in the data collection approaches for simulated versus real-world contexts, leading to distinct data quality, as elaborated upon in detail.   ### 4.5. Sim-Real Consistency C. We have also realized a cutting-edge method for grasping, known as AnyGrasp (Fang et al., 2023), integrating it with script primitives to perform the task of picking up and dropping a bottle into a basket for comparative purposes. This approach is unique in that it predicts only the grasp pose rather than the entire trajectory for grasping, which limits its application to other tasks. The numerical findings presented in Table 2 illustrate that leveraging data produced by RE3SIM allows the policy to achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, exhibiting robust performance when compared to existing real-to-sim and top-notch grasping methods. Moreover, policies that have been trained using our extensive dataset can achieve performance comparable or even slightly superior to those trained exclusively on real-world data.   This highlights the effectiveness and immense potential of high-fidelity simulation data. Generating High-Fidelity Simulation Data via 3D-Photorealistic Real-to-Sim for Robotic Manipulation wrist view third view Figure 3 provides a visual comparison between the real and simulated environments. The rendering results from our hybrid method stand in stark contrast to photos taken by real-world cameras, underscoring the high level of fidelity and realism our approach can achieve.   Table 2 offers quantitative evaluations of real-to-sim-to-real performance for tasks involving real-world manipulation. Each task underwent 20 trials where no retries were permitted following a failure. The policies were distinctly trained using 100 episodes with simulation data (RialTo+IL and RE3SIM+IL) and 50 episodes with actual data (Real+IL). Comparative testing in the picking-only scenario was also conducted with AnyGrasp combined with script primitives (AnyGrasp+Prim). The RE3SIM approach notably diminishes the discrepancy between simulation and reality, allowing for successful deployment in real-world settings and achieving an average success rate of 58% in zero-shot sim-to-real scenarios. Real-World Task RialTo+IL AnyGrasp+Prim. Real+IL RE3SIM+IL Pick and drop a bottle to the basket 0.4 0.9 0.8 0.75 Stack cubes 0 - 0.15 0.25 Place a vegetable on the board 0.45 - 0.6 0.75 Thus, the policies trained on our synthetic dataset can match or slightly exceed the performance of those trained solely on real-world data, underscoring the substantial promise and effectiveness of high-fidelity simulation data.   ### 4.6. Pipeline Efficiency To explore the full potential of employing synthetic data for tackling real-world manipulation problems as questioned in Q3, we focus on a clear-the-table task with distinct objects: the robot must tidy up by picking and placing all items, which are scattered randomly on a table within a 40cm × 50cm area, into a basket. This is a task that spans a long horizon, requiring the policy to sequentially select and manage both familiar and unfamiliar objects one at a time. To thoroughly assess the system, we created four separate setups: Seen—features four objects (the bottle, cucumber, corn, and eggplant) that were included in the training data. Unseen—involves four objects (the green pepper, banana, red bowl, and momordica charantia) that were not seen during the training phase. Cluttered—incorporates all eight objects from both seen and unseen categories. Darkness—where testing is conducted at a brightness level significantly dimmer than that of the simulation data. The model's performance is gauged using four previously seen objects. The results, shown in Fig. 4, were gathered from ten trials for each setup, with an allowance for two additional automatic grasp attempts for each object in case of initial failure.   Upon analyzing the results, we noticed that although the policy was trained on just five items, it successfully generalized to grasp newly encountered objects of a similar size, despite variances in shape and color. We postulate that the robot utilizes the static nature of the scene, recognizing objects by distinguishing their color from the background. Additionally, objects with distinct forms often share similar grasp points, which facilitates successful grabbing actions by the robot. Having access to a larger dataset that includes multiple objects enables the policy to sustain a relatively higher success rate; conversely, a smaller dataset limits the policy's skillset in this respect. The robustness of the policy in handling changes in lighting conditions was also notable. We further investigated the impact of data volume on success rates in both simulated and real-world environments. As illustrated in Fig. 5, expanding the size of the synthetic dataset, created using RE3SIM, considerably enhances imitation learning outcomes. In scenarios where the amount of simulation data is restricted, the performance in real-world conditions is nearly insignificant. Doubling the dataset size frequently leads to a marked improvement in success rates until it levels off at strong performance metrics.   ### 5. Related Work We undertook an evaluation of the consistency in policy performance when comparing simulated environments to real-world settings, using the ACT policy. For this experiment, we assessed policies at various training stages, specifically from 0 up to 120,000 training steps, utilizing three distinct random seeds on the task of picking up and dropping a bottle into a basket. As depicted in Fig. 1 (d), the Pearson correlation coefficient stands at 0.924, signifying a robust correlation between simulation and real-world performance metrics. Notably, models that demonstrate higher success rates within simulation environments tend to mirror these success rates in real-world trials. Conversely, when the success rate in simulation environments is low, the model usually struggles to achieve high success in real-world contexts. This may be attributed to alignment errors, resulting in a minor gap between simulation and reality, or possibly because the quantity of real-world test instances is significantly lower compared to simulations, which could introduce a form of bias. This observed consistency suggests that the policies trained with RE3SIM are highly conducive to real-world application, illustrating a minimal gap between simulation and reality.  Table 3 outlines the human effort required for reconstruction activities. It illustrates estimated times for reconstruction at a table level, alongside the human efforts needed for object reconstruction using ARCode. The input categories include Video, Images, and ARCode, with corresponding human effort times recorded as 51.5, 84.5, and 60.5 seconds, respectively.  Table 4 details the time cost for simulation data collection. It specifies the time necessary to gather 100 episodes of simulation data for each task, utilizing a machine equipped with 8 RTX 4090 GPUs. Each GPU is capable of running two Isaac Sim processes. The tasks and their respective time costs in minutes are as follows: Picking and dropping a bottle into a basket takes 12.35 minutes; placing a vegetable on a board requires 13.78 minutes; and stacking blocks takes 6.45 minutes. These results underscore the effectiveness of policies developed through RE3SIM, indicating their suitability for deployment in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by the nominal gap between simulated and actual performance.   ### 6. Conclusion To substantiate Q4, we have meticulously recorded and calculated the time taken by RE3SIM to reconstruct both the background and the objects, as well as the time needed to create demonstrations, highlighting the significant human involvement in reconstruction processes. In the context of RE3SIM, reconstructing the background entails the use of a series of images or a brief video of the background. This is complemented by an additional image equipped with depth information to aid in alignment. Considering the pronounced human effort required, we estimate the time necessary for reconstructing the foreground and background separately. Table 3 provides a summary of the time required based on different input formats: video versus images. While utilizing video might induce a slight compromise in quality due to effects like motion blur, employing images generally yields superior results, albeit at the cost of necessitating a bit more time. Moreover, we detail the time needed to reconstruct an object using ARCode. The overall scene reconstruction duration is derived by adding together the times for background and object reconstruction. When considering data collection expenses, Table 4 illustrates the time involved in gathering 100 simulation episodes for each task outlined in Section 4.3, all conducted using 8 RTX 4090 GPUs. The data collection time is notably less than the duration required for teleoperation in real-world settings—especially as RE3SIM largely relies on machine runtime, whereas the latter predominantly depends on the availability of data collection experts. This disparity underscores our efficiency in generating large-scale simulation data cost-effectively. In relation to generating high-fidelity simulation data through 3D-photorealistic real-to-sim processes for robotic manipulation, Table 5 outlines average time consumption per step, detailing the time consumed by each specific process. Recorded in milliseconds, the time spent on various processes includes 26.64 for physics simulation, 12.93 for Gaussian splatting rendering, 0.36 for motion planning, and 1.53 for other operations, summing up to a total time of 41.46 milliseconds. We specifically tracked the average time allocated to each phase during the data collection for the task of picking up and dropping a bottle in the simulator over 60 steps, as demonstrated in Table 5. Rendering 480p images from two camera viewpoints contributes an additional 12.93 milliseconds, accounting for one-third of the total time per step. RE3SIM achieves approximately 24 frames per second (FPS) with two cameras, ensuring that performance remains both real-time and visually fidelity-focused.   ### Limitations Sim-to-real transfer processes are dedicated to developing methodologies that allow policies to transition effectively from simulation environments to real-world applications. The most straightforward method involves enhancing the accuracy of simulators, as illustrated by the work of Todorov et al. (2012), Makoviychuk et al. (2021), Mittal et al. (2023), and Xiang et al. (2020), thereby narrowing the gap between simulated scenarios and real-life contexts. Additional strategies include domain randomization, referenced in studies such as Tobin et al. (2017), Mehta et al. (2020), Chen et al. (2021), Tremblay et al. (2018), and Loquercio et al. (2019), as well as Tobin et al. (2018). System identification methods also contribute to minimizing this divide, as shown by Ramaswamy and Tangirala (2024), Allevato et al. (2020a, 2020b), and Song et al. (2024).  Alternatively, the real-to-sim-to-real approach utilizes data from the real world to refine simulation models. Techniques that combine reconstruction methods with grasping skills, like Evo-NeRF (Kerr et al., 2023) and LERF-TOGO (Rashid et al., 2023), enable object manipulation using standard RGB image inputs. Concurrently, methods such as GaussianGrasper (Zheng et al., 2024), SplatMover (Shorinwa et al., 2024), and GraspSplats (Ji et al., 2024) employ 3D Gaussian splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) to achieve quick rendering and clear representation in robotic tasks. Furthermore, approaches such as URDFormer (Chen et al., 2024), Digital Cousins (Dai et al., 2024), and Articulate Anything (Le et al., 2024) allow for immediate environment reconstruction from a single image, facilitating the collection of extensive data sets for imitation or reinforcement learning by modifying articulations and utilizing various articulations from simulation databases to train adaptable, real-world deployable models.  Alongside these methods, 3DGS advancements, like RoboStudio (Lou et al., 2024), SplatSim (Qureshi et al., 2024), and RoboGSim (Li et al., 2024a), employ multi-view images or video to enhance world reconstruction. They refine multi-view rendering quality while incurring minimal costs, proving particularly effective in manipulation tasks involving multiple objects or where occlusions are common. Specifically, RoboStudio dedicates efforts to reconstructing a robot's URDF, ensuring both photorealistic rendering outcomes and precise collision meshes. Meanwhile, SplatSim uses pre-existing 3D models of items and settings to compile trajectories within a physics simulator, after which it re-renders these trajectories using 3DGS to mitigate the visual discrepancies between simulated scenarios and real environments. However, acquiring such 3D models can be challenging across numerous tasks. RoboGSim, on the other hand, assesses rendering quality, supports high-fidelity rendering outcomes for new pose synthesis, and demonstrates promising potential for appraising diverse manipulation algorithms, even though its sim-to-real validation remains somewhat restricted. Distinctively, RE3SIM reconstructs both geometric and visual elements whilst maintaining minimal gaps, validating robotic policies trained on simulated datasets through comprehensive real-world experiments.   ### Impact Statement We presented RE3SIM, an innovative Real-to-Sim-to-Real framework that seamlessly combines Gaussian splatting with the PhysX engine from NVIDIA Isaac Sim. This approach enhances both scene reconstruction and the sim-to-real transfer in robotic manipulation exercises. Comprehensive experiments underline its effectiveness and scalability, proving that RE3SIM significantly narrows the sim-to-real gap, thereby facilitating dependable performance in real-world tasks. Models that are trained using vast simulated datasets attained success rates on par with those achieved by models trained using real-world datasets. This emphasizes the potential of RE3SIM to produce varied, high-caliber data suitable for pre-training large-scale robotic models.   ### References RE3SIM, as it currently stands, is restricted to dealing solely with rigid objects and has not yet been adapted for the reconstruction of objects that are articulated or deformable, nor for working with liquids. Furthermore, the system depends on physics parameters that are set manually instead of utilizing system identification methods. As the complexity of tasks increases, relying on rule-based policies for data collection becomes increasingly difficult. Tackling these limitations is something that is planned for future research endeavors.   ### Appendix The proposed RE3SIM system offers a fascinating approach for creating simulated demonstrations by robots aimed at performing tasks in real-world scenarios. This initiative is designed to alleviate the significant burden placed on humans who need to gather extensive real-world data, enhancing efficiency and working to advance the capabilities of generalist robot policies by leveraging the data scaling law. The versatility of RE3SIM allows it to be utilized in a wide array of robot applications, although this adaptability might result in potential unemployment challenges. The appendix is structured to cover the following: Section A delves into the intricate design and assessment strategies for rule-based policy tasks in Sections 4.3 and 4.4. Section B provides a comprehensive view of policy training strategies and image augmentation techniques. Section C draws a detailed comparison between properties of simulated and real datasets, thus offering an explanation for discrepancies in policy performance across these datasets. Section E encompasses additional rendering outcomes of divergent tasks viewed from distinct camera perspectives.   ### B. More Experiment Details This section outlines the design framework for a rule-based policy and explains the evaluation methodology used for each task. Let's take the task of picking up a bottle and placing it into a basket. This task is divided into two main steps: first, identifying the 6D pose of the gripper prior to picking the object up, and second, pinpointing the 6D pose of where the object will be placed. The pose used before picking is calculated from the object's point cloud data, while the placement position remains constant. In this process, motion planning in joint space directs the robotic arm from its initial starting point to two critical positions for either picking up or setting down the item. The success in picking up the object hinges on how the robotic arm is positioned in relation to the gripper and the object's height with respect to the table surface. After releasing the object, its placement is considered successful if its horizontal position falls within the defined area of the basket.  When it comes to placing a vegetable on a cutting board, the center of the board is designated as the placement site. The rule-based policy for this task mirrors the approach used for previous tasks. Success in this context is defined by the object's horizontal position being within a precise area near the board's center.  For the task of stacking blocks, this involves sequentially picking up and placing two different objects. The pre-pick pose and placement position are computed using the 3D models of these objects. The steps involved are reminiscent of those used in the bottle-to-basket task. The second block is picked up only if the first block is successfully placed; if it isn't, the trajectory ends prematurely and is considered invalid. Stacking is deemed successful if the horizontal positions of the two blocks align correctly and the height difference between them equals the height of one block.  Finally, clearing objects from the table follows a different strategy. In order to reduce variability in actions when in identical states and to simplify the training of the model, the rule-based policy prioritizes picking objects that are closest to the robot's base. Given the large volume of objects involved, randomizing their starting positions often results in point cloud overlaps, which can lead to unpredictable results in physics simulations. Therefore, during domain randomization, configurations where objects intersect are eliminated before the simulation is run. The task is marked as complete only once all objects are picked up successfully and placed in their respective designated positions.   ### C. Comparison over Simulated and Real Data Policy training involves predicting a series of future k-step actions based on single-step observations, which comprise both two-view images and proprioceptive data. To capture details from images more effectively, we have replaced the initial ResNet architecture with the DINOv2 encoder (as described in Oquab et al., 2023). Throughout the training process, we utilize visual enhancements such as Gaussian Blur, Defocus, Color Jittering, and Gaussian Noise to improve the model's robustness. Moreover, we apply a cosine decay strategy to the learning rate (lr) to facilitate smoother convergence during the training of the model. Details regarding the model's hyperparameters for tasks outlined in Section 4.3 are provided in Table 6. Given the substantial size of the dataset used for the task of clearing objects from the table, the policy is trained for a concise period of only 8 epochs. To ensure the smoothness of actions during rollouts, the evaluation incorporates the temporal ensemble technique (as outlined in Zhao et al., 2023).   Regarding image augmentation, it is acknowledged that Gaussian splatting is inherently incapable of mimicking certain visual effects such as motion blur and focus-dependent blur. Nonetheless, images captured during the actual device deployment may appear blurred due to camera movement, and room brightness can vary over time. To emulate these real-world conditions during model training, we apply random transformations to the images, utilizing techniques from (Buslaev et al., 2020), including Gaussian Blur, Defocus, Color Jittering, and Gaussian Noise. As illustrated in Table 7, appropriate use of image augmentation techniques markedly improves model performance in both simulated and actual environments. Specifically, augmentations like blur and defocus effectively simulate the type of blurring that can result from camera motion. By combining noise and blur, the model learns to identify critical features necessary for task completion, reducing its sensitivity to irrelevant information changes, which enhances its performance in real-world scenarios. These image augmentation methods result in the highest success rates in real-world environments, showcasing their role in bridging the gap between 3D Gaussian splatting rendering outcomes and real-world camera visuals.  For evaluation in simulation, a rejection sampling approach is utilized during data collection to evaluate whether a training policy has successfully completed a task. The spatial relationship between the gripper and the object’s point cloud, along with the object's proximity to the tabletop, helps ascertain successful object grasping. Additionally, the relative positioning of the object in relation to the target point confirms the correct placement of the item.   In Figure 6, we present a compression analysis involving a qualitative and quantitative examination using third-person view images. This analysis explores how varying JPEG quality parameters impact image quality, task success rates, and compression ratios for tasks such as placing a vegetable on a board. Although policies are trained on compressed data, uncompressed data is deployed to maintain higher information integrity.   For complex tasks requiring extensive simulation data, storing uncompressed image data poses a significant spatial cost. Thus, we opt for JPEG compression. During model deployment, uncompressed data is preferred to preserve maximal information. Figure 6 depicts the outcome based on different image quality settings, the success rate of the models trained on the task of placing a vegetable on a board, and their corresponding compression rates. Our experiments determined that a quality setting of 40 offers an optimal balance, achieving substantial storage saving with minimal perceptible image quality loss.   ### D. Co-training and Fine-tuning We conduct training of the policy using a combination of 100 episodes of simulation data along with 50 episodes drawn from real-world settings, ultimately achieving comparable performance within those real-world environments. In the forthcoming section, we delve into the differences and commonalities between the data derived from simulations and that gathered from real-world scenarios, seeking to unearth the underlying reasons. Variations in the distribution and quality between real-world and simulation data often arise due to disparities in scene initialization approaches and the differing trajectory preferences of human operators versus those of rule-based policies.   **C.1. Object Location**   Refer to Figure 7: Data distribution. We illustrate the starting positions of objects for each task as outlined in Section 4.3. The dataset comprises 100 episodes of simulation data (Sim) and 50 episodes of real-world data (Real). We provide a separate depiction of each cube's position within the stacking block tasks. Data Quality**   In Figure 8, we offer a visualization capturing the episode lengths and gripper angles as aligned with the direction of gravity. Due to distinct data collection methods, notable differences in the lengths of trajectories emerge. In simulations, the motion planner opts for the shortest paths leading to abbreviated trajectories but with more significant angular variations. Furthermore, it is empirically noted that the planner often adjusts the gripper's rotation and position concurrently, a scenario rarely mirrored in real-world teleoperations involving a space mouse. During scene reconstruction, we did not capture images from positions with substantial angles, which resulted in reduced rendering realism within high-angle simulations. Such discrepancies necessitate potentially greater reliance on simulated data to bridge these gaps. Conversely, longer trajectories might incorporate more pauses, adversely affecting model training due to diminished action continuity.   ### E. name of paper: Rhythmic sharing: A bio-inspired paradigm for zero-shot adaptation and learning in neural networks
author: gpt-4o
summary: The brain can rapidly adapt to new contexts and learn from limited data, a coveted characteristic that artificial intelligence algorithms have struggled to mimic. Inspired by oscillatory rhythms of the mechanical structures of neural cells, we developed a learning paradigm that is based on oscillations in link strengths and associates learning with the coordination of these oscillations. We find that this paradigm yields rapid adaptation and learning in artificial neural networks. Link oscillations can rapidly change coordination, endowing the network with the ability to sense subtle context changes in an unsupervised manner. In other words, the network generates the missing contextual tokens required to perform as a generalist AI architecture capable of predicting dynamics in multiple contexts. Oscillations also allow the network to extrapolate dynamics to never-seen-before contexts. These capabilities make our learning paradigm a powerful starting point for novel models of learning and cognition. Furthermore, learning through link coordination is agnostic to the specifics of the neural network architecture, hence our study opens the door for introducing rapid adaptation and learning capabilities into leading AI models.
