contents: ### Summary paragraph The brain possesses the extraordinary ability to swiftly adjust to new environments and learn from minimal information, an ability that artificial intelligence (AI) systems have found challenging to replicate. Taking inspiration from the rhythmic oscillations seen in the structural makeup of neural cells, we have devised a learning framework that leverages oscillations in the strengths of connections and ties learning to how well these oscillations coordinate. Our findings reveal that employing this framework enables artificial neural networks to quickly adapt and learn. The oscillations in link strengths can rapidly alter their coordination, thus empowering the network to detect subtle shifts in context without supervision. Essentially, this means the network is able to generate the missing contextual tokens it needs, allowing it to function as a versatile AI framework capable of predicting behavior across various situations. Furthermore, these oscillations enable the network to extrapolate to completely new, previously unseen contexts. Such features make our learning framework an influential foundation for crafting new models of learning and cognition. Moreover, since learning by coordinating links does not depend on the specific architecture of the neural network, our research paves the way for embedding rapid adaptation and learning capabilities into prominent AI models.   ### 1 Introduction Many of the processes that govern the natural world exhibit changes in their internal parameters, leading to non-stationary dynamics where statistical properties evolve over time. Instances of this include changes in atmospheric chemistry, the movement of tectonic plates, or the shift of a tumor from being benign to malignant. Such nonstationary factors can profoundly transform the entire probability framework, making straightforward methods like mean-centering the data inadequate. Although the initial changes in system parameters may be nearly imperceptible in the data, identifying these changes can help us foresee serious long-term outcomes, such as climate change, seismic activities, or the spread of cancer. As a result, the study and prediction of dynamics subject to parameter shifts have attracted significant interest across various fields. Machine learning, in particular, has shown to be an effective approach for predicting the behavior of complex systems even when mathematical models are unavailable. Interestingly, most machine learning approaches optimize predictions for scenarios that emerge from a singular context, usually a stationary probability distribution. This learning process involves the network's link strengths alternately increasing or decreasing during training until reaching the best configuration possible. Moreover, when it comes to predicting nonstationary data, it's crucial to first identify the different states within the data and subsequently provide these contextual cues to the machine. This allows the machine to comprehend how training data contexts shift over time. In this context, 'states' refer to groups of trajectories that belong to the same stationary probability distribution, like those of an attractor or another group with consistent long-term statistical features. Since each state signifies a unique stationary probability distribution, a state can be seen as the intrinsic 'context' of the time series. If these contextual tokens are missing, the machine struggles to grasp the various probability contexts present in the data and may end up overriding data whose context conflicts with another—leading to catastrophic forgetting. However, the brains of living organisms are highly adept at sensing minute contextual changes in their surroundings and do not fall victim to catastrophic forgetting.   ### 1.1 A new learning paradigm Drawing upon the mechanochemical interactions between astrocytes and neuronal synapses, we propose an innovative perspective on neuroplasticity. Recent studies indicate that learning processes might be influenced by biomechanics, as the compression of neuronal synapses appears to enhance synaptic transmission. With this in mind, our learning model is built around this potential role of biomechanics and unfolds in two distinct segments.   Firstly, we suggest that learning is characterized by rhythmic fluctuations in connection strength. This idea is rooted in recent research, including our own, which has shown that biomechanics exhibits inherent rhythmic patterns. Moreover, we posit that learning hinges upon the synchronization of these rhythmic changes. This aspect of our model is largely inspired by astrocytes—glial cells that are found in abundance within the brain and envelop numerous synapses. These cells showcase rhythmic hotspots of biomechanical activity, which could facilitate coordination among synapses.  These foundational ideas combine to form a robust learning model: We encapsulate these rhythms as gradual oscillations in the strength of certain connections, allowing for variability in their phases across different connections. Consequently, data traversing the network can exploit multiple subnetworks, dictated by the oscillation phases at any given moment. The second component of this model is that connection phases can evolve in response to the information being processed, such as distinct states. Our framework suggests that connections engaged in handling a specific state can swiftly alter their phases to synchronize with other connections. This synchronization is orchestrated by elements that gather information from certain connections, drawing inspiration from the integrative function of astrocytes (these elements are illustrated as stars in the reference figure).  As a new state is introduced and changes the active connections, the resulting state changes are reflected as collective modifications in the synchronization of connection phases. This means that the synchronization of connection phases also acts as an identifying marker for each state. We applied our model to an artificial neural network, demonstrating its capability to swiftly detect dynamic state changes across a variety of dynamical systems, including fundamental models of chaos, while also serving as an effective digital twin for prediction and state targeting.   ### 2 Results    ### 2.1 Unsupervised state estimation with rhythmic sharing    ### 2.1.1 Detecting simple state changes We selected the three-dimensional, cyclically symmetric system from Thomas as our initial example because it encompasses a wide array of states that vary based on its internal parameter, λThomas. In our simulation, we start with λThomas set at 0.18, leading to a chaotic trajectory. Suddenly, this is shifted to 0.29, which changes the trajectory to a periodic orbit. We feed this data frame-by-frame into a neural network, where the connection weights and phases of the links are initialized randomly. We then observe the progression of the link phases as the data is introduced into the neural network, as illustrated in Figure 2A. The collective dynamics of these link phases are described by their order parameter R, which ranges from 0 to 1, and the mean phase ⟨Φ⟩, ranging from −π to π. The order parameter R(t) indicates the extent to which the link phases are globally synchronized: R equaling 0 signifies complete decoherence or uniform dispersion of the phases, whereas R equaling 1 denotes full synchronization. We highlight two key observations regarding R(t). First, R stabilizes at a certain equilibrium value whenever the input trajectory aligns with a steady state. For example, R begins at 0 from its initial setting and achieves a stable value of 1 within approximately two cycles of the chaotic state with λThomas set at 0.18, maintaining this value subsequently. This stabilization indicates that the links have discerned the invariant measure beneath the trajectory, even in its chaotic state; essentially, the links have identified an underlying stationary probability distribution that governs the trajectory's temporal evolution. Secondly, a distinctive equilibrium value of R emerges from each state, and consequently, the evolution of R mirrors the progression of λThomas. While the dynamics of the mean phase ⟨Φ⟩(t) are not as straightforward, due to their less direct response to changes in λThomas over time, they will nonetheless play a crucial role in the network’s ability to recall and predict different states, as elaborated in section 2.2. Figure 1 presents a schematic of rhythmic sharing. In part A, we see temporal snapshots illustrating the oscillating strengths of links, demonstrated by variations in their widths. In this scenario, the degree of synchrony, or coordination, between oscillations remains constant, which means the relative phases between links do not change. Part B discusses how oscillating link strengths impact information flow throughout the network. During each timepoint, the present value of the mean phase adjusts which links are dominant, consequently redirecting the flow of information within the network. For instance, the most coherent path from an input node to an output node is shown in purple. Part C illustrates how changes in input modify the subset of active links, thus affecting the coordination among oscillating links. Initially, the link lB is activated by a periodic orbit input, prompting it to synchronize with the mean phase of its connected links (represented by the star), which predominantly remains pink. When the input shifts to represent a chaotic state, links lC and lD become active, synchronizing to their respective mean fields. Consequently, links lC and lD align their synchronization with link lA. Meanwhile, link lB, now inactive, remains unaffected by its mean field.   ### 2.1.2 Sensing continuous parameter changes on systems with memory The progression of a system over time may be intricately linked to its past states. This characteristic is quite prevalent in biological systems, most notably within the immune and nervous systems.12,13 A prime illustration of such behavior is the one-dimensional Mackey-Glass system.14 Within this system, an internal parameter referred to as λMackey, which triggers changes in the system's state, serves as an indicator of the time delay or memory inherent in the system’s dynamics. During our simulations, we adjust this parameter in a sinusoidal pattern. Figure 2B illustrates how the system's connections react to these input data variations. Although the variable R exhibits some instability, presumably due to the inherent complexity of the system and the continuous nature of alterations in the parameter, it nonetheless successfully replicates the progression of λMackey over time.   ### 2.1.3 Detecting warning signs of catastrophic phenomena Ultimately, we examine a system wherein alterations to its internal parameters are not readily visible or quantifiable using current techniques, yet detecting these changes is essential to avert the looming breakdown of the system’s dynamics. The 3D Lorenz system is a well-documented chaotic system that exemplifies this kind of behavior. In this system, the internal parameter denoted as λLorenz is crucial in governing state transformations. When λLorenz is set to 24.5, the system follows a chaotic trajectory. However, if λLorenz is abruptly altered to 23.5, the trajectory shifts to another similar yet temporary chaotic trajectory, eventually collapsing into a dead signal after a random amount of time. Indeed, as depicted in figure 3C, there is a striking resemblance in the spectral properties of these two chaotic trajectories. To discern differences in spectral peaks ranging from 0.1-0.2 Hz, one must observe at least 50-100 cycles within this frequency band. Figure 3C displays the behavior of R(t), illustrating how the connections detected the transitions from the initial chaotic trajectory to the chaotic transient and finally to the dead signal. Meanwhile, figure 2 focuses on rapid detection of dynamic state changes. In part A, a simulated path for the 3D Thomas system, which involves state variables x, y, and z, is shown in orange. The internal parameter λThomas used for this simulation is highlighted in purple. After an initial brief period of transition, R stays around an equilibrium value of 1 throughout the chaotic trajectory. When λThomas is suddenly changed to 0.29, the system transitions from a chaotic state to a periodic pathway, which is immediately sensed by R as it settles to a new equilibrium value. In part B, the same method is applied to the 3D Lorenz system. Although R displays more noise compared to the Thomas system, it converges to a different equilibrium exactly at the moment λLorenz is altered, dropping to another value as the system shifts to a dead signal. Part C describes R for the Mackey-Glass system, where the internal parameter λMackey was modified in a sinusoidal pattern during the simulation. The timeframe taken for R(t) to exit its original range of values and enter a new range linked to the chaotic transient is approximately 100 frames or 11 cycles.   ### 2.2 State transformation and recall by rerouting information flow with rhythmic sharing A prominent aspect of neural networks is their capacity to retain multiple dynamic states. When these states are marked with contextual tokens during training, it becomes possible to recall a particular state by simply entering the corresponding token. However, in the absence of these tokens, recalling specific states is extremely challenging. Although R seems to serve as the needed contextual token, the mean dynamics of the link phases, represented by ⟨Φ⟩, also play a critical role, influencing the 'neural representation' of the input. Therefore, when attempting to retrieve a state, specifying this aspect is critical. Nonetheless, the influence of ⟨Φ⟩ is not immediately apparent from Figure 2, as it does not appear to react to changes in state. To evaluate this, we will examine how variations in R and ⟨Φ⟩ affect the neural output. To generate output from the network, we train it as a reservoir computer (RC), a variant of the recurrent neural network recognized for its effectiveness in forecasting chaotic dynamics.17–20 Training an RC involves identifying the optimal blend of nodes so that their collective output faithfully predicts the subsequent timestep in the input time series. The Thomas system is employed again due to its extensive range of states, making it ideal for illustrating state targeting. In our training of the RC, we use simulated data that alternates between two values of λThomas, aiming to predict the dynamics of each state on its own (fig. 3A). Figure 3 displays the creation of a digital twin for prediction and state targeting: A. It shows training data used for the Thomas system and the response of links characterized by R and ⟨Φ⟩. B. It illustrates real-time, closed-loop predictions of different states by modifying R and ⟨Φ⟩. Predictions include previously unseen states, highlighted with pink boxes in the detailed time series, with positions also depicted in orange in coordinate space. The initial input state, portrayed in light blue, represents the periodic orbit before closed-loop prediction commenced. Various values of R and ⟨Φ⟩ explore different paths through the network. C. It highlights accurate closed-loop predictions of individual states present in the training data, free from interference by other states. The phase portrait (top) aligns closely between the predicted trajectory, which was maintained for over 5000 frames, and the true trajectory. A detailed, time-domain view of the prediction (bottom) emphasizes the precision of the forecast. ‘Start’ marks the initiation of closed-loop prediction. D. It depicts closed-loop time series predictions from a conventional RC, which, having learned all training data as one state, fails to differentiate and predict states independently. Hereafter, we refer to the λThomas of the input or training data as λinput, clarifying that this is the internal parameter of the input trajectory (xinput(t), yinput(t), zinput(t)) fed into the network. Our objective is driven by the premise that if the RC can discreetly learn stationary events through rhythmic sharing, it should also forecast each stationary event continuously without mingling other events encountered during training. State alternations are non-periodic to ensure that results are not due to resonance between the frequency of link oscillations and those of λinput(t). From Fig. 3A, it is observed that, similar to previous instances, R(t) aligns with state changes in the data: λThomas = 0.18 allows for one chaotic state, while λThomas = 0.29 gives rise to two coexisting periodic orbits, resulting in three equilibrium R values. Upon obtaining the optimal output node set, we initiate a closed-loop prediction, where network output (predicting the next frame) becomes the input for predicting the subsequent frame. We stabilize R upon reaching its equilibrium regarding the input state, then proceed with closed-loop prediction. Whilst the closed-loop prediction progresses, we manually adjust ⟨Φ⟩ to observe its impact on output. Fig. 3B presents three instances where ⟨Φ⟩(t) was altered during closed-loop prediction. In the first case, with λinput = λperiodic orbit, ⟨Φ⟩(t) changing discretely results in neuronal outputs representing different states of the Thomas system nearby λperiodic orbit. Many such states point to λThomas values unencountered by the network during training. As each ⟨Φ⟩ value symbolizes a distinct static weight configuration of the network, this effectively enables extraction of various embedded states across diverse information pathways linked to each configuration. In the second scenario, with λinput = λperiodic orbit but ⟨Φ⟩ evolving linearly, it’s clear that λoutput(t) (relating to the output trajectory (xoutput(t), youtput(t), zoutput(t))) aligns with ⟨Φ⟩. This demonstrates that ⟨Φ⟩ can reliably guide neural states to desired trajectories corresponding to several λoutput; thus, accessing different network paths recalls diverse states. These observations hold for a third instance, where λinput = λchaos results in another extrapolation curve near λchaos. Findings reveal that mean-field phase parameters offer predictive insights into how the time series evolves when its state or context shifts in real-time—essentially functioning as a digital twin. Armed with these results, reaching our initial goal becomes feasible: by properly securing R values and ⟨Φ⟩ such that λoutput = λinput, the network can separately forecast each training data state without interference, as showcased in fig. 3C. Although its predictiveness doesn’t match that of an RC refined on individual states, an RC with rhythmic sharing accurately anticipates long-term dynamics for each distinct context or state. In contrast, a standard RC lacking contextual tokens cannot differentiate distinct states in non-stationary training data, treating it as one unified stationary event. This is evident in fig. 3D, where the RC emerged with a trajectory whose λoutput sits between the two distinct λinput values of training data. That it unified events in the training data is clear from its delivery of the same trajectory for both test states.   ### 3 Conclusion Inspired by the interactions between neurons and glial cells in the brain, we devised a learning framework consisting of two primary components: the gradual oscillations of connections and the capacity to alter their coordination. We incorporated this model into an artificial neural network to explore the significance of these mechanisms in neural representation. Within our model, connections swiftly modify their synchronization to determine the current dynamics of the state. In this way, the sync of these connections captures the real-time state of dynamics within the dataset. By autonomously adjusting the rhythms of link strength for various states, the network effectively learns to handle nonstationary dynamics. This is an exceptional capability, as traditional machine learning algorithms are unable to manage such dynamics without manually provided contextual tokens, even though nonstationary dynamics are prevalent in actual data. Our findings reveal that the network is proficient in swiftly detecting unusual events within data and raising alerts for potential upcoming crises. Notably, it achieves this in real time, without the necessity for prior training. The slow rhythms of link strength facilitate the projection of dynamics in numerous unobserved states, and by training the network equipped with rhythmic sharing, we can forecast the stationary dynamics of each state. This feature allows the network to function as a digital twin, adapting its predictions when the physical twin undergoes changes in state. Our application of the algorithm was limited to systems where nonstationarity arises from a single parameter, because changes involving multiple parameters cannot be distinctly separated based solely on the R(t) plot, as it merges all sources of system changes. In the future, one could aim to create a model where various clusters can individually monitor the nonstationary progression of different internal parameters within a system, thus forming small-world networks of connections.   ### 4 Methods    ### 4.1 The input systems    ### 4.1.1 Thomas’ cyclically symmetric system The equations that dictate the behavior of the three-dimensional Thomas system are as follows:11 ˙x = sin(y) − b * x ˙y = sin(z) − b * y ˙z = sin(x) − b * z (1). The system's dynamics are influenced by the parameter b, which acts as a catalyst for bifurcations within the system. In the principal text, this parameter is referred to as λThomas. 6   ### 4.1.2 Mackey-Glass system The normalized version of the one-dimensional Mackey-Glass system is described by the equation: ˙x(t) = β x(t − τ) / (1 + x(t − τ)^n) − γx(t). Here, the precise time dependency of the state variable x is clearly specified. The parameter τ represents the time delay, which is crucial for causing bifurcations in the attractor. This is characterized by the phase space coordinates (x(t), x(t − τ)) and is referred to as the parameter λMackey in the main body of the text. In our setup, we set β to 0.2, γ to 0.1, and n is given a value of 10. Furthermore, τ oscillates sinusoidally, ranging between 20 and 24, with a gradual angular frequency equal to 0.007 during the data simulation process.   ### 4.1.3 Lorenz system The equations that outline the dynamics of the 3D Lorenz system can be expressed as follows: ˙x = σ(y −x), ˙y = x(ρ −z) −y, ˙z = xy −βz (2). Within this framework, the parameter ρ plays a critical role in triggering bifurcations within the system, which is represented as the parameter λLorenz in the primary text. For the purpose of our entire simulation, we have standardized the values of the other parameters, setting σ at 10 and β at 8/3. Meanwhile, ρ is varied suddenly as it is within the Thomas system. When ρ is approximately equal to or exceeds 24.06, the system supports a globally stable strange attractor that exists alongside two stable fixed points. However, the trajectories of the attractor do not reach the basin boundary of these fixed points. Conversely, when ρ falls within the range of approximately 13.93 to 24.06, the behavior of the strange attractor changes, transforming into a chaotic saddle. This saddle continues to coexist with the fixed points, but its trajectories will eventually intersect with the boundary of the saddle after a probabilistic interval. In our simulation, we altered the value of ρ from 24.5 to 23.5. We specifically chose ρ = 23.5 due to its proximity to the bifurcation threshold, which is around ρ ≈24.06. By reducing this difference, we aim to minimize any noticeable alterations in the trajectory as the chaotic attractor evolves into a saddle.   ### 4.2 Rhythmic sharing We describe the dynamics of link interactions using the governing equation as follows:   \[ \frac{d\Phi}{dt} = \omega_0 + (\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 \hat{Q}Tn^*) \circ \sin(\Psi - \Phi + \gamma) \]  Here, \(\circ\) represents the Hadamard product. The vector \(\Phi\) consists of phases \([\varphi_1 \ldots \varphi_{N_l}]^T\) where \(N_l\) denotes the total number of links. The vector \(\omega_0\) embodies the initial natural frequencies designated for these links. Each link is coupled to a vector of local mean fields \(\Psi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_l}\), which is determined by:  \[ r(t) \circ e^{i\Psi(t)} = \hat{A}_\Phi e^{i\Phi(t)} \]  where \(r \in \mathbb{R}^{N_l}\) represents the vector of local order parameters, detailing the degree to which synchronization occurs within each specified local mean field for respective links. Specifically, \(\hat{A}_\Phi{ij} \equiv A_\Phi{ij} / |A_\Phi{i\cdot}|\), with \(A_\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{N_l \times N_l}\) being a random phase adjacency matrix, binary for simplicity, where elements denote connection (1 if links are connected, 0 otherwise). The normalization factor \(|A_\Phi_{i\cdot}|\) is based on the L1 norm of a given row of \(A_\Phi\). A tunable hyperparameter modulates the density of non-zero elements within the \(A_\Phi\) matrix. Importantly, although our focus is on 1:1 synchronization, different synchronization orders such as \(p:q\) (for clusters) can be introduced by altering the argument on the right-hand side of eq. 3, substituting \(\sin(\Psi - \Phi)\) with \(\sin(p \circ \Psi - q \circ \Phi)\). Vectors \(p\) and \(q\) are composed of positive integers with each element \(q_i\), \(p_i\) dictating the intended synchronization order between \(\Phi_i\) and its interacting mean field \(\Psi_i\). However, careful arrangement of \(A_\Phi\) might be necessary to diminish competition among differing synchronization orders among links. The phase-lag vector \(\gamma\) functions similarly to the one in the Sakaguchi-Kuramoto model, facilitating asymmetric communication. The global synchrony across all link phases can be defined via the scalar global order parameter \(R(t) \in [0, 1]\):  \[ R(t)e^{i\langle\Phi\rangle(t)} = \frac{1}{N_l} \sum_{k=1}^{N_l} e^{i\varphi_k(t)} \]  where \(\langle\Phi\rangle(t)\) is the equivalent scalar global mean phase. This definition mirrors that for local mean fields, except that every \(A_\Phi\) element is replaced by 1. The coupling amplitude \(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2 \hat{Q}Tn^*\) captures the causal direction of nodal activity influencing link interactions. Here, elements of the normalized incidence matrix \((\hat{Q}T)_{ij} \equiv (QT)_{ij}/|(QT)_{i\cdot}|\) stem from the incidence matrix \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{N_n \times N_l}\), where the numerator equals 1 for links incident to a node (including self-loops), and 0 otherwise. The norm \(|(QT)_{i\cdot}|\) is the L1 norm of the \(i\)-th row in \(QT\). We adjust node states \(n \in (-1, 1)\) to \(n^* \in (0, 1)\) where \(n^* \equiv (n + 1_{N_n})/2\) (and \(1_{N_n} = (1, 1, \ldots, 1) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_n}\) represents a vector of ones). Notably, inactivity of a \(i\)-th node, \(\inf(n_i) = -1\), equates absence in link interactions, with \(\inf(n^*_i) = 0\). The hyperparameter \(\varepsilon_1\) modulates phase coherence disparity across states, yet should remain zero if \(\varepsilon_2 = 0\); setting otherwise could asymptotically promote or demote global synchronization across the link network. Finally, \(\omega_0\) acts as a hyperparameter denoting slow natural frequencies’ vectors. While values and distributions are not predetermined, we consider a straightforward binary state where a percentage of links share non-zero frequency (\(\omega_0 \ne 0\)), and the remainder hold zero frequencies. The density of links with non-zero frequencies is denoted as \(\Lambda(\omega_0) \in (0, 1]\), another hyperparameter.   The evolution of node states within our recurrent neural network—a reservoir computer, more specifically an echo state network—obeys the following equation:  \[ n(t + \Delta t) = \alpha n(t) + (1 - \alpha) \tanh \left(An(t) + W_{in}u(t) + \xi \right) \]  The activation function \(\tanh[\cdot]\) operates on each independent vector component within its argument. Reference to a node, neuronal, or reservoir state specifically identifies a point within \(n \in (-1, 1)^{N_n}\); other uses of ‘state’ refer explicitly to invariant setups, like attractors. The leakage hyperparameter \(\alpha\) dictates update speed and memory of \(n\), while \(An \in \mathbb{R}^{N_n \times N_n}\) constitutes another random adjacence matrix among nodes, scaled by its spectral radius (a hyperparameter). The input matrix \(W_{in} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_n \times N_u}\) includes elements chosen uniformly from the span \([-δ, δ]\), setting \(\delta\) as the input scaling hyperparameter, with \(u(t) \in N_u\) as input. \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^{N_n}\) serves as a node bias hyperparameter to offset neuronal node activation function. This equation \((6)\) encapsulates non-linearity of each node's activation, equating to other recurrent network updates up to coordinate transformation. Therefore, choosing an echo state-type network won’t compromise generality. Utilizing this network for a reservoir computer involves projecting neuronal states’ latent space onto the original domain through a linear map \( \tilde{u}: \mathbb{R}^{N_n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N_u}\), expressed by:  \[ \tilde{u}(t) = W_{out} n(t) \]  \(\tilde{u}(t + \Delta t)\) anticipates \(u_{data}\) post time step \(\Delta t\), striving to calibrate matrix \(W_{out}\) so \( \tilde{u}(t + \Delta t)\) best estimates \(u(t + \Delta t)\) under selected hyperparameters. For incorporating varying link strengths with constant relative amplitude in the neural network, equation (6) can be altered to involve \(A_n\) presenting a basic oscillating dependence \(\tilde{A}_n(t)\):  \[ \tilde{A}_n(t) \equiv A_n \circ \left(1 - \frac{m}{2} \left(1 + \sin[\Phi(t)]\right)\right) \]  Here, \(m\) quantifies relative link strength alteration during oscillations. This modulation ensures link strength bounds between its original state \(A_{nij}\) and a reduced form \((1-m)A_{nij}\) to limit peak spectral radius, thus protecting the echo state property from unintended disruptions. Finally, the phase matrix \(\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{N_n \times N_n}\) compiles individual link phases into a format matching the adjacency matrix structure:  \[ \Phi(t)_{ij} :=  \begin{cases}  \varphi_{j \to i}, & \text{if } A_{nij} \ne 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } A_{nij} = 0  \end{cases} \]  Consequently, vector \(\Phi\) in Equation (3) is the collection of all non-zero elements from \(\Phi\), arranged as phases \([\varphi_1 \ldots \varphi_{N_l}]^T\) with \(N_l\) representing the cumulative link count, i.e., for any \(j, k \in [1, N_n]\), we can portray \(\varphi_i := \varphi_{j \to k}\) for all index \(i \in [1, N_l]\). We preassume a 1:1 link strength modulation phase and link phase alignment, theoretically leading to synchronized link modulation echoing in neuronal dynamics. This assumption simplifies implementation, yet is empirically supported as chemical oscillations in astrocytes often 1:1 sync with biomechanical oscillations typical in astrocyte hotspots. Although function \(f\) might mirror alternate conversions of astrocytic chemical dynamics to such mechanical waves, our model proceeds in the continuous time threshold \(\Delta t \rightarrow 0\). We simulate our model—including discussed modifications via first-order forward Euler discretization, retaining \(\Delta t\) consistency with Equation (6).   ### 4.2.1 Oscillation death for isolated links In models akin to the Kuramoto framework, each oscillator is independently connected to a selection of other oscillators within the network. Should an oscillator end up not being coupled with any others, its phase will naturally progress according to its intrinsic frequency, denoted as ω0. Nevertheless, we have opted to link each oscillating connection to the average field of its linked oscillators, granting the system the characteristic that any isolated, active link will eventually cease its oscillations if the condition |ω0| < |ε| holds true. To understand the occurrence of oscillation cessation in our model, let's focus on a single oscillator, labeled ϕ (we will omit indices for clarity), that develops without any direct interaction between links: ˙ϕ = ω0 + ε sin(Ψ0 − ϕ) (equation 10), where Ψ0 is the constant atan2(0./0.), a value that is mathematically indeterminate but computationally yields a numeric output due to precision in floating-point representation. Here, ε is defined as ε1 + ε2(QT n ∗)ϕ, representing the force of interaction for this particular oscillator, generally constrained within ε1 ± ε2. For simplicity and to facilitate an analytic solution, ε is considered static as a constant. Through a translation of ϕ → ϕ − Ψ0, equation 10 simplifies to ˙ϕ = ω0 + ε sin(−ϕ) (equation 11). By applying a half-tangent transformation, we can demonstrate the solution as: ϕ(t) = 2 tan−1[εω0 + ∆ ω0 tan(∆2 t + ξ0)] (equation 12), where ∆ ≡ √(ω0^2 − ε^2) and ξ0 ≡ 2 tan−1[-ε/(∆ + (ω0/∆) tan(ϕ0/2))], ϕ0 being the initial phase. It is sufficient to show that if the argument within the tan−1 function achieves a real limit for extensive time periods given a small ω0 (compared to ε, which will generally be approximately one for synchronization), then tan−1 (and thus ϕ) will settle to a real value as t approaches infinity. For |ω0| < |ε0|, both ∆ and ξ0 are entirely imaginary, rendering both the magnitude and the argument of the nested tangent within the expression for ϕ(t) purely imaginary as well. Therefore, ϕ(t) continues as 2 tan−1[a + b tanh(ct + d)], where a, b, c, d are real constants. Since tanh(ct + d) reaches a real limit as t becomes large, ϕ(t) similarly stabilizes to a real limit, indicating a cessation of oscillations. Conversely, if |ω0| > |ε0|, both ∆ and ξ0 are entirely real, causing ϕ(t) to progress as 2 tan−1[a + b tan(ct + d)], reusing a, b, c, d as general real constants. Given that the argument lacks a real limit for large t, the phase ϕ(t) will not stabilize. Thus, the condition for oscillation cessation in isolated links is |ω0| < |ε|.   ### 4.3 Overview of reservoir computing with echo state networks In this section, we offer a concise overview of the procedures involved in conducting training and making predictions using an echo state network.   ### 4.3.1 Training To start, a reservoir undergoes an initiation process referred to as the "warm-up phase," which lasts for τwarm steps, each with a duration of ∆t of the input. Due to the fact that a reservoir computer possesses leaky memory, this phase is crucial as it allows ample time for the reservoir to erase its initial blank slate state, typically marked as n = 0. In this context, the input, represented as u, is set to the training data, which means u(t) = utrain(t). This setup is designed to align n(t) precisely with the dynamics of the input data without introducing any feedback errors. Since this phase’s only purpose is to synchronize the nodes' state space with that of the corresponding data, the reservoir states generated during this phase are discarded and not utilized for training purposes. Once this step concludes, the reservoir progresses into the "training phase" for τtrain steps of ∆t. At this stage, the now-aligned states are again driven by u(t) = utrain(t), but here, every single reservoir state over this period, specifically n(t0 + ∆t), n(t0 + 2∆t), and so on up to n(t0 + τtrain∆t), is meticulously recorded. For simplicity in notation, twarm = τwarm∆t signifies the conclusion of the warm-up phase. By utilizing the concatenated states collected over this period, the optimal output matrix Wout is derived using L2 regression, achieving this by minimizing the expression: arg min Wout [sum from t=twarm+∆t to twarm+τtrain∆t of ||Woutn(t) − utrain(t)||^2 + β tr(WoutWT out)], where β serves as the regularization hyperparameter.   ### 4.3.2 Predicting Armed with the trained Wout, we are prepared to initiate the prediction stage. At this point, a segment of the test data, referred to as utest, is introduced into the reservoir. This reservoir can either be reset to an empty state or can continue from the last state it achieved during the training phase. It undergoes another warm-up period, which is necessary to help it forget the previous state and adjust itself to the new data that it needs to predict. It is important to note that the length of the warm-up period for the test data does not have to match the warm-up period used during the training phase. At the conclusion of this warm-up period, the final frame of the test data, labeled as utest(twarm), is utilized as the starting point for generating the initial prediction, denoted as ˜u(twarm +∆t). Following this, the output from this prediction is recycled as the new input to calculate the reservoir's subsequent state. This forms a closed-loop system that predicts the next timestep. This iterative process is continued until the reservoir has moved forward sufficiently to cover the entire prediction window we desire.   ### 4.3.3 State targeting and prediction by steering (R, ⟨Φ⟩) In our altered architecture, we execute a similar procedure as previously described, but with a small modification to the warm-up phase of the prediction if our goal is to forecast the time series of a singular state, as depicted in Figure 3C. While the network acclimates to the test data, the link connections reset their order parameter to align with the test state. Once the order parameter stabilizes (denoted here as R0), we maintain R by allowing the phases to evolve in any manner dictated by a predetermined vector-valued forcing function g, satisfying the equation ˙Φ(t) = g(Φ, t) for t ≥ tR0. Here, g(Φ, t) = g(t)1Nl with Φ(tR0) = ΦR0 (Equation 14). The function g is scalar-valued, and 1Nl = (1, 1, ..., 1) is a vector of ones, indicating length Nl. ΦR0 represents the phases vector at the initial moment t when R equals R0, referred to as tR0. This setup ensures adherence to the constraint R(t) = R0 for t ≥ tR0, where tR0 precedes twarm, since phase-dependence is absent in the forcing, resulting in a Lyapunov exponent of zero. This means the phases do not diverge over time. We opt for g = Ωt, with Ω equating to ω0, which allows the states to gradually evolve until the desired mean phase, ⟨Φ⟩= ⟨Φ⟩0, is achieved. When ⟨Φ⟩0 is attained, we substitute g = 0 to permanently solidify the 10 links. Determining ⟨Φ⟩0 involves solving ⟨Φ⟩0 = arg min ⟨Φ⟩ h( ˆ Woutn(Φ, t), utest(t)) ∀t ∈ [tR0, tR0 + τ] (Equation 15) for τ > 2π/Ω, ensuring comprehensive sampling of static link strength configurations given R0. The h function is a selected error measurement. We choose the warm-up prediction duration such that all earlier specified targeting of mean-field variables is completed before warm-up ends, i.e., tR0 + τ ≤ τwarm∆t. For the systems employed here, using the root mean square error is logical: h = || ˆ Woutn(Φ, t) − utest(t)||2. However, if the state topology remains stable despite the bifurcation parameter or noise interference, a differently tailored error function may be needed to discern state variations more precisely. To summarize the process, follow these steps: 1. Use Equation 3 to evolve the phase with utest until R reaches R0. 2. For a period τ, replace Equation 3's right side with Equation 14, ensuring R(t) stays at R0 while ⟨Φ⟩ undergoes at least one full rotation during τ. This helps identify the mean phase ⟨Φ⟩0 that incorporates the test state utest using Equation 15. 3. Set g = 0 at this juncture and begin the closed-loop prediction as explained in Section 4.3.2. Remember, all these procedures occur during the warm-up phase when the reservoir operates in an open loop—the reservoir's output does not feed back as input for the next step. Additionally, note that the extrapolation curve in the open-loop phase differs from that in the closed-loop stage. In the former, the network receives a constant input of a single state, acting as an external force that aligns network output to mimic the input state. This restricts the network from extrapolating across a broader range of states near the input. Conversely, in the closed-loop phase, a small deviation at one step can grow in subsequent cycles, allowing the network to transition into the basin of attraction of a state λ, where the difference λ − λinput is pronounced.   ### 4.4 Data availability The dataset utilized by the Thomas system for this particular study is available for access on GitHub. In addition to this, the manuscript contains all the equations and information required for generating the other sets of simulated data.   ### 4.5 Code availability Should anyone be interested in the algorithmic code employed in this study, they can obtain it by reaching out to the corresponding author with a reasonable request. name of paper: A Real-to-Sim-to-Real Approach to Robotic Manipulation with VLM-Generated Iterative Keypoint Rewards
author: gpt-4o
summary: Task specification for robotic manipulation in open-world environments is challenging, requiring flexible and adaptive objectives that align with human intentions and can evolve through iterative feedback. We introduce Iterative Keypoint Reward (IKER), a visually grounded, Python-based reward function that serves as a dynamic task specification. Our framework leverages VLMs to generate and refine these reward functions for multi-step manipulation tasks. Given RGB-D observations and free-form language instructions, we sample keypoints in the scene and generate a reward function conditioned on these keypoints. IKER operates on the spatial relationships between keypoints, leveraging commonsense priors about the desired behaviors, and enabling precise SE(3) control. We reconstruct real-world scenes in simulation and use the generated rewards to train reinforcement learning (RL) policies, which are then deployed into the real world-forming a real-to-sim-to-real loop. Our approach demonstrates notable capabilities across diverse scenarios, including both prehensile and non-prehensile tasks, showcasing multi-step task execution, spontaneous error recovery, and on-the-fly strategy adjustments. The results highlight IKER's effectiveness in enabling robots to perform multi-step tasks in dynamic environments through iterative reward shaping.
