contents: ### Abstract Specifying tasks for robotic manipulation in open-world scenarios presents significant challenges. It requires objectives that are flexible and able to adapt to align with human intentions, evolving through continuous feedback. To address this, we introduce a new approach called Iterative Keypoint Reward (IKER), which is a visually grounded reward function based in Python. This method provides a dynamic way to specify tasks. Our framework makes use of Visual Language Models (VLMs) to create and improve these reward functions for complex, multi-step manipulation tasks. Starting with RGB-D visual data and unconstrained language commands, we identify and sample keypoints in the environment, using them to generate a reward function that depends on these keypoints. IKER focuses on the spatial relations between keypoints, incorporating commonsense priors about expected behaviors to facilitate accurate SE(3) control. We recreate real-world environments in simulations. With the generated rewards, we train reinforcement learning (RL) policies that are subsequently tested in the real world, completing a real-to-simulation-to-real world loop. Our method demonstrates impressive capabilities across a range of scenarios, including tasks that require both holding and manipulation without grasping. It shows effective completion of multi-step procedures, immediate error correction, and the ability to adapt strategies in real-time. The results underscore the efficacy of IKER in empowering robots to carry out complex, multi-step tasks in dynamic settings through iterative refinement of reward structures. To learn more, please visit our project page: https://iker-robot.github.io/.   ### I. INTRODUCTION Imagine a scenario where a robot is assigned the task of placing a pair of shoes neatly on a rack, but finds itself dealing with an obstacle—a shoe box taking up space on that same rack (refer to Figure 1, top right). Before it can position the shoes, the robot must first relocate the box to make room. This scenario underscores the significance of task specification for robots operating in real-world, unstructured settings, where tasks often require multiple, unstated actions. In cases like this, rigid, pre-programmed instructions do not suffice to navigate the complex interactions necessary to achieve the task. For robots to be effective, task specifications should incorporate commonsense knowledge—or priors—that guide the robot's actions. For example, instead of attempting to awkwardly fit the shoes into the small remaining space, the robot should intuitively clear the area first. Recent advancements in vision-language models (VLMs) are promising for developing flexible task specifications in robotics. This promise is largely attributed to their improved capabilities in encoding extensive world knowledge, derived from training on vast, varied datasets [1–8]. VLMs excel at interpreting intricate instructions and natural language descriptions, creating a bridge between human expectations and robotic behavior, and capturing sophisticated human-like reasoning and problem-solving tactics. However, prior studies utilizing VLMs in robotics show two primary shortcomings: (1) they struggle with specifying exact targets in three-dimensional space, and occasionally (2) they find it difficult to adapt to changes in the task environment as work progresses. In our research, we present the Iterative Keypoint Reward (IKER), a visually grounded reward function designed for robotic manipulation to overcome these shortcomings. Drawing inspiration from recent findings [9], we recognize that both the positions and orientations of objects can be effectively encoded via keypoints. This allows IKER to enable precise manipulation in 3D spaces, thus supporting complex tasks that demand exact control over location and orientation. Furthermore, IKER introduces an iterative refinement process, in which the VLM updates task specifications by incorporating feedback from the robot's interactions with its environment. This mechanism facilitates dynamically adaptable strategies and intermediate operations, such as object repositioning to enhance grip. Despite VLMs' proficiency in processing visual data from the real world, training robotic policies directly in such environments is often impractical, due to constraints related to safety, scalability, and efficiency. To navigate these challenges, our approach first derives IKER from real-world observation, transfers the scenes and corresponding rewards to a simulation for training, and eventually deploys the optimized policy back into the actual environment. This method establishes a real-to-simulation-to-real loop. We illustrate the success of our real-to-sim-to-real framework with IKER through various scenarios involving commonplace objects like shoes and books. These scenarios range from prehensile tasks, such as accurately placing shoes on racks, to non-prehensile ones, like methodically sliding books to specific locations. Comprehensive evaluations—both quantitative and qualitative—are conducted to determine the system's capacity to autonomously perform intricate, long-horizon tasks. The results reveal human-like capabilities within the system, showcasing its aptitude for executing multi-step actions, recovering from errors effortlessly, and adjusting strategies flexibly in response to environmental changes.   ### II. RELATED WORK VLMs in Robotics. In the field of robotics, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have established themselves as an important tool, as evidenced by research [10–38]. The body of work focusing on VLMs in robotics is largely centered around two primary areas: task specification [10–12, 15, 16, 21] and low-level control [11, 13, 14, 39]. Our research aligns closely with the task specification domain, emphasizing the flexibility and adaptability necessary for operating in complex, real-world environments. In terms of task specification, numerous studies utilize VLMs to decompose intricate tasks into more manageable subtasks, effectively acting as a bridge between high-level instructions and robotic actions. For instance, Huang et al. [40] have shown how Large Language Models (LLMs) can function as zero-shot planners, breaking down tasks into actionable steps. Similarly, Ahn et al. [10] leverage VLMs to parse and sequence long-horizon tasks into steps that robots can execute. Moreover, Belkhale et al. [41] introduce the concept of "language motions" that serve as middle steps connecting high-level directives with specific robotic actions, allowing the capture of reusable, low-level behaviors. Our unique approach, however, centers on the flexible interpretation of tasks in dynamically changing environments. Beyond mere task decomposition, VLMs have found application in generating affordances and value maps that direct robotic actions. Huang et al. [12] apply VLMs to produce 3D affordance maps, endowing robots with spatial knowledge on which parts of their surroundings are suitable for interaction. Liu et al. [15] make use of VLMs to predict point-based affordances, facilitating zero-shot manipulation tasks. Zhao et al. [42], on the other hand, incorporate VLMs into model predictive control, where models forecast the outcomes of potential actions to guide optimal decision-making. Such work illustrates the potential of VLMs to link high-level task comprehension with the spatial and functional insights essential for robotic control. Similar to our method, Huang et al. [9] utilize keypoints and establish relationships and constraints among them for carrying out manipulation tasks, though their approach is executed in an open-loop manner. In contrast, our method employs a closed-loop system that allows dynamic adaptions of plans. Furthermore, our approach accommodates non-prehensile manipulations, like pushing. Other studies have explored the use of VLMs for generating reward functions [43–46]. Nevertheless, these methods often fall short of real-world applicability. Some lack demonstrations on actual robots [44], others are confined to a single real-world scenario [46], or focus on narrowly defined tasks such as a robotic dog walking on a ball [45]. In contrast, our work highlights the versatility and robustness of VLM-generated rewards across multiple real-world manipulation tasks. Algorithm 1 IKER Execution Framework 1: Input: Language instruction I 2: Initialize: done ← false, execution history ← [ ], i ← 1 3: Generate 3D models of objects 4: while true do 5: ({k(i) j } Ki j=1, Oi) ← GetKeypoints(3D models) 6: code ← QueryVLM(Oi, execution history) 7: (done, {ktarget(i) j } Ki j=1) ← Execute(code) 8: if done is true then 9: break 10: end if 11: si ← TransferSceneToSimulation(3D models) 12: πi ← LearnPolicy(si, {ktarget(i) j } Ki j=1) 13: ExecutePolicyInRealWorld(πi) 14: Append (Oi, code) to execution history 15: i ← i + 1 16: end while Real-to-Sim and Sim-to-Real. The concept of real-to-simulation (real-to-sim) has gained considerable attention owing to its role in facilitating agent training. By transferring a scene to simulation, it can be utilized for a variety of tasks including reinforcement learning (RL). Several methods focus on reconstructing rigid bodies for simulation purposes [47–53]. For instance, Kappler et al. [47] propose a method for reconstructing rigid objects to aid in grasping. Other works delve into reconstructing articulated objects [54–61]. Huang et al. [62] introduce strategies for reconstructing the occluded shapes of articulated objects, while Jiang et al. [55] present a framework called DITTO, designed to create digital twins of articulated objects based on real-world interactions. Our work employs the fast, state-of-the-art BundleSDF method [63] to create object meshes that are then introduced to the simulation. The sim-to-real transfer has displayed impressive performance across a spectrum of skills, such as tabletop manipulation [64, 65], mobile manipulation [66, 67], dynamic manipulation [68], dexterous manipulation [69–72], and locomotion [73, 74]. However, merely deploying trained policies directly onto physical robots frequently results in performance issues due to the sim-to-real gap. To address this gap, researchers have developed various techniques, including system identification [75–77], domain adaptation [78–82], and domain randomization [73, 83, 84, 84–88]. Our approach utilizes domain randomization, as it doesn't require any real-world interaction data during training. Instead, it relies exclusively on simulation, rendering the policies robust by exposing them to a diverse array of randomized conditions. Recently, Torne et al. [89] introduced RialTo, a full-loop real-to-sim-to-real system aimed at leveraging simulation to enhance imitation learning policies trained through real-world gathered demonstrations. In contrast to that, we concentrate on executing long-horizon tasks by training exclusively in simulation, thereby bypassing the necessity for demonstrations altogether.   ### III. METHOD In this section, we dive into the formal definition of Iterative Keypoint Reward (IKER) and delve into the process by which it is automatically crafted and honed by Vision-Language Models (VLMs), continuously incorporating feedback from the environment. Following this, our comprehensive framework, which employs IKER within a real-to-sim-to-real cycle, will be explained. Our method is visually summarized in Figure 2, where you will find detailed procedural steps outlined in Algorithm 1.   The Iterative Keypoint Reward Generation process involves several critical stages: Real2Sim Reconstruction, Sim2Real Deployment, and Reinforcement Learning (RL) Training, as indicated in Fig. 2: Framework Overview. The IKER concept rests on the idea of a visually grounded reward, produced by VLMs as a means of task specification. In this setup, the real-world scenario is reconstructed within a simulation environment. Subsequently, the reward created is utilized for the training of RL policies, which are then applied back to real-world scenarios.  As depicted in Fig. 2 — Framework Overview, the process begins with Real2Sim Reconstruction, which leads into Sim2Real Deployment and culminates in RL Training. This iterative process revolves around the core principle whereby the Iterative Keypoint Reward is intricately generated by VLMs from visual task specifications. It entails reconstructing the real-world context within a simulated environment. The crafted reward is then instrumental in training reinforcement learning policies, which operators can effectively implement in physical scenarios.  To illustrate the Iterative Keypoint Reward Generation in more detail, refer to Fig. 3. In the initial phase, mentioned as the first step in Figure 2, keypoints within the scene are identified. These keypoints, alongside a directive from a human and a record of execution history, are processed by a VLM to produce a code that links these keypoints to a reward function. There is an even more detailed portrayal of these keypoints and the ensuing code in Figure 7.   ### A. Iterative Keypoint Reward (IKER) Provided with an RGB-D view of the environment and an open-vocabulary language instruction I for a multi-step task, our objective is to develop a series of policies, denoted as πN i=1, to effectively complete the specified task. Importantly, there is no preset limit to the number of policies N, which gives the robot flexibility in its approach to the task. To illustrate, consider the example in Fig. 3: the initial policy, represented by π1, involves moving a shoe box to open up space, while the subsequent policies are responsible for positioning each shoe accordingly. For every step i, the RGB observation is labeled as Oi. We assume the presence of a set of Ki keypoints {k(i) j }Ki j=1, which we will describe further in Sec. III-B, each indicating a 3D position within the task space. By utilizing these keypoints, our aim is to autonomously generate a reward function, named IKER, that translates the positions of keypoints into a scalar reward function f (i) : RKi×3 →R. The formulation of the reward function f (i) relies on a Vision-Language Model (VLM), specifically GPT-4o [1] in this instance, which receives the following context: (1) the provided human instruction I outlining the task, (2) the current RGB observation Oi, which has keypoints marked with numerical labels, and (3) the sequence of past observations and reward functions up to the point of step i−1, namely {O1, f (1), . . . , Oi−1, f (i−1)}. The VLM is further influenced by a prompt that instructs it to develop a Python function for the reward f (i). This prompt guides the VLM to deconstruct the task into executable steps, forecast which object should be engaged with, define the movement of objects by determining where their keypoints ought to be placed concerning other keypoints, and conduct arithmetic operations on these keypoints to project their final positions. It is worth noting that we do not explicitly designate which keypoint pertains to which object, leaving it to the VLM to deduce this information. The prompt also requires the VLM to format all outputs in a specified code format and to set the flag done = True if the task is accomplished. Through code prediction, the VLM can execute any required calculations on the current keypoint positions, which would not be feasible if restricted to mere textual descriptions. Appendix C contains the comprehensive prompt, and Figure 7 provides a meticulous walkthrough of RGB observations and the crafted reward functions relevant to the example shown in Figure 3. By executing the generated code to obtain the ultimate keypoint positions, we calculate a scalar reward to assess the policy's effectiveness. The reward function, f (i), aids learning by integrating these elements: • Gripper-to-object Distance Reward (rdist): Inspires the robot to close the gap with the object of interest by penalizing significant distances. • Direction Reward (rdir): Steers the robot to direct the keypoints toward the targeted locations. • Alignment Reward (ralign): Prompts the robot to place the keypoints near their designated target locations. • Success Bonus (rbonus): Dispenses an extra reward when the average distance between the keypoints and their intended positions stays within a predetermined threshold over specific timesteps, signifying successful task completion. • Penalty Term (rpenalty): Imposes penalties for unfavorable actions like excessive movements, dropping objects, or applying substantial force. The reward function f (i) is expressed as f (i) = αdistrdist + αdirrdir + αalignralign + αbonusrbonus + αpenaltyrpenalty.   ### B. Transferring real-world scene to simulation To transition a real-world scene within a workspace boundary into a digital simulation, we initially create 3D meshes for the manipulable objects, like the shoe box and shoes depicted in Figure 3. This is done by capturing video footage of each item while moving them around, ensuring that the camera records all sides. These videos enable precise 3D mesh reconstruction through the use of BundleSDF [63], and multiple objects can be scanned simultaneously, which significantly accelerates the scanning process. Once an object’s mesh is created, it can be reused in various contexts, eliminating the need to recreate it for every new scenario. With the meshes developed, we employ FoundationPose [90] to estimate the positions of the objects, allowing for exact placement of the corresponding meshes within the simulated environment. For static components, such as the workspace table and shoe rack illustrated in Figure 3, a point cloud is captured to construct their meshes for simulation usage. These generated meshes are further utilized to determine potential keypoints. For movable items like shoes or books, keypoints are placed at the object’s extremities along its axes, defined relative to the object’s center and independent of human instructions. For static items such as shoe racks that are part of the environment, keypoints are evenly distributed across their surfaces. Numerical labels assigned to the keypoints are grouped by object. As demonstrated in Figure 7, for instance, keypoints 1–4 are related to the box, 5–8 to the left shoe, 9–12 to the right shoe, and the remaining keypoints pertain to the rack. Keypoints that are too close together in the projected image are omitted. Specifically, background keypoints (e.g., those of the rack) that are near object keypoints are removed initially. Among overlapping object keypoints, only the one carrying the lower numerical label is preserved. It’s worth mentioning that the VLM is not explicitly informed of this information but instead has to deduce the relationship between the keypoints and the objects based on the input image.   ### C. Policy Training in Simulation We oversee the robot's movements within the end-effector space, which encompasses six degrees of freedom. This includes three prismatic joints enabling movement along the x, y, and z axes, and three revolute joints responsible for rotation. The fingers of the gripper typically remain closed, only opening when needed to grasp objects. For an in-depth explanation on grasping mechanisms, please consult Appendix A. State Space: Our policy's state space efficiently encapsulates the vital information necessary for task execution. The input is a vector, denoted as st, which includes the pose of the gripper’s end-effector (pe, qe) within R7, the pose of the object being manipulated at any given moment (po, qo) also in R7, a series of keypoints for the object Ko = {k(i) j }Ki j=1 ∈ RKi×3, and their corresponding target positions Kt = {k(i) tj }Ki j=1 ∈ RKi×3. The keypoints Ko are computed by applying rigid body transformations to the object's keypoints defined in its local coordinate frame, which are then mapped to their positions in the global frame. Kt is derived from the reward function f (i) determined by the VLM. Rotations are represented using quaternions for qe and qo. This state space, st = (pe, qe, po, qo, Ko, Kt), effectively encapsulates essential details about relevant objects and the policy's goal. Rather than directly incorporating raw RGBD data into the state space, we extract object poses and keypoints from RGBD inputs using a vision-based pose estimation method, which is thoroughly examined in Section III-D. This preprocessing eliminates the need to include raw RGBD data in the policy. Action Space: We define the action space in relation to the gripper’s existing position and orientation. Our policy outputs actions, denoted as at = (∆pe, ∆re), where ∆pe ∈ R3 and ∆re ∈ R3 correspond to changes in translation and rotation, respectively. Training Algorithm & Architecture: Policies are trained using the IsaacGym [91] simulator, paired with the PPO [92] algorithm. An actor-critic architecture [93] with a shared backbone forms the basis of the network. It features a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) comprising hidden layers of 256, 128, and 64 units, with each layer followed by ELU [94] activations. Currently, each task requires approximately 5 minutes for training, which can pose challenges for some applications. However, this training duration can be diminished by boosting the number of parallel environments and employing more robust GPUs. Domain Randomization (DR): To tackle the difficulties associated with transferring policies from simulation to the real world, we employ DR as a means to plug the sim-to-real gaps. DR is applied to various object properties, such as friction, mass, restitution, compliance, and geometry. Moreover, we randomize the object's position, the gripper’s location, and the grasp within specified ranges. These factors are particularly crucial for tasks involving non-prehensile actions like pushing. Detailed parameter ranges are provided in Appendix B, with an evaluation of DR's efficacy presented in Section IV-E.   ### D. Deployment of Trained Policy The reinforcement learning policy, denoted as πi, is directly implemented in real-world scenarios. Since this policy determines the end-effector's pose, we apply inverse kinematics in order to calculate the joint angles at each timestep effectively. Operating at a frequency of 10Hz, the RL policy generates action commands which are then adjusted to ensure the end effector stays within the established workspace limits. For tracking keypoints, we make use of FoundationPose [90], which is instrumental in estimating the pose of the object. These pose predictions are then employed to ascertain the locations of keypoints, which are set in relation to the objects themselves. When the Vision-Language Model (VLM) forecasts an object grasp, AnyGrasp [95] is employed to identify grasping positions in real-world situations.   ### IV. EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS Our objective is to explore the capacity of Iterative Keypoint Reward to accurately depict reward functions applicable to a broad array of manipulation skills in the context of our IKER pipeline, designed for real-to-sim-to-real transfer. Additionally, we seek to determine whether this pipeline can manage multi-step tasks within dynamic environments by utilizing Iterative Keypoint Reward as a form of feedback to assist in replanning processes.   ### A. Experimental Setup, Metrics and Baselines Figure 4 presents the experimental setup and the objects involved in our study. We conduct all our experiments using the XArm7 robotic arm. Our configuration includes four stationary cameras along with one camera mounted on the wrist. For tasks involving shoes, we experiment with five pairs of shoes and two shoe racks. Additionally, for stowing tasks, we utilize nine different books. Task results are organized by whether they were obtained with human-labeled rewards or automatically through Visual Language Model (VLM) generated rewards, both in simulation and the real world: using our IKER method and traditional pose-based approach.   For the Shoe Place task, the results show an efficiency of 0.945 for our method in simulation and 0.938 in real-world configurations, significantly higher compared to the 0.8 and 0.9 success rates of the traditional pose approach. The Shoe Push task yielded results of 0.871 and 0.850 for our approach in simulation and real-world, while the conventional method achieved 0.7 in both. For the Stowing Push, our method scored 0.901 in simulation and 0.914 in real-world, while the pose-based approach showed 0.8 in simulation and 0.7 in the real-world test. Finally, for Stowing Reorient, our approach achieved 0.848 in simulation and 0.859 in real-world scenarios, greatly surpassing the conventional method, which scored 0.8 and 0.7, respectively. Table I summarizes the performance of the IKER method in both simulation and the real-world.  IKER, which leverages visual keypoints, shows significantly improved performance over conventional pose-based methods, notably when using VLMs to generate reward functions automatically. Our experiments conducted with the XArm7 integrated with four stationary RealSense cameras, showcase the setup and the objects in use as seen in Figure 4. These cameras gather point clouds that help build the simulation environment and supply data for AnyGrasp to predict grasp actions. Besides, a wrist-mounted camera is included to capture images that are essential for querying the VLM.   As a baseline comparison, we employed an annotated version of the IKER system using human-labeled reward functions to allow assessments free from VLM impact. We juxtaposed our keypoint-based method with a pose-based baseline, where reward functions are traditionally crafted in reinforcement learning [71, 96–99]. This pose-based method involves the VLM generating a function f that links the initial object poses, defined by xyz coordinates and RPY angles, to their final target poses. Details of the baseline prompt are detailed in Section C.  We evaluated our approach across four key scenarios, shown in Figure 1 (left): these include Shoe Place, Shoe Push, Book Push, and Book Reorient. In the Shoe Place scenario, the robot picks up a shoe from the floor and places it on a rack. In Shoe Push, it maneuvers a shoe towards another to form an aligned pair. In the Book Push task, the robot pushes a book to align with another or towards the table's edge. Lastly, in the Book Reorient task, it adjusts a book's position on a shelf. Each of these scenarios consists of 10 start/end configurations.   In simulated environments, success rates are calculated across 128 randomized environments for each start/end configuration, totaling 1280 trials per scenario. Real-world success is directly assessed on the 10 start/end configurations. In both realms, a trial is deemed successful if the average distance of key points to the target points is within 5 centimeters.   ### B. Policy Training with IKER for Single-Step Tasks We carried out a series of experiments to compare reinforcement learning (RL) training utilizing keypoints against object pose in reward functions. The scope of our experiments covers four significant tasks, as outlined in Table I. Within the annotated method framework, the success rates for shoe placement utilizing IKER and object pose are 0.945 and 0.938, respectively. A comparable pattern emerges in tasks such as shoe push, stowing push, and reorient, where performance differences are negligible. These findings highlight that when target locations are specified through human annotations, both keypoints and object poses proficiently capture those targets and serve as effective strategies for RL policy training.   Conversely, in the automatic method, IKER demonstrates substantially improved performance over object pose representations. For instance, in shoe placement, IKER achieves a 0.7 success rate, whereas object poses manage only 0.3. Comparable outcomes are observed across other tasks. The success of object pose is restricted to elementary scenarios devoid of orientation alterations, since VLMs encounter challenges with rotations within the SO(3) space. By contrast, keypoints reduce complexity by restricting VLM reasoning to Cartesian space, thereby eliminating the requirement for handling object poses within the SE(3) space. Table I also highlights a slight decline in success rate transitioning from simulation to the real-world scenario. In particular, for shoe placement, IKER’s success drops from 0.945 in simulation to 0.8 in reality. For the shoe push task, the success rate decreases from 0.871 to 0.850.   These results imply that the domain randomization noted in Section III-C assists the model in generalizing to real-world contexts, though real-world performance is still impacted by factors like inaccuracies in environment reconstruction, perception errors, and difficulties in simulating extreme object dynamics. A significant portion of failures within our framework arises from discrepancies between heuristic grasps used in simulation and those generated by AnyGrasp in reality, along with erroneous VLM predictions. Regarding incorrect VLM predictions, the model may mistakenly choose the wrong keypoints or fail to leverage all available keypoints on an object when assessing its relationship to another object. For example, if an object presents four keypoints, the VLM might utilize only one, resulting in poorly aligned placement. These problems can be mitigated by providing additional in-context examples when querying the VLMs. These challenges may diminish further with the integration of advancements such as [100], which improve the spatial reasoning abilities of VLMs. Additionally, some failures stem from the physical dynamics encountered during the pushing of objects. These issues can be somewhat alleviated by precisely estimating dynamic parameters during the transfer from real to simulation environments.   ### C. Iterative Replanning for Multi-Step Tasks We illustrate the robot's ability for iterative chaining through a sequence of three crucial actions: initially pushing a shoe box to create enough space, followed by placing a pair of shoes onto a rack. A failure in one step inevitably leads to a failure in the subsequent step. To evaluate this process, we experiment with 10 different initial and final configurations, thoroughly iterating through each scenario to gauge overall effectiveness. Our approach is compared with VoxPoser [12], which utilizes large language models (LLMs) to generate code responsible for creating potential fields that aid in motion planning. VoxPoser is an excellent baseline due to its capacity to generate motion plans for a range of manipulation tasks based on free-form language commands. However, it is important to note that VoxPoser plans are open-loop, meaning they lack the feedback mechanism essential for adjusting to disturbances: adjusting plan robustness, proposing new plans, and ultimately achieving the desired objective. For example, the human directive "Place shoes on rack" results in the placement of the right shoe on the rack, followed by the left shoe—although slightly misplaced at first—which is then readjusted to complete the task successfully. Another scenario involves the human instructing to "Stow book to shelf," where the initial attempt to grasp the book fails, necessitating a replanning of the action to complete the task. These scenarios, depicted in Fig. 5, showcase the capabilities of our framework, which remains resilient to disturbances and is able to adapt to unexpected events, even suggesting new plans when the original ones become infeasible. Fig. 6 provides a comparison of multi-step task chaining with VoxPoser. Our proposed framework consistently outperforms VoxPoser at each phase of the task sequence, refining specifications at each step. To tailor VoxPoser to suit our tasks, we made two significant adjustments: (1) VoxPoser originally utilized OWL-ViT [101] to detect object bounding boxes, but faced challenges in differentiating between left and right shoes, prompting us to provide precise ground-truth object locations. (2) We also furnished VoxPoser with the full plan since the initial version struggled with multi-step tasks. This gave VoxPoser an advantage over our method by providing access to privileged information. Figure 6 illustrates the results of iterative chaining. Across the three tasks, our method persistently performed better than VoxPoser. In the first task, we achieved success in 8 out of 10 attempts, compared to VoxPoser's 5 successes. During the second task, we recorded 5 successes while VoxPoser only managed 1. In the final task, our method succeeded on 4 occasions, whereas VoxPoser failed every time. The failures of VoxPoser can be attributed to several factors, such as pushing the shoe box either excessively far or insufficiently. Additionally, its grasping technique is overly simplistic, relying on a heuristic that places the robot’s end effector near the object center prior to closing the gripper, which frequently leads to grasp failures. VoxPoser also faces challenges with collisions during object manipulation, as it lacks consideration for environmental obstacles. Furthermore, incorrect shoe placements—like stacking one shoe atop the other, leading to them falling—highlight its inherent limitations.   ### D. Robustness, Adjusting Plans, and Re-Planning Unlike earlier approaches that depend on open-loop planning, our method utilizes closed-loop plans, allowing for real-time adjustments during task execution. This capability unlocks a range of functions, as illustrated in Figure 5. In the first scenario, while the robot is placing shoes on the floor, it is interrupted by a human. The framework shows its robustness by swiftly recovering from this interruption. The robot re-grasps the shoe and accomplishes the task by successfully placing both shoes on the rack. In another scenario, as the robot attempts to position the left shoe, it notices that the shoe is not sufficiently close to the right shoe. To resolve this issue, the VLM suggests a remedial action, instructing the robot to nudge the left shoe so that it aligns properly next to the right shoe, forming a correct pair. In the final scenario, the robot is assigned the task of storing a book on a shelf. Unfortunately, the initial grasping attempt fails due to the book's size rendering it too large to hold. The VLM then predicts an alternative approach, adapting the strategy to ensure the successful placement of the book.   ### E. Effect of Domain Randomization We detail the outcomes of implementing our framework both with and without Domain Randomization (DR) for the tasks of shoe placement and pushing. The performance metrics presented are averaged over ten separate trials. In the simulation setting, when DR is not utilized, the performance stands at 0.964. However, incorporating DR results in a slightly decreased performance level of 0.945. This indicates that in a solitary and controlled environment, the policy tends to perform more efficiently without DR. Contrastingly, in real-world applications, the performance without DR significantly declines to 0.6. When DR is applied, the performance improves to 0.8, underscoring the utility of DR in diverse real-world scenarios. As shown in Table II, the specific outcomes are as follows: for the place task, simulation performance without DR is 0.964 and in real-world conditions, it drops to 0.5. With the DR methodology, these metrics are 0.945 for simulation and 0.8 for real-world application. For the push task, the simulation performance without using DR stands at 0.923, declining to 0.2 in a real-world setting. Utilizing DR, the performance for the same task is 0.871 in simulation and increases to 0.7 in real-world settings. DR, while it may slightly reduce simulation performance, markedly enhances the task's performance in real-world applications across various situations. For the placement task without DR, it is evident that the policy exhibits less robustness to the discrepancies between simulation and real-world execution, often resulting in collisions with the shoe rack during transportation of objects. Furthermore, failures also tend to occur immediately post object pickup, possibly due to variations in pose estimation. The pushing task presents even more significant challenges: without DR, the success rate plummets to 0.2, while it surges to 0.7 with DR. Without DR, the policy has a tendency to inaccurately handle the shoe, either pinching it too aggressively or misaligning it during the push action. These insights collectively underscore the crucial role of DR in ensuring dependable performance in real-world conditions.   ### V. CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS In this study, we presented the Iterative Keypoint Reward (IKER), a framework designed to utilize Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in crafting visually grounded reward functions for the manipulation of robots in open-world settings. By incorporating keypoints derived from RGB-D observations, our approach allows for precise SE(3) control and seamlessly incorporates VLM-based priors without the need for rigidly structured instructions. IKER effectively connects simulation and real-world execution through a real-to-sim-to-real loop, facilitating the training of policies within simulation which are then deployed in physical scenarios. Through experiments conducted on a variety of tasks, the framework has shown its capability to tackle complex, long-term challenges by employing adaptive strategies while also allowing for error rectification. This research constitutes a progression towards more intelligent and adaptable robots that can function effectively in dynamic, real-world environments. Although these advancements are significant, our methodology has certain limitations. For instance, in order to obtain object meshes, we are required to capture objects from all possible angles. However, future developments might alleviate this requirement by using methods such as those referenced in [52], which are capable of generating meshes from a singular image. Additionally, our real-to-sim transfer does not consider dynamics parameters, which could potentially be modeled with greater precision using system identification techniques. Furthermore, while our framework successfully reconstructs multiple objects within the environment, we have not factored in tasks that require complex multi-object interactions, which results in our evaluations predominantly focusing on single-object manipulation at various stages.   ### VI. name of paper: SwiftSketch: A Diffusion Model for Image-to-Vector Sketch Generation
author: gpt-4o
summary: Recent advancements in large vision-language models have enabled highly expressive and diverse vector sketch generation. However, state-of-the-art methods rely on a time-consuming optimization process involving repeated feedback from a pretrained model to determine stroke placement. Consequently, despite producing impressive sketches, these methods are limited in practical applications. In this work, we introduce SwiftSketch, a diffusion model for image-conditioned vector sketch generation that can produce high-quality sketches in less than a second. SwiftSketch operates by progressively denoising stroke control points sampled from a Gaussian distribution. Its transformer-decoder architecture is designed to effectively handle the discrete nature of vector representation and capture the inherent global dependencies between strokes. To train SwiftSketch, we construct a synthetic dataset of image-sketch pairs, addressing the limitations of existing sketch datasets, which are often created by non-artists and lack professional quality. For generating these synthetic sketches, we introduce ControlSketch, a method that enhances SDS-based techniques by incorporating precise spatial control through a depth-aware ControlNet. We demonstrate that SwiftSketch generalizes across diverse concepts, efficiently producing sketches that combine high fidelity with a natural and visually appealing style.

contents: ### Abstract Recent progress in large vision-language models has paved the way for generating highly expressive and varied vector sketches. Current leading techniques, however, depend on a lengthy optimization process that requires repeated feedback from a pretrained model to decide where strokes should be placed. As a result, even though these methods produce remarkable sketches, their utility in practical situations remains limited. In our study, we present SwiftSketch, a diffusion model designed for image-conditioned vector sketch generation that achieves high-quality sketch outputs in under a second. This model functions by gradually removing noise from stroke control points initially sampled from a Gaussian distribution. The transformer-decoder architecture of SwiftSketch is specifically crafted to adeptly manage the discrete nature of vector representation while capturing the essential global dependencies that exist between strokes. For training SwiftSketch, we have compiled a synthetic dataset of image-sketch pairs, overcoming the drawbacks of current sketch datasets, which often lack professional quality and are typically produced by non-artists. To create these synthetic sketches, we introduce ControlSketch, a method that enhances techniques based on SDS by incorporating precise spatial control through a depth-aware ControlNet. We provide evidence that SwiftSketch can generalize across a wide array of concepts, efficiently generating sketches that merge high fidelity with a naturally appealing visual style.   ### 1. Introduction Over the last few years, numerous studies have delved into generating sketches from images, addressing both scene-level and object-level sketching challenges [6, 46, 47, 55]. This process involves converting an input image into a line drawing that effectively encapsulates its essential characteristics, such as structure, contours, and overall visual impression. These sketches can be manifested either as pixel images or as vector graphics, with vector graphics often favored due to their resolution independence, improved editability, and capacity to capture the sequential and abstract nature of sketches. Current methods for generating vector sketches frequently involve training a network to learn the distribution of human-drawn sketches [56]. Nevertheless, assembling datasets of human-drawn sketches is a laborious endeavor, and contributors recruited via crowdsourcing often do not possess artistic proficiency. This situation results in datasets predominantly filled with amateur-style sketches (refer to Fig. 2, left). Conversely, datasets crafted by professional designers or artists tend to be limited in size, typically containing just a few hundred examples, and they are often constrained to particular domains like portraits or product design (refer to Fig. 2, right). Consequently, existing data-driven methods for sketch generation are often confined to specific areas or reflect the amateur style prevalent in the training data. Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [57] have given rise to new methodologies within the sketch domain. These methods have shifted sketch generation from a dependency on datasets drawn by humans to utilizing the priors of pretrained models [11, 46, 47, 54]. Such techniques produce sketches that are professional in appearance by optimizing parametric curves to represent an input concept, guided by the pretrained VLM. However, these techniques face a significant challenge: the generation process is heavily reliant on repeated feedback (backpropagation) from the pretrained model, which is inherently time-intensive. It often takes several minutes or sometimes more than an hour to create a single sketch. This limitation renders these methods impractical for interactive applications or for generating sketch data on a large scale. In response, we present SwiftSketch, a diffusion-based method for object sketching that is capable of creating high-quality vector sketches in less than a second per sketch. SwiftSketch is versatile, able to generalize across a broad array of concepts while maintaining high fidelity to the input image, as illustrated in Figure 1. Drawing inspiration from the latest developments in diffusion models for data that is not pixel-based [29, 43, 44], we train a diffusion model that learns to map a Gaussian distribution in stroke coordinate space to the data distribution (see Figure 1, top). To tackle the discrete nature of vector graphics and the complex global topological relationships among shapes, we implement a transformer-decoder architecture that includes self- and cross-attention layers, which are trained to accurately reconstruct ground truth sketches in both vector and pixel spaces. The integration of the image condition into the generation process occurs via the cross-attention mechanism, where meaningful features are initially extracted from the input image with the help of a pretrained CLIP image encoder [36]. Given the scarcity of professional-quality paired vector sketch datasets, we have assembled a synthetic dataset to train our network. The input images for this dataset are created using SDXL [33], and the matching vector sketches are generated using a new optimization-based method we introduce, termed ControlSketch. ControlSketch advances the SDS loss [34], commonly employed for text-conditioned generation, by incorporating a depth ControlNet [58] into the loss, which allows for generating object sketches with spatial control. Our dataset includes over 35,000 high-quality vector sketches spanning 100 categories and is structured to be scalable. We showcase SwiftSketch's ability to produce high-quality vector sketches of diverse concepts, striking a balance between fidelity to input images and the abstract, natural look of sketches.   ### 2. Related Work Existing sketch datasets predominantly consist of sketches created by humans and serve a variety of sketch-related purposes. Among these, class-conditioned datasets are quite prevalent, especially the QuickDraw dataset, which is the largest of its kind, boasting a collection of 50 million sketches across 345 categories. Various styles characterize image-referenced sketch datasets, including (a) QuickDraw, (b) Sketchy, (c) OpenSketch, and (d) the Berger et al. Figure 2 collection, illustrating the contrast between amateur and professional sketches. Both QuickDraw and Sketchy are expansive datasets; however, Sketchy offers sketches with finer detail than QuickDraw, although both maintain a non-professional aesthetic. OpenSketch and the Berger et al. set, by comparison, contain professional-grade sketches but are considerably smaller and tailored to specific fields. These datasets might include image tracing and contour depictions or abstract yet detailed forms, and some very abstract sketches, which are generally developed by individuals who are not professional artists. There have been attempts to gather sketches from professional artists, yet such collections are limited in size and often confined to specific categories, such as portrait or household item sketches. As a result, they are not ideal for developing generative models that need to be broadly applicable across diverse concepts.  The advent of these datasets has enabled the exploration of data-driven methods for addressing sketch-related challenges. A range of generative frameworks and architectures have been tested for generating vector sketches, including RNNs, BERT, Transformers, CNNs, LSTMs, GANs, reinforcement learning, and diffusion models. Yet, these techniques fundamentally operate in a class-conditioned context, which constrains their ability to generate sketches beyond the classes in the training datasets. Moreover, they often depend on datasets sourced from the public, which primarily contain sketches of an amateur nature, thus limiting their capacity to produce more intricate or artistically nuanced styles. Efforts to create sketches with a more professional appearance are often domain-specific or limited to pixel-based output. Notably, converting images to sketches can be akin to a style transfer task. Recent advancements utilizing text-to-image diffusion models have shown promising results with high artistic fidelity; however, even these approaches are confined to pixel space. Our focus, contrastingly, is on vector sketches due to their scalable resolution, clean and smooth appearance, customizable abstraction, and editable properties.  To circumvent dependence on existing vector datasets, recent studies have explored the power of large pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for zero-shot sketch generation. Initial approaches harness models like CLIP to facilitate image- and text-driven generation, optimizing a set of random strokes through a differentiable renderer to align vector and pixel representations. More recent models have employed text-to-image diffusion backbones, integrating SDS loss for optimization and achieving superior outcomes, although still limiting to text-based contexts. While these produce artistic results across a wide range of concepts, they are resource-intensive, necessitating iterative backpropagation.  Diffusion models have emerged as robust generative frameworks, extending beyond pixel-centric data handling. Emerging research underscores their flexibility across different tasks, such as synthesizing human movement, generating 3D point clouds, and reconceptualizing object detection as a generative task. Some prior work has applied diffusion models specifically to vector graphics creation. For example, VecFusion adopts a two-step diffusion approach for font generation, yet its intricate architecture and font-specific vector representation confine its adaptability to other vector-based applications. Meanwhile, SketchKnitter and work by Ashcroft et al. leverage diffusion models trained on datasets like QuickDraw and Anime-Vec10k for creating vector sketches, albeit without using image or text conditioning for inputs.   ### 3. Preliminaries Diffusion Models Diffusion models, as referenced in works [20, 41], represent a category of generative models designed to learn distributions by incrementally denoising a Gaussian input. These models consist of a couple of processes: a forward process denoted as q(xt|xt−1), which adds noise to data samples x0 that are drawn from a probability distribution pdata over various time steps t ranging from 1 to T, and a backward, or reverse, process represented by p(xt−1|xt), which incrementally removes noise from the signal. This reverse process functions as the generative component and is approximated using a neural network indicated by ϵθ(xt, t). Throughout the training phase, a noised signal is generated at various time steps from a sample x0 using the formula: xt = √¯αtx0 + √ 1 −¯αtϵ, (1) where ϵ follows a normal distribution N(0, I), and ¯αt, defined as Qt s=1 αs, acts as the noise scheduler. A standard method for training this model is employing the simplified objective: Lsimple = Ex0∼q(x0),ϵ∼N(0,I),t∼U(1,T ) ϵ−ϵθ(xt, t) 2. (2) During inference, generating a new sample begins with a Gaussian noise sample xT from N(0, I) and the denoising network is iteratively applied over T steps to produce a final result x0. SDS Loss The Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [34] is utilized to extract insights from a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model to fine-tune a parametric representation. In the context of vector graphics, the parameters ϕ defining an SVG file can be optimized using the SDS loss to encapsulate a specified text concept. A differentiable rasterizer [26] transforms ϕ into a pixel image x, which is subsequently noised to obtain xt at a particular time step t. This noised image, when conditioned on a text cue c, is processed through the pre-trained diffusion model, ϵθ(xt, t, c). The difference in the diffusion loss as outlined in Eq. (2) serves to approximate the gradients for the parameters of the initial image synthesis model, ϕ, in order to better synchronize its results with the conditional text prompt. Specifically, the gradient of the SDS loss is expressed as: ∇ϕLSDS =  w(t)(ϵθ(xt, t, y) −ϵ)∂x ∂ϕ  , (3) where w(t) is a constant related to αt. This optimization procedure iteratively refines the parametric model.   ### 4. Method Our approach is built on three essential elements: First, there is ControlSketch, an innovative optimization-driven technique designed to produce high-quality vector sketches from input objects. Second, we establish a synthetic paired image-sketch dataset that is developed using the ControlSketch technique. Third, the foundation is completed by SwiftSketch, a diffusion model that has been trained on the dataset we created, allowing for the swift and efficient generation of sketches.   ### 4.1. ControlSketch When presented with an image I showcasing an object, our objective is to produce a sketch S that mirrors the input with high fidelity while maintaining a natural, sketch-like quality. As widely accepted in the field, we portray S as comprising n strokes {si}n i=1, each represented by a two-dimensional cubic Bézier curve: si = {pi j}4 j=1 = {(xj, yj)i}4 j=1. We refine the strokes through the typical SDS-based optimization pipeline, elaborated in Section 3, introducing two significant enhancements: a superior initial stroke setup and the application of spatial control. Our technique leverages the image’s attention map Iattn, depth map Idepth, and accompanying caption y, obtained through DDIM inversion [41], MiDaS [5], and BLIP2 [24], respectively. Prior methodologies [47, 54] typically employ the attention map for initial stroke placement, yet we have noticed this can lead to incomplete sketch areas, notably when spatial control is introduced. To address this issue, we suggest a refined initialization approach (see Fig. 3, left) that ensures a more comprehensive coverage. We segment the object area into k = 6 equally-sized regions (Fig. 3c), using a K-Means approach weighted by attention metrics alongside pixel positions. We equitably distribute n/2 points among these regions, with the remaining n/2 points allocated in proportion to the mean attention score in each sector. This strategy allocates more points to regions with higher attention and uniformly spaces points within each area for robust coverage. This method defines the starting control points for the strokes, ready for optimization, as illustrated in Figure 3d. The stroke refinement is further visualized in Figure 3, right. During each iteration, the rasterized sketch R({si}n i=1) is intentionally disrupted based on t and ϵ, subsequently processed through a depth-ControlNet-based text-to-image diffusion model [58]. This model forecasts the noise ˆϵ by considering both the caption y and depth map Idepth. We regulate the balance between spatial and textual conditions to attain the best compromise between “semantic” fidelity—rooted in y to ensure the sketch is identifiable—and “geometric” fidelity—originating from Idepth to maintain spatial structural precision.  As demonstrated in Figure 4, (a) begins with the input image. (b) illustrates the object mask. (c) exhibits the extraction of the object’s contour via morphological operations, assigning greater weight to the sketch pixels intersecting this contour. (d) shows the attention map, while (e) depicts sorting the strokes by a blend of contour intersections and attention scores. (f) presents a visualization of the initial 16 strokes in the arranged sketch, highlighting the efficacy of our sorting method. In this manner, more points are dedicated to attention-intensive areas, with even spacing within each region assuring good coverage.   ### 4.2. The ControlSketch Dataset We employ ControlSketch to create a dataset composed of paired image-vector sketches. Each entry in this dataset is represented by the set {I, Iattn, Idepth, Imask, S, c, y}, encompassing the actual image, its associated attention map, depth map, object mask, the vector sketch of the object, as well as the class label and caption that accompany it. For image generation, we use SDXL [33], paired with a prompt template crafted to generate images tailored to each specific class c (an example for the class “lion” is depicted in Figure 3a). Following this, ControlSketch is applied to the masked images to produce corresponding vector sketches. Further particulars can be found in the supplementary materials. Approaches that rely on optimization, such as ControlSketch, naturally lack predetermined stroke sequences. However, learning an internal stroke order allows the creation of sketches with variable abstraction levels by adjusting the stroke count produced. Therefore, we introduce a heuristic stroke-sorting method that gives precedence to contour strokes and those that depict key regions, as shown in Figure 4. As a result, each vector sketch S is systematically arranged as an ordered sequence of strokes (s1, . . . , sn).   ### 4.3. SwiftSketch The ControlSketch dataset is instrumental in training our generative model, Mθ, which is designed to adeptly convert an input image, I, into a vector sketch. We conceptualize Mθ as a transformer decoder, ensuring it can manage the distinct and expansive dependency patterns found in vector sketches. The training process leverages the well-established conditional diffusion framework, which we detailed in Section 3, but incorporates modifications tailored to the nuances of vector data and the specific image-to-sketch transformation task. Notably, the model is trained to effectively denoise the (x, y) coordinate arrays that typify the strokes within the sketch. The entire training workflow is visually detailed in Figure 5.   During each training cycle, a dataset pair (I, S0) is extracted, where S0, existing in the vector domain as R2×4×n, represents the pristine sketch, and R(S0) is its rasterized variant in pixel terms, produced via a differentiable rasterizer [26]. The image I undergoes feature extraction through a pretrained CLIP ResNet [36], specifically tapping into its fourth layer, which excels in capturing both geometrical and semantic data [47]. Subsequent refinement by a lightweight CNN adjusts these features, optimizing them for compatibility with Mθ, and resulting in the image embedding Ie. Each iteration involves selecting a timestep t randomly from a uniform distribution U(1, T) and noise ϵ from a normal distribution N(0, I) to shape St:   \[ St = \sqrt{\alpha_t}S0 + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t}\epsilon \]   as shown by equation (4), with αt acting as the noise scheduler dependent on t. Within Figure 5, St is portrayed as a noised transformation of S0 in vector terms, with noise contingent upon the timestep t. The control points {st_1, ..., st_n} are introduced into a linear layer (illustrated in green) and, with traditional positional embeddings, channeled through a transformer decoder (signified in pink) comprising 8 cross-attention and self-attention layers. The encoded timestep t with the image attributes Ie becomes engaged within the transformer via cross-attention. The decoder then reverts the output to its primary points dimension using a linear layer, arriving at the prediction Mθ(St, t, Ie) = ˆS0.   We utilize a dual-objective training scheme for Mθ: Lpoints and Lraster, addressing both vector and raster sketch manifestations:   \[ Lpoints = \|S0 - ˆS0\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|s0_i - ˆs0_i\|_1 \]   \[ Lraster = LPIPS(R(S0), R(ˆS0)), \]   as stipulated in equation (5), where Lpoints pertains to the L1 distance between the original sketch control points S0 and its forecasted counterpart ˆS0, while Lraster refers to the perceptual distance (LPIPS) [59] between the raster versions of the sketches. Lpoints enhances stroke-level precision, whereas Lraster aligns the generated sketch with the broader structure of the original. Our cumulative loss takes the form L = Lpoints + λLraster, administering λ = 0.2. A typical practice is to adopt classifier-free guidance [19] at the inference phase, prompting Mθ to learn both conditioned and unconditioned distributions through random assignment of I = ∅ for 10% of training steps. Figure 6 outlines the inference mechanics. Model Mθ generates novel sketches by systematically denoising random Gaussian signals, ST ∼ N(0, I). With each t, Mθ forecasts the clean sketch ˆS0 = Mθ(St, t, Ie) based on Ie and t. St−1, the subsequent interim sketch, emerges from ˆS0 via Equation (4). This step is iterated over T stages. It's observed that final sketches might exhibit residual noise, attributed to the model's primary focus on rectifying heavily noised inputs, with slight inaccuracies at finer stages lacking significant impact on the loss. To rectify this, we introduce a refinement network, Mθ∗. As illustrated in Figure 7, this additional step is aimed at purging minor residual noise. This refinement network is structured akin to Mθ but targets enhancement of slightly noised sketches, conditioned on unchanged input image features, and fixing the timestep condition at 0. Further elaboration is available in the supplementary section. This refinement process draws inspiration from analogous approaches in pixel domain techniques [33, 39], where post-processing elevates image sharpness and resolution. After Mθ's denoising is complete, ˆS0 passes through Mθ∗ for fine-tuning, enhancing the final output as shown in Figure 6.   ### 4.4. Implementation Details ControlSketch converges after about 2,000 steps, requiring roughly 10 minutes on a typical RTX3090 GPU to complete the process. On the other hand, SwiftSketch undergoes training with T set to 50 noising steps, enabling rapid generation. To ensure the model hones in on fine details, we tweak the noise scheduler so that the signal is perturbed more gently at smaller timesteps than what the cosine noise schedule proposed in [32] suggests. The model is trained using images drawn from 15 distinct classes, with each class comprising 1,000 samples. This extensive training routine extends over 400K steps, taking nearly six days to run on a single A100 GPU. During inference, we apply a guidance scale set at 2.5. Our synthetic dataset is further enriched with an additional 200 test samples for each of the 15 training classes, along with 85 supplementary object categories, each with 200 samples as well. For more detailed implementation insights, as well as comprehensive class labels and dataset visualizations, please refer to the supplementary material.   ### 5. Results We start by highlighting the impressive capability of SwiftSketch in producing high-quality vector sketches from a wide array of input images. SwiftSketch effectively extends its functionality to new images from the categories used during training, as demonstrated in Figure 11. Here, it generates sketches that accurately reflect the input images with convincing detail and realism. When faced with images from entirely new categories that traditionally prove more challenging, SwiftSketch excels by capturing the fundamental features of these input images, creating sketches that are abstract yet remain true to the source (see Figure 12). Remarkably, each sketch is created in vector format and the whole process—including 50 diffusion steps followed by a single refinement step—is completed in under a second. Figure 7 illustrates the denoising steps in the generation process, where the method starts with a Gaussian distribution and gradually refines it until it matches the data distribution. Figure 8 showcases how our method achieves varying levels of abstraction using an ordered stroke technique, visualizing the sequential stroke additions as presented in the resulting SVG file. One can observe that even the initial strokes effectively communicate the intended concept. Additional results from both SwiftSketch and ControlSketch can be found in the supplementary materials.   ### 5.1. Comparisons We assess the efficacy of SwiftSketch and ControlSketch methods in image-to-sketch generation by comparing them against top-tier approaches like Photo-Sketching [25], Chan et al. [6], InstantStyle [48], and CLIPasso [47]. For our analysis, InstantStyle, XDoG, Chan et al., and other techniques are used to generate sketches, with timing and format (Pixel or Vector) indicated above each sketch. In Figure 9, we provide a qualitative comparison: on the left, input images are displayed, followed by sketches created using XDoG [52], a well-regarded edge detection method. ControlSketch and SwiftSketch, our novel methods, appear on the right, employing a sketch image as a style reference. The figures illustrate distinct outputs from each method, with XDoG serving as the baseline technique. Chan et al. and InstantStyle deliver detailed sketches that accurately map the structure of input images but closely adhere to the left-side edge maps. Comparatively, Photo-Sketching (in the fifth column) offers more abstract results but struggles to represent image content naturally. Although these methods are efficient, producing raster sketches in under a minute, our approach emphasizes vector sketches. These are resolution-independent, easily modifiable, and exhibit smoothness and clarity. Meanwhile, CLIPasso (sixth column) generates vector sketches that balance detail and semantics well but takes 5 minutes per sketch and can introduce overlapping stroke artifacts, notably in complex examples. ControlSketch (seventh column) excels in creating high-fidelity, abstract, yet clear sketches that depict input images without artifacts, although it progresses slower than CLIPasso due to the inherently time-consuming SDS process, which limits interactive use. By contrast, SwiftSketch (rightmost column) effectively learns from ControlSketch samples to generate sketches in real time, closely matching the quality of optimization-heavy techniques. Additional examples can be found in the supplementary materials.  For quantitative analysis, we selected 4,000 images from our dataset—2,000 from categories seen during training and 2,000 from new categories—and added 2,000 more from the SketchyCOCO [14] set to test generalization on external data. Each set includes 10 randomly picked categories with 200 images per category. Using the CLIP zero-shot classifier [36] for class recognition, MS-SSIM [51] for image-to-sketch fidelity as in CLIPascene [46], and DreamSim [13], we evaluate performance. Results in Table 1 show scores for each type of data separately, with human sketches from SketchyCOCO as a control. Chan et al. and InstantStyle rank highest across several metrics, attributed to their detailed sketches mirroring edge maps, ensuring high recognition (CLIP score) and fidelity. SwiftSketch shows strong performance on seen test categories, akin to ControlSketch (our ground truth), but struggles with unseen categories, particularly in class recognition. This is more pronounced in SketchyCOCO, challenged by low-resolution and poor lighting. SwiftSketch’s training was limited to 15 categories due to resource constraints, pointing to more training as a means for better generalization.  ControlSketch sketches stand out in recognizability and fidelity, performing well on SketchyCOCO data. To emphasize ControlSketch's superiority over CLIPasso, a perceptual study with 40 participants was conducted. Participants viewed pairs of sketches made by both methods, shown with the input image in random order, and rated the one perceived as higher quality. The study, featuring 24 sketches from each method, spanned 24 object classes. Participants favored ControlSketch sketches in 89% of cases, as depicted in Figure 13.   ### 6. Ablation In order to assess the contribution of SwiftSketch’s primary components, we methodically remove each element and retrain the network from scratch. Our analysis involves evaluating the models without the LPIPS loss, the L1 loss, and the sorting mechanism, as well as considering the impact of adding the refinement network. These findings are detailed in Table 2: "Full" signifies our entire diffusion pipeline before introducing the refinement phase, while "+Refine" indicates that the refinement stage has been added. Notably, the absence of the L1 loss causes a substantial decline in performance, underscoring its critical role in the training process. Omitting the LPIPS loss also adversely affects performance, particularly concerning classes that the model has not previously encountered. The metrics show similar performance levels even when the sorting phase is omitted. Although the produced sketches may seem visually alike, the sorting phase plays a pivotal role in accommodating different abstraction levels. While the network can be trained without the sorting phase and still yield satisfactory results, the development of an internal stroke order is crucial for enabling training across varying abstraction levels, where sketches inherently convey the importance of the strokes. The refinement stage significantly enhances recognizability, especially for categories not present in the training data, where sketches from the diffusion phase tend to be less clear. The influence of the refinement network is further illustrated in Figure 14, and more examples are included in the supplementary material. For a comprehensive understanding, scores calculated based on a total of 4000 sketches—split equally between seen and unseen categories—are presented. The metrics used include CLIP Top-1 and Top-3 accuracy, MS-SSIM, and DreamSim across seen and unseen categories: without LPIPS, scores are 0.88 for seen and 0.36 for unseen in CLIP Top-1, 0.94 and 0.49 in CLIP Top-3, 0.58 and 0.52 in MS-SSIM, and 0.58 and 0.72 in DreamSim. Excluding L1 leads to 0.03 for seen and 0.01 for unseen in CLIP Top-1, 0.06 and 0.03 in CLIP Top-3, 0.24 and 0.22 in MS-SSIM, and 0.80 and 0.84 in DreamSim. Without sorting, scores are 0.93 for seen and 0.63 for unseen in CLIP Top-1, 0.97 and 0.76 in CLIP Top-3, 0.62 and 0.57 in MS-SSIM, and 0.55 and 0.68 in DreamSim. The complete pipeline achieves 0.94 for seen and 0.61 for unseen in CLIP Top-1, 0.97 and 0.73 in CLIP Top-3, 0.62 and 0.57 in MS-SSIM, and 0.54 and 0.68 in DreamSim. The addition of refinement boosts scores to 0.95 for seen and 0.70 for unseen in CLIP Top-1, 0.98 and 0.82 in CLIP Top-3, 0.62 and 0.56 in MS-SSIM, and 0.53 and 0.66 in DreamSim.   ### 7. Limitations and Future Work SwiftSketch demonstrates efficiency in generating vector sketches from images, yet it does have certain limitations. Firstly, although the tool excels in categories it has been trained on, our evaluation shows a marked decline in performance when it encounters new, unseen categories. This drop is especially significant in categories that markedly differ from those it was trained on, such as non-human or non-animal objects. For instance, failure cases often present themselves with a noisy appearance or as completely unidentifiable forms, much like the carrot depicted in Figure 10. Future work aimed at increasing the training category count could potentially improve the model’s ability to generalize. Secondly, the refinement stage includes a process intended to correct the noisy appearance, but it might inadvertently over-simplify the sketches, leading to a loss of crucial details, evident in the cow’s facial features like the nose and eyes, as shown in Figure 10. Lastly, for the scope of this paper, we restricted training of SwiftSketch to sketches with a fixed number of strokes (32). However, training with sketches that have varying stroke counts, across multiple abstraction levels, opens up a promising avenue for subsequent research. Our transformer-decoder architecture is naturally adept for this kind of expansion, and our findings suggest that the network is capable of capturing essential characteristics from sorted sketches, underscoring its potential to effectively manage more complex levels of abstraction. (a) Noisy, unrecognizable sketches (b) Refinement stage omits fine details Figure 10. Limitations. (a) Sketches may present as unrecognizable (e.g., carrot) or noisy (e.g., Eiffel Tower). (b) The refinement stage can result in the omission of fine details, such as the cow’s nose and eye.   ### 8. Conclusions We introduced SwiftSketch, a novel approach for sketching objects, capable of crafting believable vector sketches in just under one second. SwiftSketch utilizes a diffusion model integrated with a transformer-decoder architecture, which generates sketches by gradually denoising a Gaussian distribution within the realm of stroke control points. In light of the limited availability of datasets featuring professional-quality paired vector sketches, we curated a synthetic dataset consisting of 100 distinct categories and more than 35,000 sketches. This comprehensive dataset was developed using ControlSketch, an enhanced sketch generation method based on SDS, now improved with a depth ControlNet for superior spatial manipulation. We showcased, both visually and numerically, that ControlSketch is capable of producing sketches of exceptional quality and fidelity. Furthermore, SwiftSketch not only effectively captures the data distribution of ControlSketch but also achieves remarkably high-quality sketch production, while drastically slashing the generation time from about 10 minutes to a mere 0.5 seconds. We are convinced that this work marks a significant advancement towards the goal of real-time, high-quality vector sketch generation, with the promise of facilitating more interactive artistic processes. Moreover, we intend to make our scalable dataset construction methodology publicly available to aid and inspire future research efforts within this area.   ### 9. summary: Sample selection arises endogenously in causal research when the treatment affects whether certain units are observed. It is a common pitfall in longitudinal studies, particularly in settings where treatment assignment is confounded. In this paper, I highlight the drawbacks of one of the most popular identification strategies in such settings: Difference-in-Differences (DiD). Specifically, I employ principal stratification analysis to show that the conventional ATT estimand may not be well defined, and the DiD estimand cannot be interpreted causally without additional assumptions. To address these issues, I develop an identification strategy to partially identify causal effects on the subset of units with well-defined and observed outcomes under both treatment regimes. I adapt Lee bounds to the Changes-in-Changes (CiC) setting (Athey & Imbens, 2006), leveraging the time dimension of the data to relax the unconfoundedness assumption in the original trimming strategy of Lee (2009). This setting has the DiD identification strategy as a particular case, which I also implement in the paper. Additionally, I explore how to leverage multiple sources of sample selection to relax the monotonicity assumption in Lee (2009), which may be of independent interest. Alongside the identification strategy, I present estimators and inference results. I illustrate the relevance of the proposed methodology by analyzing a job training program in Colombia.
