contents: ### Abstract In causal research, sample selection can occur internally when the treatment influences which units are included in an analysis. This issue frequently arises in longitudinal studies, especially in contexts where the assignment of treatments is mixed with other variables. This paper discusses the limitations of one of the most widely used identification strategies under these circumstances: the Difference-in-Differences (DiD) approach. Using principal stratification analysis, I demonstrate that the standard ATT estimand might lack a clear definition; furthermore, the DiD estimand requires additional assumptions for a causal interpretation. To overcome these challenges, I propose a strategy that can partially identify causal effects on the subgroup of units that have well-established and observed outcomes across both treatment conditions. I refine Lee bounds within the Changes-in-Changes (CiC) framework (as put forward by Athey & Imbens, 2006), utilizing the temporal aspect of data to ease the assumption of unconfoundedness in Lee's (2009) original trimming method. Notably, this framework encompasses the DiD identification strategy as a specific example, which I also explore in the study. Moreover, I investigate how utilizing various sources of sample selection can relax the monotonicity assumption established in Lee's work (2009), potentially offering broader insights. Beyond this identification approach, I present estimators and inference results pertinent to this context. To showcase the applicability of the proposed method, I examine a job training initiative in Colombia. JEL-Code: C14, C21, C23. Keywords: Difference-in-Differences, Changes-in-Changes, Sample selection, Panel Data, Repeated Cross-Sections, Principal stratification, Partial identification. aDepartment of Economics, European University Institute, Via delle Fontanelle 18, 50014 Fiesole, Italy. Email: javier.viviens@eui.eu. There is an ongoing development of an R package to implement the described methodology. I extend my gratitude to Fabrizia Mealli, Andrea Ichino, and Alessandro Tarozzi for their insightful discussions and guidance. I also thank Ellen Greaves for her thought-provoking discussion during the 2024 EUI May Forum, along with Miguel Nunes, Jörn-Steffen Pischke, and those present at seminars at the European University Institute for their valuable feedback and suggestions. Any errors remain my own responsibility. arXiv:2502.08614v1 [econ.EM] 12 Feb 2025.   ### 1 Introduction Difference-in-differences (DiD) is a frequently employed method for estimating causal effects in observational studies. However, its application becomes problematic in samples subjected to endogenous selection. Typically, researchers operate under the assumption that missing observations occur completely at random. In reality, though, missingness often correlates with the distribution of potential outcomes, resulting in endogenous sample selection. While this issue has been thoroughly analyzed in experimental contexts, less attention has been given to its implications in non-randomly assigned treatments, such as those encountered in DiD frameworks. This paper brings to light the limitations of using DiD as an identification strategy under endogenous sample selection and suggests an alternative approach for estimating causal effects when faced with non-ignorable sample selection.  In longitudinal research, sample selection can result from various scenarios, including the loss of follow-up for some participants. A prominent example is censoring due to death, as noted by Rubin (2006). In such instances, outcomes for certain individuals become indeterminate during the study and ultimately go unrecorded. This dilemma is often prevalent in clinical studies, where patients may pass away before outcomes are assessed (Ding et al., 2011; Comment et al., 2019). Similarly, censoring due to death is also seen in social science research. Examples include job training program evaluations, where wages apply only to those employed (Ham & Lalonde, 1996), and educational policy assessments where outcomes aren't clearly defined for students who drop out (Krueger, 1999; Cornwell et al., 2005).  Attrition presents another frequent cause of sample selection, particularly in survey-based studies, due to non-response issues (Nunan et al., 2018; Gröger & Zylberberg, 2016; Braghieri et al., 2022). Here, the outcome for missing participants isn't observed although it remains theoretically determinable. Sample selection can also occur in repeated cross-sectional studies when the treatment modifies the sample composition. A classic illustration by Card and Krueger (2000) highlights this: when a minimum wage hike stimulates new restaurant openings, the restaurant sample evolves selectively over time.  In evaluating the DiD identification strategy's challenges under sample selection, principal stratification analysis is employed (Frangakis & Rubin, 2002). This method acknowledges selection into the sample as a post-treatment variable, categorizing each unit by its potential selection status (observed or missing) under both treatment arms. The combined values of these potential selection states classify the sample into four principal strata, despite these strata being latent due to their potential selection states being never observed together. Should the distribution of potential outcomes vary across these strata, the sample selection is non-ignorable.  The DiD methodology may encounter two principal issues under sample selection. First, the standard goal estimand, the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), may lack clear definition when sample selection stems from censoring due to death. In such cases, outcomes for missing participants aren't well-defined, such as wages for jobless individuals, academic metrics for dropouts, or health data for deceased patients, leading to undefined causal outcome comparisons. For instance, if a control group student drops out but stays enrolled in the treatment group, their GPA increase is undefined due to the lack of a control group GPA. Consequently, average treatment effects can only pertain to units with clearly defined treatment effects, namely those not censored under any treatment condition.  The second issue is that the DiD estimand loses its causal meaning; it fails to compare potential outcomes within a common set of units. Rather, it contrasts mixtures of different principal strata having diverse potential selection patterns. This misalignment might instigate Simpson’s paradox—where overall comparisons mislead due to intrinsic group disparities. For example, assessing job training programs by comparing wages of trained versus untrained employed workers might inadvertently reflect descriptive, not causal, relationships unless potential outcome distributions match across strata, indicating non-ignorable employment.  To tackle related sample selection conundrums in experimental settings, Zhang and Rubin (2003) suggest estimating causal impacts on units maintaining consistent selection patterns across treatment groups. While conditioning on observable selection involves post-treatment variables, principal strata serve more as confounding pre-treatment covariates, unaffected by treatment assignments. Specifically, the authors advise focusing on the Always-Observed principal stratum, concerning units with observable and defined outcomes under both treatment and control groups. Yet, identifying principal causal effects on this subpopulation remains challenging due to latent principal strata.  This paper formulates an identification strategy to estimate causal effects on the Always-Observed principal stratum—the units observed irrespective of treatment status. I expand the trimming strategy known as Lee bounds (Lee, 2009) into a Changes-in-Changes (CiC) framework (Athey & Imbens, 2006), not presuming unconfounded treatments. Instead, the strategy assumes that all unobservable factors affecting outcomes for the Always-Observed units are encapsulated within a single index, whose distribution may vary across these units in treatment and control groups, yet steadfastly remains constant over time within each group. Under this condition, coupled with the proportions of principal strata in each group, I achieve partial identification of two causal estimands: the ATT for the Always-Observed stratum and the Quantile Treatment Effect on the Treated (QTT) for the same stratum. Notably, the QTT proves crucial when policymakers aim to assess not just average policy impact but its distributional outcomes. By transitioning from average to distributional focuses, the CiC framework facilitates probing treatment effect heterogeneity across the outcome spectrum.  Furthermore, this paper showcases results for the DiD identification strategy nested within the CiC framework. The primary identification assumption—principal parallel trends—is a subset of the CiC outcome model. Despite CiC enforcing weaker assumptions and accommodating distributional effect identification, DiD persists as the predominant tool for estimating average effects when treatments are confounded by unobserved individual traits. Therefore, I adapt the proposed methodology for the DiD scenario too.  I introduce estimators valid for the two-group, two-period situations and deduce their asymptotic distributions to enable robust inference for both the CiC and the DiD methods. A crucial facet of the identification strategy involves estimating the principal strata proportions using the CiC model combined with a monotonicity assumption. This allows for the pinpoint identification of principal strata proportions, assuming treatment affects selection unidirectionally for all units, excluding one of the strata (e.g., units observed solely when treated). I relax this condition in the presence of several sample selection sources, positing each as monotonic, yet permitting contrary signs. This expansion preserves point identification for all four principal strata, potentially extending applicability of the original Lee bounds to experimental contexts.  To illustrate the proposed methodology, I examine a Colombian job training program's effects using data from Attanasio et al. (2011), focusing on salaried earnings for Always-Observed workers, those consistently in paid employment irrespective of training reception. The null hypothesis suggesting the policy did not alter this subpopulation's average outcome wasn't rejected. Nonetheless, examining the QTT demonstrated outcome distribution variance indicating possible heterogeneous effects with distributional ramifications.  This paper bridges two research domains: exploring causal impacts in longitudinal settings (see Arkhangelsky and Imbens (2024) for reviews) and assessing partially identified causal impacts when outcomes are censored due to ‘death’. The former typically leans on unconfoundedness, but recent focus emphasizes settings with treatments confounded by unobservable characteristics. Concurrently, Rathnayake et al. (2024) and Shin (2024) expand Lee bounds to DiD settings, sharing the estimand (ATT on Always-Observed stratum) and identifying assumption (principal parallel trends) with my paper. Nevertheless, three principal distinctions emerge between their work and mine. Firstly, principal parallel trends represent a special, flexible design case within the general CiC framework presented herein, enabling identification of diverse effect types. Secondly, my contribution extends the identification of principal strata proportions in Rathnayake et al. (2024) and Shin (2024), identifying these proportions under looser conditions with probabilities confined to the unit interval. Finally, I develop an extension relaxing monotonicity assumptions yet maintaining point identification, unlike Rathnayake et al. (2024) and Shin (2024), who partially relax this assumption leading to partially identifiable strata proportions.  The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 covers notation and the DiD design under sample selection; Sections 3 and 4 discuss the proposed methodology, with Section 3 detailing identification strategies and Section 4 covering estimation and inference results. Section 5 applies these strategies using job training data from Attanasio et al. (2011). Finally, Section 6 offers concluding remarks.   ### 2 Difference-in-differences under sample selection In this section, I discuss the difference-in-differences framework as it relates to situations with sample selection. For the sake of clarity and simplicity, I focus on the scenario involving two groups over two periods. Imagine a random sample of N units that are tracked across two time periods. A foundational body of literature was developed by Zhang and Rubin (2003), Imai (2008), Lee (2009), and Zhang et al. (2009), introducing a structured method to estimate effects on the Always-Observed stratum. This scholarly conversation has since expanded in numerous ways, such as estimating effects for other strata (Huber & Mellace, 2015), refining bounds using covariates (Grilli & Mealli, 2008; Long & Hudgens, 2013; Semenova, 2023), incorporating instruments (Mattei et al., 2014), utilizing longitudinal data (Comment et al., 2019; Grossi et al., 2023), integrating sample selection with noncompliance (Chen & Flores, 2015; Blanco et al., 2020), targeting varied estimands (Bartalotti et al., 2023), and exploring non-binary treatment regimes (Lee & Liu, 2024). Notably, all of these studies assume that treatment effects are not confounded. This paper also contributes to a broader literature on sample selection, which was initially spurred by the pivotal work of Heckman (1979). A segment of this research is concerned with correcting for selection bias in panel data environments (Bhattacharya, 2008; Semykina & Wooldridge, 2010; Carlson & Semykina, 2024; Ghanem et al., 2024).   Let's denote t ∈ {1, 2}. Suppose wit indicates the treatment status of unit i at time t. Initially, no unit receives the treatment, so wi1 = 0 for all i. However, in the following period, a subset of units receives the treatment, wi2 ∈ {0, 1}. The variable G is used as an indicator for the treatment group, with Gi = 1 if unit i receives treatment in the second period, otherwise it is zero, such that Gi ≡ wi2. The outcome for unit i at time t, denoted as Yit, is analyzed using the potential outcome framework, assuming the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) as proposed by Rubin (1980, 1990). This assumption excludes interference between units and variations of treatment, allowing the observed Yit to be connected to unit i's potential outcomes, Yit(wi1, wi2): Yit = Yit(0, 1)Gi + Yit(0, 0)(1 − Gi). When sample selection is in play, some outcomes might be unobserved and undefined. A binary selection indicator, Sit, marks if unit i's outcome is observable and defined at time t, being 1 if so and 0 if not. An important consideration in this setup is that the selection indicator, S, acts as a post-treatment variable. Therefore, the observed selection outcome, Sit, must relate to potential selection outcomes: Sit = Sit(0, 1)Gi + Sit(0, 0)(1 − Gi). The assumption of no treatment anticipation, a standard in prior literature (Arkhangelsky & Imbens, 2024), is maintained here for both outcome and selection: Assumption 1 No treatment anticipation Si1(wi1, wi2) = Si1(wi1, w′ i2) = Si1 for all wi2, w′ i2 for all i, Yi1(wi1, wi2) = Yi1(wi1, w′ i2) = Yi1 for all wi2, w′ i2 for all i. Assumption 1 stipulates that treatment does not alter outcomes or selection in the earlier period. Since no unit is treated initially, it suffices to reference the second-period potential outcomes with wi2: Si2 = Si2(1)Gi + Si2(0)(1 − Gi), Yi2 = Yi2(1)Gi + Yi2(0)(1 − Gi). As selection is post-treatment, the population is dividable into subpopulations defined by potential selection indicator values in the second period, (Si2(1), Si2(0)), following the principal stratification approach (Frangakis & Rubin, 2002). Each unit falls into one of four principal strata, presented in Table 1, where Vi indicates the principal stratum for unit i. As potential outcomes aren't influenced by treatment, principal strata pre-exist treatment assignment. Even though selection status is a post-treatment result, the principal strata serve as pre-treatment attributes.  4 Table 1: Principal Strata. Therefore, expectations throughout the document are intended to reflect sampling variability (Abadie et al., 2020).   ### 2.1 Canonical difference-in-differences In the traditional difference-in-differences framework that involves comparing two groups over two time periods, the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) stands out as the most widely used causal estimand. This estimand, referred to as Causal Estimand 1, is symbolized as the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT), expressed mathematically as E[Yi2(1) − Yi2(0) | Gi = 1]. The core identification assumption underlying this model is known as the parallel trends assumption, designated as Assumption 4 Parallel Trends. Mathematically, it is stated as E[Yi2(0) − Yi1 | Gi = 1] = E[Yi2(0) − Yi1 | Gi = 0]. Assumption 4 essentially asserts that, in the absence of any treatment, there exists a consistent difference in the expected outcomes between the groups over time. A frequently cited result in this context is that, when Assumption 4 is satisfied, the ATT can be effectively identified using the Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimand, as articulated by Arkhangelsky and Imbens in their 2024 study: Estimand 1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD) E[Yi2 − Yi1 | Gi = 1] − E[Yi2 − Yi1 | Gi = 0].   ### 2.2 Issues arising from sample selection Upon selecting the sample, when the outcomes for certain units are either not well-defined or not observed, the Difference-in-Differences (DiD) identification strategy may encounter a couple of significant issues. To begin with, if sample selection emerges as a result of censoring due to an event like death, the outcome for the missing units isn't properly defined. In such instances, the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) itself becomes ambiguous. Take, for example, a job training program. Unemployed individuals lack a clearly defined 'wage' variable. This means that at least one of their potential outcomes isn't properly specified—the scenario under which they remain unemployed while receiving treatment. If these potential outcomes are not explicitly defined, then the causal contrast represented by Yi2(1) − Yi2(0) is also left undefined. A worker who may be unemployed under control but gains employment under treatment does not have a clearly measurable treatment effect on wages. Average causal effects, such as those aimed at by Causal Estimand 1, implicitly presuppose that a causal contrast is available for all units. When this assumption falters, a common alternative approach is to estimate the average causal effect for the subgroup of units possessing a clearly defined causal contrast—those categorized within the Always-Observed stratum (Zhang & Rubin, 2003; Rubin, 2006), specifically where Si2(1) = Si2(0) = 1.   The second issue shows itself even if the outcome is well-defined for every unit. This typically happens with survey data, where there's attrition because of non-response to the survey itself. Although the outcome isn't recorded for those who don't respond, the causal contrast remains theoretically valid. In such cases, the ATT is still a well-defined estimand. Yet, the foundational DiD estimand utilized in complete case analysis loses its causal meaning. To illustrate this, consider a researcher who ignores sample selection and aims to estimate the DID estimand using solely the units for which outcomes are recorded in both time periods: E[Yi2 − Yi1 | Gi = 1, Si2 = 1] − E[Yi2 − Yi1 | Gi = 0, Si2 = 1] = E[Yi2(1) − Yi1 | Gi = 1, Si2(1) = 1] − E[Yi2(0) − Yi1 | Gi = 0, Si2(0) = 1] = E[Yi2(1) − Yi1 | Gi = 1, Vi ∈ {AO, OT}] − E[Yi2(0) − Yi1 | Gi = 0, Vi ∈ {AO, OC}] (1). For an estimand to maintain its causal stature, it must compare potential outcomes among a common set of units. Yet, as highlighted in equation (1), in the face of sample selection, the DiD estimand evaluates two different sets of units: an amalgamation of AO and OT strata against a mixture of AO and OC strata. This comparison lacks a causal interpretation because it's confounded by the differing distributions of potential outcomes across principal strata. This complication directly arises from conditioning on an auxiliary variable that the treatment also influences. Thus, without any supplementary assumptions, the DiD estimand ceases to be causal.   Introducing Assumption 5, Ignorable Sample Selection, Yi2(wi2) − Yi1 ⊥⊥ Vi | Gi ∀wi2 ∈ {0, 1}, highlights that, by the premise of Assumption 2, if Si2 = 1, then Si1 = 1, hence there's no need for additional conditioning on Si1. The assertion of Assumption 5 is that the distribution of potential outcomes does not depend on the principal strata when considering the treatment. Given this assumption, equation (1) transforms into E[Yi2(1) − Yi1 | Gi = 1] − E[Yi2(0) − Yi1 | Gi = 0], and with the application of Assumptions 1 and 4, this equates to E[Yi2(1) − Yi2(0) | Gi = 1], (2), which is the ATT. Assumption 5 brings back the causal interpretation of the DiD estimand, asserting its equivalence to the ATT by presuming that the principal strata are ignorable—in other words, that the membership of unit i in a principal stratum is independent of their potential outcomes, (Yi1(0), Yi2(0), Yi2(1)), and thus independent of their treatment effect, Yi2(1) − Yi2(0).   Remark 1 underscores that, in many practical situations, researchers estimate the average treatment effect on selection, noted as E[Si2(1) − Si2(0)]. If they do not reject the null hypothesis indicating that this effect is zero, they tend to conclude that the missing observations are completely random, allowing them to proceed with the complete case analysis.   ### 3 Principal causal effects under non-ignorable sample selection It is important to recognize that not rejecting a null hypothesis does not equate to accepting it. In particular, when considering Assumption 5, it's vital to understand that a treatment effect of zero on selection neither suffices as proof of nor is required for this assumption to hold. Additional insights on this are provided in Appendix A.1. Assumption 5 specifically pertains to situations where the potential outcomes are unobserved yet still clearly defined. Within such contexts, it is possible to correct for attrition bias, and the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) can still be pinpointed without depending on Assumption 5 (as elaborated by Ghanem, Hirshleifer, et al. in 2024, and Shin in 2024). Nevertheless, when the potential outcomes for certain units are not well-defined, the ATT itself loses its definition. Under these circumstances, it becomes essential to aim for a new causal estimand since no assumption would suffice to define the ATT. In the section that follows, I will introduce an identification strategy designed to estimate causal effects even when non-ignorable sample selection is a factor. The causal estimands proposed here remain well-defined regardless of the sample selection type, as they specifically target the latent subpopulation for which causal effects are clearly established. This approach is generally applicable, as in many real-world scenarios, this particular subpopulation is key to interpreting treatment effects from a policy perspective, as discussed by Zhang & Rubin in their 2003 work.   ### 3.1 Identification in the DiD setup This section introduces an innovative identification strategy designed to estimate causal effects within longitudinal contexts where sample selection is not ignorable. Unlike the traditional literature on sample selection that often assumes treatment unconfoundedness, my approach does not require this assumption. Instead, I acknowledge that the treatment may be entangled with unobservable characteristics at the unit level. Nonetheless, I impose certain restrictions regarding the distribution of these unobservables over time. In the following discussion, I propose two causal estimands that retain well-defined properties even under sample selection, and I delve into their identification under various assumptions.  Causal Estimand 2 focuses on the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated Always-Observed units (ATTAO) expressed as E[Yi2(1) − Yi2(0) | Gi = 1, Vi = AO]. This particular estimand represents the ATT for those consistently observable units, capturing the average effect on treated units whose outcomes are clearly defined under both treatment conditions. Yet, due to the latent nature of this subpopulation, this estimand can only be partially determined. In numerous situations where treatment effects demonstrate heterogeneity, policymakers might be interested not only in the average effect but also in understanding how it is distributed. For example, consider a job training program. A positive ATTAO implies, on average, that the training enhances wages for workers employed regardless of program participation. However, this positive average effect may predominantly benefit workers with lower baseline wages or, alternatively, those with higher initial wages. Such diverse scenarios entail significant policy repercussions since the distributional effects of the training vary considerably. To bridge this gap, I put forward a new estimand aimed at the treatment effect across different quantiles of the outcome distribution for Always-Observed treated units.  Causal Estimand 3—Quantile Treatment Effect on the Treated Always-Observed units (QTTAO)—is defined as QTTAO(q) = F −1 Y2(1)|G=1,V=AO(q) − F −1 Y2(0)|G=1,V=AO(q), where F −1 Y (q) = inf{y : FY (y) ≥ q}, q ∈ [0, 1]. Here, FYt(w)|G=1,V2=AO signifies the cumulative distribution of the Potential Outcome Yt(w) at time t for units within the treatment group, G = 1, and belonging to the Always-Observed category, V = AO (where S2(1) = S2(0) = 1). Causal Estimand 3 contrasts the quantile q of the treated potential outcome distribution against the control potential outcome distribution at the same quantile for these units. For instance, QTTAO(0.5) relates to the treatment effect for the median treated AO unit. Due to both terms involving conditioning on a latent category, they remain only partially identifiable. Additionally, the distribution F −1 Y2(0)|G=1(q) does not occur directly in observations and necessitates imputation. I proceed to present the assumptions needed for the partial identification of these estimands.  To begin, I will talk about the partial identification of ATTAO within a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework. Then, I expand the discussion by loosening the central identification assumption, moving into a Changes-in-Changes (CiC) setting. In this CiC framework, I also consider the partial identification of QTTAO. Lastly, I explore how to identify the proportions of the principal strata, a critical element of the proposed methodology, under varying assumptions.   ### 3.2 Identification in the CiC setup The current body of research assessing the impacts on Always-Observed units typically relies on assuming treatment is unconfounded. Nonetheless, this assumption proves often unrealistic in Difference-in-Differences (DiD) frameworks, as treatment assignment is generally non-random and likely linked to underlying unobserved factors (Ghanem, Sant’Anna, & Wüthrich, 2024). To overcome this limitation, I propose an extension of Lee bounds (Lee, 2009) by substituting the unconfoundedness assumption with an assumption akin to parallel trends. This alternative method aligns more closely with the common identifying assumptions found in DiD frameworks. One major limitation, highlighted in Assumption 6, is its dependence on scale, meaning that if Assumption 6 is valid in terms of levels, it inherently does not hold true when expressed in logarithmic terms. Additionally, the DiD framework presupposes additivity and linearity in the potential outcomes, which may not always represent complex realities accurately. To overcome these issues, Athey and Imbens (2006) proposed a method known as Changes-in-changes (CiC), which extends the DiD strategy to embrace nonlinear and scale-invariant models.   In the CiC model, the inclusion of individual and time 'fixed effects' offers the possibility of influencing outcomes in more intricate ways than the linear and additive methods typically employed in DiD. The advantages of using the CiC model are substantial. First, by redirecting focus from average treatment effects to distributional effects, it becomes possible to identify distributional treatment effects, such as the Quantile Treatment Effect on the Treated Always-Observed units (QTTAO). Second, the earlier trimming strategy depends heavily on the differentiated outcome's distribution, denoted as ¨Yi = Yi2 −Yi1, restricting its application to panel data. In contrast, the CiC strategy does not depend on ¨Yi, enabling its application more freely to repeated cross-section data.  Assumption 7 concerns the outcome model: (Yit(0) | Vi = AO) = m(Uit, t), where the function m(u, t) is strictly increasing with respect to u for all t, and Uit represents an unobservable scalar characteristic of unit i at time t. Uit maintains a constant distribution over time within groups, such that Ui1 | Gi, Vi = AO and Ui2 | Gi, Vi = AO follow similar structures, and the treatment group's support lies within the control group's distribution support. Assumption 7 parallels assumptions 3.1 to 3.4 outlined by Athey and Imbens (2006), modeling the untreated potential outcome as a function dictated by the unobservable characteristic, Uit. This framework imposes several constraints on the unobservable, its distribution, and the outcome function m(·). It should be noted that these assumptions do not place any restriction on the observable data, making them inherently untestable. Within this model, all relevant individual characteristics affecting outcomes are captured in a single index, Uit. The condition that m(·) is strictly increasing suggests that individuals with a larger value of the unobservable will generally exhibit higher outcomes. Such an assumption appears intuitive if the unobservable characteristic is interpreted in terms of ability or productivity, and it naturally applies in models that separate variables additively, like the DiD model, though it also supports various non-additive and nonlinear outcome functions.  Notably, the unobservable's distribution can vary between treatment and control groups; however, it remains stable over time within each group. This consistency is vital as it means that the change in outcomes in the control group can be linked to shifts in the function m(·). Accurately estimating the trend in m(·) enables the identification of the potential missing outcomes for the treatment group.  Example 1 tackles a two-way fixed effects model: assume a separable additive model where m(Uit, t) = Uit + λt, positing that Uit = αi+εit, wherein εit is random disturbance. Consequently, the untreated potential outcome can be represented as: Yit(0) = αi + λt + εit. This example underscores that the conventional two-way fixed effects model is a specific case under the broader CiC framework, showing how DiD's identification is situated within the CiC structure. When assumptions inherent in the DiD model are met, Assumption 7 holds true as well, though the reverse doesn't necessarily apply. I then introduce additional assumptions regarding the selection mechanism that allow us to pinpoint these proportions. Assumption 8 introduces Monotonicity: for every individual i in the dataset, it either satisfies Positive Monotonicity, Si2(1) ≥ Si2(0), or Negative Monotonicity, Si2(1) ≤ Si2(0). This assumption eliminates one of the four principal strata. Positive monotonicity excludes the OC stratum, suggesting that the control units present in both periods are entirely composed of Always-Observed units: Si2(1) ≥ Si2(0) implies Pr(Si2(1) = 0 | Si2(0) = 1) = 0, leading to π0 = 1. On the flip side, negative monotonicity rules out the OT stratum and presumes that all treated units observed during both periods are AO stratum members. Despite seeming restrictive, this assumption is common in the literature and is essential for accurately identifying the principal strata proportions. It parallels the monotonicity assumption that excludes the presence of defiers in instrumental variable contexts. In section 3.4, I present a new method that allows this assumption to be relaxed when various sample selection sources exist within the data. Choosing between positive or negative monotonicity hinges on the study's context. For instance, when a researcher is evaluating the impact of job training on salaries, it's plausible to assume that an employee employed without training would also have a job with training, making positive monotonicity a more suitable assumption. On the other hand, if a study explores how increased tuition fees affect college students’ success and considers dropout due to higher costs, negative monotonicity is sensible. Here, if a student continues their studies despite tuition hikes, it’s plausible they would remain enrolled under usual fees. When assuming positive (negative) monotonicity, π0 (π1) becomes one, requiring only the trimming of the treatment (control) group. I employ the CiC (Athey & Imbens, 2006) technique to deduce the proportion of AO units in this group. This identification strategy presumes that an unknown function of individual hidden factors dictates potential selection outcomes. This approach is less limiting compared to assuming identical trends in selection outcomes. Indeed, the changes-in-changes framework encompasses the difference-in-differences model as a special instance, as illustrated in Example 1. This methodology offers added benefits when applied to selection: it enables the determination of the missing potential selection outcomes for both groups. This is particularly important when trimming the control group under negative monotonicity. Furthermore, it guarantees that all the estimated probabilities fall within the unit interval. Assumption 9 introduces a Selection Model: Sit(0) = h0(Uit, t) Sit(1) = h1(Uit, t), where Uit represents an unobservable scalar specific to unit i at time t, and hw(u, t) is a non-decreasing function of u for all t ∈ {1, 2} and w = {0, 1}. The unobservable U is continuously distributed and maintains the same compact range in both groups. Its distribution holds constant over time within groups Ui1 | Gi ∼ Ui2 | Gi. Additionally, once the selection outcome is realized, the distribution of U is not influenced by the group within a specific time frame. Uit ⊥⊥ Gi | Sit, t Assumption 9 frames the selection mechanism around an unobservable personal characteristic, Uit. In this context, this selection model closely resembles the outcome model described in Assumption 7. A shared central component in both models is the unobservable scalar, U, for selection, and U for the outcome. Even when they are independent, the possibility of a correlation between unobserved elements influencing selection and those impacting the outcome is a central issue in the non-ignorable sample selection challenge. Despite both models rooting in the core logic of a CiC model, there are three significant differences between the outcome model in Assumption 7 and the selection model in Assumption 9. First, estimating the missing potential selection outcomes is crucial for both the treated and control units, necessitating specific functions for S(1) and S(0). Unlike this complex requirement, only the missing potential outcome Y(0) needs to be estimated for treated units in the outcome model, making it unnecessary to model Yit(1). Second, the unknown function m(·) must be strictly increasing concerning the unobservable, whereas, for S (since it’s binary), such an equivalent assumption cannot be imposed on h0(·) and h1(·). Nonetheless, the assumption of non-decreasing nature ensures that observed units do not possess lower unobservable values compared to those exiting the sample. Third, Assumption 9 specifies that Uit ⊥⊥ Gi | Sit, t. This parallels the notion although the exact assumption, Uit ⊥⊥ Gi | Yi, t, is not overtly stated, it’s implicit in Assumption 7. Given m(u, t)’s strict increase over u, we get Uit = m−1(Yit, t), simplifying U’s distribution to be uniform and therefore equal for both groups. Consequently, the conditional independence assumption easily holds. However, when several sources of sample selection are present, the monotonicity assumption can be eased by permitting each source to independently display monotonicity, possibly with differing signs. Consider, for example, a scholarship program intended to improve university students' performance. Such a scholarship might affect selection within the treatment group through two unique mechanisms: it could lower dropout rates, illustrating positive monotonicity, and simultaneously boost graduation rates, demonstrating negative monotonicity. Assume there are J distinct sources of sample selection, where \( s_j^{it} \) is a binary variable equivalent to 0 if unit i exits the sample due to source j and 1 otherwise. In this scenario, J equals 2, with \( s_1^{it} = 0 \) if student i drops out at time t, and \( s_2^{it} = 0 \) if they graduate. By definition, these sources are mutually exclusive, signifying that when a unit exits the sample, it is due to one particular source j. For instance, students might leave because they graduated or dropped out before completing their degree, yet both events cannot happen at the same time. This structure allows the generic selection indicator to be expressed as the product of the varying sources of selection: \( S^{it} = \prod_{j=1}^{J} s_j^{it} \), with the mutual exclusivity of sources implying that \( \sum_{j=1}^{J} s_j^{it} \in \{J-1, J\} \forall i, t \). This notation also extends to potential selection indicators: \( S^{it}(w) = \prod_{j=1}^{J} s_j^{it}(w) \). The four strata detailed in Table 1 are defined for each source j. We can similarly define a variable \( V_j^i \) indicating the principal stratum of unit i characterized by the joint values of the potential selection indicator for source j, \( (s_j^i(1), s_j^i(0)) \).   **Assumption 10 Source-specific Monotonicity**: For each source \( j \in \{1, ..., J\): s_j^{i}(1) \geq s_j^{i}(0) \forall i \) for Positive Monotonicity, or \( s_j^{i}(1) \leq s_j^{i}(0) \forall i \) for Negative Monotonicity. Assumption 10 is analogous to Assumption 8, but it is specified for each particular source of selection, negating the presence of a single stratum for any source j (\( V_j^i = OC \) if positive monotonicity is assumed and \( V_j^i = OT \) if negative monotonicity is assumed). Let \( X_j \) represent the set of units belonging to stratum X according to source j. For instance, \( AO_j = \{i : V_j^i = AO\} \equiv \{i : s_j^{i}(1) = 1, s_j^{i}(0) = 1\} \).   **Assumption 11 No Intersection of OC and OT Strata**: \( OT_j \cap OC_k = \emptyset \forall j, k \in \{1, ..., J\} \). Assumption 11 excludes the possibility where a unit falls into the OT stratum defined by source j and the OC stratum defined by another source. Accordingly, if a unit is part of the OC or OT strata by source j, it can only be in the AO stratum according to all the other sources. Formally, if \( s_j^{i}(1) \neq s_j^{i}(0) \), then \( s_k^{i}(1) = s_k^{i}(0) = 1 \forall k \neq j \). Consider a student who drops out in the control group but stays enrolled if treated (\( s_1^{i}(0) = 0, s_1^{i}(1) = 1 \)). Given the mutual exclusivity and \( s_1^{i}(0) = 0 \), it concludes that the student does not graduate in the control group, \( s_2^{i}(0) = 1 \). Assumption 11 rules out the possibility that this student, who dropped out in the control group, graduates in the treatment group, hence \( s_2^{i}(1) = 1 \) is assumed. Thus, as the student falls into the OT stratum characterized by the dropout source's joint values, \( (s_1^{i}(0), s_1^{i}(1)) = (0, 1) \), they must be in the AO stratum defined by the joint values of the graduation source, \( (s_2^{i}(1), s_2^{i}(0)) = (1, 1) \). While Assumptions 10 and 11 are indeed restrictive, they alleviate Assumption 8, permitting the existence of the four principal strata. This poses no negative impact since the proportion of AO units within each group remains point-identified. Nonetheless, a significant limitation is the necessity for different sources to be present and identifiable within the data, which may not always be feasible.   **Lemma 2**: When Assumptions 10 and 11 hold, the four principal strata defined by the joint values of \( (S^{i}(1), S^{i}(0)) \) that divide the population are represented by: \( AO = \bigcap_j AO_j ; NO = \bigcup_j NO_j ; OT = \bigcup_j OT_j ; OC = \bigcup_j OC_j \). Conversely, if a unit is part of the NO, OT, or OC stratum from any source, it also aligns with the equivalent principal stratum defined by the overarching selection indicator S. I demonstrate that these proposed estimators not only exhibit consistency but also follow an asymptotically normal distribution. Additionally, I provide a discussion on the methodology for constructing confidence intervals pertaining to these estimated bounds. The development of the estimators is based on the sample analogues of the elements laid out in Propositions 1, 2, 3, and 4. For the sake of clarity and without diminishing the breadth of generality, this section specifically examines the scenario where there are two distinct sources of sample selection. In the first instance, where j equals 1, a condition of positive monotonicity is assumed. Conversely, for the second instance, where j equals 2, negative monotonicity is considered the prevailing condition. All the summations that appear throughout this section pertain to the entire size of the sample.   ### 4.2 Asymptotic Normality Let us denote the sample size as \( N \), and let \( N_0 \) represent the count of units in the control group, while \( N_1 \) indicates the number of units in the treatment group. They propose the following expression for these intervals: CIα =  [ ∆LB − Zα ˆσLB √n , [ ∆UB + Zα ˆσUB √n  (18), where Zα is determined such that: Φ(Zα + √n [∆UB − [∆LB]/max{ˆσUB, ˆσLB}) − Φ(−Zα) = α. In this scenario, Φ(·) represents the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. According to the equation (18), the interval encompasses the range [∆LB, ∆UB] at least α% of the time. Intuitively speaking, when the bounds are significantly separated and the standard errors of these bounds are relatively small, the confidence interval is determined by adding or subtracting a one-side critical value that corresponds to a confidence level α (for example, 1.645 for a 95% confidence interval) multiplied by the standard error of the bound. This critical value becomes larger when the bounds are in close proximity or when they have substantial standard errors. In a special case where [∆LB equals [∆UB and the Average Treatment effect on the Treated Adjusted Observables (ATTAO) is precisely identified, the confidence interval simplifies to become the standard one constructed around a precisely identified parameter, using Z0.95 ≈ 1.96.   ### 6 Conclusion and extensions In this section, the methodology is illustrated by examining a job training initiative conducted in Colombia. This program offered disadvantaged youth an opportunity to enhance their prospects in the labor market through three months of classroom instruction followed by three months of practical, on-the-job training. The program has been subject to analysis by Attanasio et al. (2011), who observed a positive impact on women’s wages and likelihood of securing paid employment. For men, the program slightly improved job quality, but no notable change in earnings was recorded. Continuing this line of inquiry, Attanasio et al. (2017) later explored the long-term implications of the program, detecting enduring positive effects on both earnings and job quality across genders. Recently, Possebom and Riva (2024) returned to this topic, utilizing principal stratification analysis to partially pinpoint the program’s impact on women's employment in the formal sector, particularly for those employed irrespective of their treatment status. Within this stratum, the results do not allow the researchers to dismiss the hypothesis that the training did not affect formal employment.  In the current study, I leverage experimental data from Attanasio et al. (2011), encompassing survey responses from 3,955 participants. These participants were surveyed twice: initially in January 2005, prior to the commencement of training, and subsequently between August and October 2006, following the completion of training. Based on this baseline data, I created a panel dataset conducive to Difference-in-Differences (DiD) and Changes-in-Changes (CiC) analyses. For a comprehensive overview of the data collection method and program execution, refer to Attanasio et al. (2011). My analysis focuses on assessing the training’s effect on salaried wages, which is a pertinent outcome only for those in paid employment as neither unemployed nor self-employed participants possess defined salaried earnings. Of the 3,955 sample individuals, 1,453 were observed to have paid jobs during the pre-treatment phase. Amongst these individuals, 20% were no longer in salaried positions during the post-treatment phase, and 19% were unreachable during the post-treatment survey. Consequently, I could ascertain salaried earnings for both observation periods for 888 participants, forming the cohort for my DiD estimation. Specifically, it points out that the Average Treatment effect on the Treated (ATT) estimate becomes ill-defined when sample selection results from data being censored due to mortality. In such situations, without additional assumptions, the causal interpretation of the DiD estimate is compromised. To tackle these challenges, this paper introduces new estimands—ATTAO and QTTAO(q)—that stay well-defined regardless of any sample selection issues. The study investigates the partial identification of these causal measures within a broad Change-in-Composition (CiC) framework that accommodates treatment confounders, which may include unobserved traits. The proposed approach allows researchers to assert causal conclusions even when facing non-ignorable sample selection. Nonetheless, there are still several avenues for further research extensions. The estimands put forward in this study mainly address the treatment group. Given that the treatment is not unconfounded, its effects will potentially vary between the treatment and control cohorts. However, the CiC framework can be further developed to infer the missing potential outcomes for control units, facilitating the estimation of the average treatment effect for this cohort. As a result, the proposed methodology has the potential to aid in identifying two more estimands, namely ATEAO and QTEAO(q), thereby enhancing the external validity of inferences drawn from the investigation. This study confines its scope to a two-group, two-period scenario. However, the reality of most applications is that they encompass numerous pre- and post-treatment periods. Including this data is crucial for scrutinizing the identification assumptions and achieving a fuller comprehension of the policy's impacts. Furthermore, many policy implementations occur in a staggered manner. Though the proposed methodology can be seamlessly applied to a setting with multiple groups and periods through the estimation and aggregation of pairwise comparisons (as discussed by Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021; Sun & Abraham, 2021), a more innovative and worthwhile research trajectory would be to merge it with doubly robust estimators that blend outcome modeling with propensity score weighting (as per Sant’Anna & Zhao, 2020; Arkhangelsky & Imbens, 2022). This paper does not delve into the contribution of covariates, even though they possess significant potential to bolster the identification strategy in two distinct ways. Firstly, integrating covariates could make the bounds more precise, thereby more informative. Secondly, basing assumptions on covariates might enhance their credibility and resilience, offering a sturdier basis for the analysis. A limitation of the suggested methodology is that the derived bounds might sometimes lack informativeness. When the proportion of Always Observer (AO) units decreases, the bounds broaden. Yet, even when this proportion nears 1, certain outcome distributions can still yield expansive bounds. Embracing a Bayesian approach might assist in determining where the target estimand is most likely positioned within these bounds. Lastly, this paper mitigates the monotonicity assumptions while preserving the point identification of principal strata proportions. This adjustment could also be valuable in experimental contexts. However, it hinges on the presence of multiple sources of sample selection and sustains the monotonicity assumption for each available source. Investigating methods to further relax the monotonicity assumption while producing informative bounds remains a fertile area for future research exploration.   ### A Proofs Abadie, A., Athey, S., Imbens, G. name of paper: Separating Advertising and Marketplace Functions of E-commerce Platforms: Is it Social Welfare Enhancing?
author: gpt-4o
summary: The use of sponsored product listings in prominent positions of consumer search results has made e-commerce platforms, which traditionally serve as marketplaces for third-party sellers to reach consumers, a major medium for those sellers to advertise their products. On the other hand, regulators have expressed anti-trust concerns about an e-commerce platform's integration of marketplace and advertising functions; they argue that such integration benefits the platform and sellers at the expense of consumers and society and have proposed separating the advertising function from those platforms. We show, contrary to regulators' concerns, that separating the advertising function from the e-commerce platform benefits the sellers, hurts the consumers, and does not necessarily benefit the social welfare. A key driver of our findings is that an independent advertising firm, which relies solely on advertising revenue, has same or lesser economic incentive to improve targeting precision than an e-commerce platform that also serves as the advertising medium, even if both have the same ability to target consumers. This is because an improvement in targeting precision enhances the marketplace commission by softening the price competition between sellers, but hurts the advertising revenue by softening the competition for prominent ad positions.

contents: ### 1. INTRODUCTION The explosive growth in both the size and reach of e-commerce platforms, like Amazon and eBay, has significantly reshaped online retail and advertising landscapes. These platforms do not merely function as intermediaries connecting buyers and sellers; they have evolved into major advertising centers, featuring elements such as sponsored product listings (CNN Business, 2024). Sellers vie for ad placements to enhance product visibility, with their success largely hinging on one crucial element: the precision of consumer targeting. The more precisely a platform can comprehend consumer preferences, the better it can direct advertisements to pertinent users, thereby boosting sales and maximizing profits for both the sellers and the platform itself (Goldfarb and Tucker, 2011). Nevertheless, this also brings up significant questions concerning its broader impacts on pricing strategies, consumer welfare, and market efficiency at large (Bakos, 1998). In recent times, apprehensions about the concentration of power within dominating platforms have caught the attention of regulators and policymakers alike. For example, Amazon, which wields substantial control over both retail and advertising spheres, is facing growing scrutiny regarding its market dominance (Khan, 2019). Consequently, there have been advocated proposals to segregate its advertising operations from its marketplace functions to mitigate monopolistic practices and bolster competition, thereby safeguarding smaller sellers (Claburn, 2022). Advocates for this separation believe it could diminish conflicts of interest, create a more level playing field, and provide sellers with increased autonomy. However, these proposals often overlook vital economic repercussions (Dippon and Hoelle, 2022), especially considering the potential advantages of enhanced consumer targeting and the wider repercussions for consumer welfare and market dynamics (Belleflamme and Peitz, 2015). This research note endeavors to provide valuable insights to regulators engaged in the ongoing discourse around the merits and drawbacks of their proposals to divide the advertising and marketplace roles of retail platforms. Our insights are derived from a stylized model of an online market involving two competing sellers. In scenarios where the platform integrates its advertising and marketplace functions, a consumer visiting the platform is shown sponsored listings based on sellers' bids. On the contrary, in scenarios where the advertising segment operates independently, a separate advertising entity displays sponsored listings during a consumer's visit. Both the platform and the independent advertising firm possess imperfect knowledge of consumer preferences; however, they possess the capability to refine this knowledge, thereby enhancing the accuracy of targeted sponsored listings. This research note indicates that separating the advertising operations from the platform might not fulfill the anticipated objectives. Contrary to regulators' assumptions, such a separation could disadvantage sellers and potentially diminish social welfare, albeit benefiting consumers. The fundamental factor driving these findings is that an independent advertising entity has equal or lesser incentives to enhance targeting precision compared to an e-commerce platform that doubles as an advertising medium. Improved targeting precision increases the platform's marketplace commission by reducing price competition among sellers but decreases advertising revenue by easing the competition for prime ad positions. The social welfare may only be higher under the proposed separation if consumer preference is weak or if the probability of clicking on products for ultimate purchase is low. This study adds to the ongoing discourse regarding the optimal structure of online platforms from a social welfare perspective, challenging the assumption that detaching the advertising business from dominant platforms will yield more favorable outcomes for sellers and consumers. Our findings offer invaluable insights for regulators, platform operators, and policymakers striving to balance market power and economic efficiency in the rapidly evolving digital marketplaces.   ### 2. LITERATURE REVIEW The academic community has recently started to pay significant attention to sponsored advertising within online marketplaces. Various studies have delved into scenarios where sellers possess better insights into consumer preferences than the marketplaces themselves (Long et al., 2019; Choi and Mela, 2019). Some research papers explore how this seller knowledge can affect the outcomes of sponsored ads (e.g., Chen and Stallaert, 2014; Zhang and Katona, 2012). For example, Chen and Stallaert (2014) demonstrate that when online publishers leverage consumer information for targeted advertising, there are considerable benefits, especially as user diversity and the number of competing advertisers for sponsored positions increase. Similarly, Zhang and Katona (2012) illustrate that when an advertising intermediary allows advertisers to target specific consumer segments, competition among advertisers intensifies, and this interplay significantly hinges on the number of comparison shoppers. Furthermore, Kannan et al. (2021) investigate how an online trading platform profiles sellers to decide which one will make it to a sponsored slot for each buyer.  Distinctly diverging from the stream of research that views advertising as the sole revenue mechanism for platforms, our study investigates platforms that also derive income through sales commissions. In this regard, targeting accuracy influences not only the competition among sellers for ad positions but also the dynamics of their price competition. An additional noteworthy deviation in our work from existing literature is our focus on settings where the platform possesses consumer information, transparently sharing it with sellers bidding for sponsored product listings. This scenario eliminates information asymmetry between sellers and the marketplace during bid placement. Consequently, the impacts of detaching the advertising business from the marketplace stem solely from altered incentives to refine targeting precision.  The foundational literature on the economics of digital business models has traditionally focused on the interlinks between advertising and the operational aspects of online platforms (Weyl, 2010; Brousseau and Penard, 2007). This body of work suggests that integrated platforms gain from synergies between advertising and marketplace functions, benefiting from factors like economies of scale, strengthened network effects, and enhanced ad targeting due to access to marketplace data. More recent studies addressing the economic ramifications of the enforced structural separation of advertising from marketplaces due to regulatory changes (Belleflamme and Peitz, 2018) propose that such a division could hamper data collection, thereby diminishing the platforms' capacity to deliver personalized, efficient services. Dippon and Hoelle (2022) emphasize the potential for increased market inefficiencies. Khan (2019) argues that eliminating cross-subsidization could negatively impact consumers and sellers, as platforms like Amazon might not be able to utilize advertising revenue to offer price reductions or promotional deals for consumers. Our research distinguishes itself by highlighting differing motivations for enhancing targeting accuracy under variant structures, even when data availability remains unaffected.   ### 3. MODEL SETUP We explore a scenario where third-party vendors utilize a leading retail platform, referred to as R, to connect with their buyers. In this context, we have two sellers, named A and B, with products also labeled as A and B for clarity. The platform acts not only as a commerce facilitator and marketplace but also as a promotional medium for these vendors. It levies a sales commission for providing marketplace facilities and charges an advertising fee for promotional services. The offerings from both sellers are imperfect substitutes, competing within the same product category. Seller i, where i is either A or B, sets their product price denoted as pi and pays a commission of rpi to the platform per sale, with r being the commission rate that lies within the interval (0, 1).   We consider a complete mass of consumers, each with unique preferences modeled through Hotelling’s linear city concept. This means consumers are uniformly arrayed along a line of unit length, with products A and B placed at points 0 and 1, respectively. A consumer positioned at z along [0, 1] derives utility UA(z) = v - zt from product A and utility UB(z) = v - (1 - z)t from product B. Here, v represents the utility or value a consumer places on their ideal product, whereas t (where t > 0) reflects the cost of preference misalignment, indicating the consumer's intensity or strength of preference bias. Consumers demand exactly one unit.   The platform offers two advertising positions for sellers to showcase their products. By clicking an advertisement, consumers can visit the related product page, gaining insights about the product’s location and pricing. This analysis emphasizes the advertising dynamics by assuming shoppers discover products solely by interacting with ads. Following established research on internet position auctions (Varian, 2007; Edelman et al., 2007), every ad spot comes with a click-through rate (CTR), denoting the chance a consumer will click the ad in that specific position. Studies have demonstrated variation in CTRs based on position. For example, the top (or left) ad slot often has a superior CTR compared to the bottom (or right) slot in vertical (or horizontal) displays (Lu et al., 2015; Ghose and Yang, 2009; Agarwal et al., 2011). The ad post with the superior CTR is identified as the “more-prominent position,” characterized by a CTR α, where 0 < α ≤ 1, while the lower CTR position is termed the “less-prominent position” with a CTR δ, where 0 < δ < α.  Consumers’ purchase decisions hinge on their ad-clicking patterns. A consumer who clicks on a single ad position—either the more or less prominent—will either purchase that product or exit the marketplace without buying anything. Specifically, if A appears in one position and a consumer at z clicks only on A, she buys A if and only if z ≤ zA = (v - pA)/t, assuming no alternative options. On the flip side, if B is displayed and clicked on alone by a consumer at z, they purchase B only if z > zB = (v - pB)/t. When a consumer clicks on both ads, they choose the product providing the higher net utility. Thus, if a consumer situated at z interacts with both ads, she opts for A if z ≤ zAB and for B if z > zAB, where zAB = 1/2 + (pB - pA)/(2t). Should a consumer not click either ad, no purchase occurs.  The platform possesses insights into consumer preferences, delivered as a signal s indicative of an individual's position along Hotelling’s line. Referring to Li et al. (2020) and Kwark et al. (2014), we propose that the signal accurately reflects the true location z of a consumer with probability β and lacks informativeness otherwise. This β, ranging from 0 to 1, is referred to as the platform's targeting precision. The probabilities P(s = y|z = y) = β and P(s ≠ y|z = y) = 1 - β describe this precision. Both sellers understand this targeting accuracy. The platform allocates advertising positions through a second-price auction system. The vendors develop bidding tactics to submit bids based on the consumer signals they've received; vendors A and B can place bids bA(s; β) and bB(s; β), respectively, conditional upon the signal.  This particular targeting method aligns with industry practices, where advertisers can bid considering user demographics, browsing habits, and purchase histories. The vendor placing the higher bid secures the more-prominent position, while the lesser bid lands the less-prominent spot. Identical bids result in positioning aligned with consumer-product fit, wherein the product better aligned with the consumer's expected location wins the premier spot. The winning vendor in the auction pays the losing vendor’s bid amount as an advertising fee on a per-click basis, whereas the losing vendor pays a preset reserve price, effectively normalized to zero.  We consider a scenario where the platform houses both marketplace and advertising capabilities as our benchmark, calling it the Integrated Setup, symbolizing current technological configurations on many platforms. Alternatively, we also examine a regulatory proposal aimed at bifurcating marketplace and advertising functions. This alternative, termed the Independent Setup, positions the marketplace with the platform and the advertising function with an independent advertising entity. The Independent Setup retains similar position auction methods as the Integrated Setup. By holding consumer behavior, CTRs, and the auction system constant across both configurations, we isolate the impact of the regulatory proposal to separate these functions. Furthermore, operational and targeting precision improvement costs for the platform and advertising firm, along with the production costs for sellers, are assumed negligible.  In this multi-stage game, stage 1 sees regulators choosing whether the Integrated Setup or the Independent Setup will dominate the market. In stage 2, dependent on stage 1's outcome, the platform or advertising entity selects targeting precision. Stage 3 involves the sellers concurrently deciding their pricing and bidding methodologies. In the last stage, stage 4, the platform or advertising entity gathers consumer signals and assigns ad slots based on auction outcomes. Consumers engage with ads, make purchasing decisions, and the merchants alongside the platform reap any profits. This structured sequence mirrors real-life observations attentively.  In terms of informational structure, signals indicating individual consumer positioning are confidential to the entity procuring them, either the platform or the advertising firm; however, sellers understand the targeting precision. Neither platforms, advertising firms, nor sellers can predict individual consumer clicking tendencies, though they are aware of the expected CTR for each ad location. Without engaging with product ads, consumers lack product knowledge. Sellers, platforms, and advertising firms know sellers' locations. All other parameters, consumer distribution, and auction rules are considered communal knowledge. We assume valuation lies within the moderate range, v ∈ t(α(2-α)δ + 1/2), 2t—ensuring zA, zB, and zAB reside between (0, 1), fulfilling conditions where the market remains incompletely covered, meaning not all consumers who click will invariably make a purchase.   ### 4. EQUILIBRIA IN THE INTEGRATED AND INDEPENDENT SETUPS In this segment, we aim to establish the subgame perfect equilibrium through the application of backward induction for both the Integrated Setup and the Independent Setup. We will commence by outlining the purchasing choices made by consumers alongside the demand functions of sellers, which we will tackle in Section 4.1. This will then be succeeded by an exploration of the decisions related to product listings and their respective pricing, as discussed in Section 4.2. Following that, in Section 4.3, we will focus on the decisions regarding the precision of targeting.   ### 4.1. Consumers’ Purchase Decisions and Sellers’ Demand Functions In the final phase of the game, a consumer's decision to buy is influenced by her location, the positioning of products in the listing, and the prices set for these products. Let's assume the consumer is at location z, with product A placed in a more eye-catching position and product B in a less noticeable one. From the standpoint of both the platform and the sellers, if we consider a probability of α(1 − δ), this consumer is likely to click only on product A and proceed with buying it, provided that z ≤ zA. Conversely, with a probability of (1 − α)δ, her click would be exclusively on product B, and she'd buy it only if z > zB. There's also a probability of αδ that she'd click on both product listings, opting to buy product A if z ≤ zAB, or going for product B if z > zAB. Otherwise, she might exit the platform without making any click or purchase. If the roles reverse, placing product B in the more appealing position and product A in the less favorable one, the consumer's action would shift: she'd click only on product B with a probability of α(1 − δ), buying it if z > zB, or click only on product A with probability (1 − α)δ if z ≤ zA. Alternatively, she'd click both listings with a probability of αδ, choosing product A if z ≤ zAB and product B if z > zAB. Once more, she might simply leave without engaging further. Within the Integrated Setup of the platform, or the Independent Setup involving the advertising firm, there is a signal s related to consumer location z. We denote the probability of the consumer deciding to purchase product i, also referred to as the expected demand for product i, contingent on the signal s and the position of product A being more prominent (denoted with a superscript A) as dA_i(s). Similarly, we denote the expected demand for product i, conditional on a signal s with product B in the key position (indicated via a superscript B), as dB_i(s). We illustrate dA_i(s) and dB_i(s) in Table 1 under certain circumstances: C1 represents 0 ≤ s ≤ zB, C2 indicates zB < s ≤ zAB, C3 denotes zAB < s ≤ zA, and C4 signifies zA < s ≤ 1. Additionally, Table 2 shows the differential in demand between positions, specifically dA_A(s) - dB_A(s) for product A, and dB_B(s) - dA_B(s) for product B.   Table 1 outlines the expected demands for products A and B when A occupies the more dominant spot and when B does. For dB_A(s):   - s: βδ + (1 − β)((1 − α)δzA + αδzAB); (1 − β)(α(1 − δ)(1 − zB) + αδ(1 − zAB)) for C1, - βδ + (1 − β)((1 − α)δzA + αδzAB); βα(1 − δ) + (1 − β)(α(1 − δ)(1 − zB) + αδ(1 − zAB)) for C2, - β(1 − α)δ + (1 − β)((1 − α)δzA + αδzAB); βα + (1 − β)(α(1 − δ)(1 − zB) + αδ(1 − zAB)) for C3, - (1 − β)((1 − α)δzA + αδzAB); βα + (1 − β)(α(1 − δ)(1 − zB) + αδ(1 − zAB)) for C4.  Table 2 presents the variation in expected demand between more ample and less favorable positions for both products:  - dA_A(s) − dB_A(s): (α −δ)((1 − β)zA + β) and dB_B(s) − dA_B(s): (α − δ)(1 − β)(1 − zB) for C1, - (α − δ)((1 − β)zA + β); (α − δ)((1 − β)(1 − zB) + β) for C2, - (α − δ)((1 − β)zA + β); (α − δ)((1 − β)(1 − zB) + β) for C3, - (α − δ)(1 − β)zA; (α − δ)((1 − β)(1 − zB) + β) for C4.  Some key insights from Table 2 are worth emphasizing. Firstly, it aligns with expectations that dA_A(s) − dB_A(s) > 0 and dB_B(s) − dA_B(s) > 0 for any s, with 0 ≤ β ≤ 1 and 0 < δ < α ≤ 1, indicating higher expected demand when a product is placed in a more prominent position. Secondly, for a seller, the difference is larger when the consumer signal aligns closely with the seller's location than when it stands apart. More precisely, dA_A(s) − dB_A(s) is notably higher in scenarios C1, C2, and C3 (0 ≤ s ≤ zA) than in scenario C4 (zA < s ≤ 1), and similarly, dB_B(s) − dA_B(s) is greater in scenarios C2, C3, and C4 (zB < s ≤ 1) than in C1 (0 ≤ s ≤ zB). Thirdly, given the signal s, the discrepancy in expected demand for a seller's product between a prominent position and a less-prominent placement depends solely on the product's price, as zA is influenced by pA and zB by pB. Essentially, gains in demand from holding a more-prominent position arise solely from consumers clicking and weighing only the prominently positioned product, while losses in demand when occupying a less-prominent spot stem from consumers who regard only the latter. Ultimately, this gain or loss in demand linked with product listings is contingent exclusively upon the respective seller's pricing. Lastly, the difference in expected demands for a seller elevates when the value of α − δ increases, since a consumer is more inclined to click and review merely the more-prominent product if α rises or less likely to do so for a less-prominent one if δ diminishes.   ### 4.2. Sellers’ Pricing and Bidding Strategy In both the Integrated and Independent Setup scenarios, the auction is won by the seller who submits the higher bid, and their product is consequently shown in the more prominent position. It's important to remember that the price of a seller's product has a direct impact on the predicted difference in demand between the two positions. This dynamic, in turn, shapes their willingness to pay (WTP) for the premium position and influences their bidding strategy. In the third stage of the game, sellers make their pricing and bidding decisions at the same time.
