Child Protective Services (CPS) inquiries can occasionally be invasive and distressing, with past studies highlighting significant racial discrepancies—sometimes unjustified—in CPS interactions nationwide (Kim et al. 2017, Edwards et al. 2021, Baron et al. 2023). According to our dataset, Black children are nearly twice as likely to face investigation compared to other children, even after factoring in algorithm risk scores (see Table A.9). Conversely, after adjusting for algorithm-predicted risk, there is no evidence of disparities in screening based on gender, ethnicity, or socioeconomic factors (Table A.9), prompting a focused analysis on racial disparities, particularly comparing Black children to non-Black children (predominantly white). Figure 2 illustrates that in the control group, Black children with risk predictions below the median were 60 percentage points more likely to be screened in than their similarly-ranked non-Black (primarily white) counterparts. However, with the algorithm's availability, Black children with below-median risk were screened at significantly lower rates, aligning with the rates for other children. These outcomes suggest that access to the algorithmic tool mitigated unwarranted racial disproportionality in investigations among low-risk children. Despite the trial county's relatively small Black population, the complete sample using CPS-derived race included 170 Black children, with no fewer than 23 children in each race-by-treatment-status grouping. Regression outcomes in column 1 of Appendix Table A.10 validate a reduction in screenings for low-risk Black children, numbering 26. Figure 2 underscores that the algorithm reduced racial disparities in CPS surveillance among low-risk children: (i) Below Median Algorithm-Predicted Risk (ii) Above Median Algorithm-Predicted Risk. These visuals show CPS screening rates (investigations) by race and tool access. Predicted risk is categorized using the algorithm referral risk score, with race defined as noted by Child Protective Services. The 90% confidence intervals are included, and randomization controls are in place throughout. Our theoretical framework implies that workers will better assess risk when they can rely on algorithmic data rather than group averages (Proposition 3). Our data align with this thesis. The notably large reduction in racial disparities in screenings among children with low-risk scores suggests the algorithm tool might also influence shifts in group stereotypes that guide assessments. This supports theoretical models by Bordalo et al. (2016) on stereotype formation based on a representative agent. For low-risk Black children, the algorithm may have encouraged workers to revise their reference points to align with those of other low-risk children: possibly using a different α value in model equation 1 for both low- and high-scoring Black children. Appendix Table A.10 confirms that the reductions in surveillance disparities from the tool are robust across various tests and design considerations: such as permutation tests, omitting Hispanic children, excluding children with unreported race, recoding missing race as either white or Black, and using a combined CPS and hospital-reported race approach, alongside using algorithm score levels (1-20) instead of a binary median score measure. Although the precise magnitude, and related sensitivity to detect significant effects, of the disparity in screens for below-median-risk children varies with the specifications, providing the algorithm universally reduces surveillance inequalities based on risk, or eliminates them entirely when taking the raw estimates at face value. Black children are nearly twice as likely to present an above-median algorithm risk score compared to the overall sample. We thus assess the influence of the algorithm on racial disparities in absolute metrics; basically, not adjusting for predicted risk. Column 2 of Appendix Table A.10 shows the algorithm tool reduced screening by 13 percentage points for Black children across the sample, primarily by sharply reducing screenings among low-risk Black children. The availability of the tool roughly cut racial disparities in screenings by half, but the estimate lacks statistical significance due to the relatively small number of Black children in the sample. Crucially, reducing screenings for low-risk Black children did not clearly result in adverse child harm outcomes. We lack the power to rule out a rise in harm, but harm levels among low-risk Black children were comparable regardless of tool use (Appendix Figure A.10i). The reductions in racial surveillance disparities may stem from the synergy of human judgment and algorithmic input: a composite of algorithm-revealed information and comprehensive worker training. Social workers in the study region received cultural competency training, which emphasized fair treatment of all families and sensitivity towards equity across race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, and linguistic lines. Post-trial discussions with social workers suggest that a low algorithm score might have empowered workers to forego investigations that might have been previously leveraging group racial risk averages (model proposition 3, Section 2.4). While this exploration provides a notable case of human-algorithm collaboration, further research is needed to ascertain how such disparity reductions might apply to environments with varying family demographics and differing worker beliefs or underpinning training. We revisit this analysis in Section 6.3, considering the equity benefits of human-algorithm decisions in contrast to hypothetical algorithm-alone decision rules.   ### 5.1 Algorithm Improves Worker Allocation of Screen-Ins Providing workers with an algorithm designed to forecast child risk has led to enhanced child outcomes and has also contributed to narrowing racial disparities. According to our theoretical framework, these positive effects are primarily due to enhancements in how workers assess risks to children, as indicated in Proposition 1. In this segment, we present evidence supporting the notion of enhanced decision-making among workers and eliminate a range of other possible explanations.   ### 5.2 Improvements in Targeting Reduce Child Harm and Harm Disparities The intervention failed to elevate the total amount of investigations, referred to as "screen-ins," or increase any other quantifiable level of services (refer to Figure A.11). The workers did not augment the overall level of intervention, nor did they prefer one type of intervention over another, which sometimes occurs due to the asymmetric valuation of false positives and false negatives, as noted by Almog et al. (2024) and Fitzpatrick et al. (2022). In the context of our study, intervention levels might be relatively inflexible due to legal, financial, and time limitations.   Figure 3 highlights that workers did not ramp up investigations into children with high-risk scores as predicted by the algorithm. The diagram illustrates that the association between screen-in rates and the risk score remains relatively minor within the control group and is not markedly altered by the tool's introduction. Often, a caller's immediate concerns about a child are more crucial in making screen-in decisions than the child's family history. Figure A.12 estimates the impact of other types of CPS interventions when algorithm access interacts with algorithm risk score. An earlier draft of this paper noted a slight reduction in the gradient of screen-in by risk score, which was marginally significant (p = 0.098) when workers had algorithm access compared to the control group. This reduction resulted from including 544 children sent to a residual overflow group where the tool was not used. Including these children created a misleading statistical anomaly, prompting their exclusion from the current analysis. Text data confirm that workers in these overflow groups did not consult the tool.   Notably, the availability of the algorithm tool did not make interventions for children with high algorithm scores more likely. The only observable change was that workers tended to open more preventive cases for children with low scores and fewer for those with high scores, but these adjustments do not account for the observed reduction in child harm. However, when aided by the algorithm, workers began targeting investigations toward children at higher risk of different types of harm. Randomization allows us to draw inferences about improvements in decision-making by comparing outcomes for children who were screened out. Conceptually, the potential risk of harm levels is equal in both the algorithm and control groups before the intervention, so a decrease in child harm for those screened out suggests reallocating screen-ins toward riskier children. This outcome aligns with a CPS objective of identifying children at low risk of harm who do not require visitation. This analysis represents our primary test of targeting efficacy, as reported in Column 1 of Table 3. This data came from CPS rather than hospital documentation, granting an independent assessment of all screened-in children. The variations suggest differences in the types of children screened in instead of investigator behavior, as investigators did not know the algorithm score during standard procedures. Secondly, the tool facilitated workers in focusing screen-ins on children who had suffered more maltreatment-suggestive hospitalizations before the screen-in decision, even though teams could not directly access the child's medical history (Column 3). This finding is relevant to children in the highest algorithm risk quartile (scores 16-20), comprising many children with previous hospitalizations. For children in the lower three score quartiles, harm levels in the 180 days prior to the referral are too minor to discern an effect. Finally, Column 4 indicates that workers increased screen-ins of children with a higher predicted harm index. This index is calculated using a comprehensive set of characteristics outlined in Table 3’s footnote and constructed with the leave-one-out approach detailed by Abadie et al. (2018) to prevent overfitting in the control group. Children screened in with the algorithmic tool had a predicted harm index 0.116 standard deviations higher than those screened without such support.   In summary, columns 2-4 in Table 3 demonstrate that with algorithm aid, workers became more adept at investigating cases where children showed recent injuries, underwent more previous harm, and had greater predicted future harm risks. While theoretically, screen-in targeting could improve without significant impacts on these dimensions (such as targeting children at high risk who haven't exhibited tangible harm signs yet, like not suffering recent injuries or hospitalizations, or future harm caught by our prediction model), the findings affirm that algorithmic information refined CPS's screen-in allocation decisions. It might be surprising that workers improved their investigation allocations based on potential child harm without increasing investigations for high algorithm risk score children. These facts allow for various hypotheses and negate others (refer to Table A.11). The most consistent hypothesis with these findings is that workers leverage expertise that complements the algorithmic tool, to be elaborated in Section 5.3. Echoing Bhatt et al. (2024), social workers might focus screen-ins based on anticipated treatment effects (proverbially ˆβ) instead of expected outcomes (ˆy). Essentially, not every child with high algorithm scores will benefit from CPS intervention, and vice versa. Ultimately, the improvements in screen-in targeting seen in columns 1 and 4 of Table 3 (around 0.1 SD) could potentially account for the entire 0.06 SD decrease in child harm observed with algorithm support. Enhanced screen-in targeting might also have better directed subsequent CPS actions, though our study lacks adequate power to confirm this. Targeting other concurrent interventions (e.g., law enforcement, community services) could have also improved; however, screen-ins remain the central focus for CPS. In either case, child outcomes improved with algorithm support due to workers' enhanced abilities in assessing child risk and making more informed screening decisions, as further detailed in Section 5.2.   ### 5.3 Worker Discussion Text: Changes in Worker Attention Historically, certain disadvantaged groups have exhibited a broader range of mortality rates and child maltreatment risks (as detailed by Currie and Schwandt, 2016; Putnam-Hornstein et al., 2021). Our model anticipates notable improvements in the accuracy of how workers assess risks for individuals within these groups. This enhancement is expected to result in significant reductions in harm compared to other groups (see Propositions 1.2 and 2.2). Supporting our model, the data reveals that children from demographics that underwent substantial targeting improvements via the algorithm showed the most considerable declines in documented harm (as illustrated in Figure 4). Figure 4 illustrates the impact of integrating algorithmic support on both the harm index (on the vertical axis) and the effectiveness of screen-ins (on the horizontal axis; harm is measured conditionally on screen-outs) across various notable groups. Notably, the introduction of the tool led to more significant targeting enhancements for girls compared to boys, as indicated. The point estimates in Figure 4 almost perfectly align along a fitted line. This enhancement corresponded with greater harm reductions among children, ultimately decreasing disparities in child harm. These findings more generally imply that reductions in harm can be attributed, at least partially, to improved targeting of screen-ins.   **Figure 4: Groups with Most Improved Targeting had Greatest Reductions in Child Harm**   Notes: This chart demonstrates that those groups which achieved the most significant advances in screen-in targeting also saw the largest declines in overall child harm. In this section, we delve into some compelling evidence on how access to algorithmic information altered workers' decision-making processes. We do this by utilizing comprehensive, unstructured administrative text data gathered from a partnered child welfare agency, specifically from notes taken during workers' decision-making discussions. With the support of the algorithm, workers potentially made fewer errors in combining family or child histories, gained a clearer understanding of family histories, contextualized incoming reports more effectively, or adopted a more comprehensive focus on household dynamics, including all siblings and alleged perpetrators. (2022) regard cognitive load as a key factor in determining if algorithmic tools can enhance human expertise. Overly complex interfaces or excessive alerts from algorithmic decision-support systems can lead to cognitive overload. Conversely, a machine learning tool crafted in partnership with users might lower what cognitive theory identifies as extraneous (modifiable) cognitive load, as described by Sweller (2011). In our context, an algorithm that organizes large volumes of unstructured historical data could enable workers to shift their focus to more inherently challenging aspects of their decision-making tasks, which relates to intrinsic cognitive load. According to cognitive load theory, one might anticipate more significant welfare improvements when cases are intricate and when workers can greatly benefit from algorithmic support to make family history easier to understand. As the use of machine learning tools to support decision-making becomes increasingly common, questions regarding the value human experts add to decisions and when it's appropriate to rely on machine-generated decisions also increase. In this particular study, the results improved when workers were granted access to an algorithm. Surprisingly, the workers did not focus their investigations on children who had higher risk scores according to the algorithm. Instead, they effectively utilized complementary information. Considering how well the algorithm's risk score forecasts significant outcomes (refer to Appendix Figure A.3), one might reasonably wonder if outcomes could have seen even greater enhancement if workers had made decisions more aligned with the algorithm’s risk score. In this part, we perform two innovative hypothetical exercises to estimate the impact of delegating decision-making to an algorithm. We examine whether child harm and equity might have been better addressed under two scenarios: first, if investigation decisions were guided solely by algorithm predictions, and second, if there was a slight increase in dependence on those algorithm predictions. This approach can be adapted to other experimental contexts to determine if users are making full use of algorithmic data. Elements of this approach can also be utilized to examine speculative, alternative decision-making rules beyond the existing algorithm.   ### 6.2 Counterfactual 2: Marginal Increased Reliance on Algorithm The initial counterfactual analysis employs a bounding strategy to assess the effects of completely deferring screening decisions to an algorithm. Due to legal limitations, the experiment lacked an algorithm-exclusive treatment group: statutory requirements for a screen-in do not consistently correlate with high risk predicted by the algorithm. The role of the algorithm was to predict child risk levels, not to make decisions on screening them in. We hypothesize that algorithmic recommendations would adhere to a straightforward rule, prioritizing the screening of children with the highest predicted risks. The counterfactual analysis is conducted in the following manner: First, children are sorted by their risk scores predicted by the algorithm. Next, by maintaining screen-in rates at 30 percent, consistent with other treatment groups, the riskiest 30 percent of children, according to the algorithm, are screened in. Finally, child outcomes are estimated based on these revised screening decisions. To predict counterfactual outcomes under this algorithm-centered decision framework, we categorize children from the control group into a 2-by-2 matrix defined by the observed screen-in decisions by humans and hypothetical algorithm recommendations inferred with minimal assumptions. This matrix is detailed in Table A.13 and comprises four scenarios: both the algorithm and humans decide to screen in, both decide to screen out, humans choose to screen in while the algorithm screens out, and humans screen out but the algorithm screens in. Direct observation of child health outcomes is possible when both humans and algorithms concur on the screen-in decision (both screen in or screen out). For children screened in by human decision-makers yet screened out by the algorithm, an assumption favorable to the algorithm is made, positing that these children's health would remain unharmed even if screened out, allowing us to estimate this counterfactual outcome using observed child harm. This assumption defines a best-case boundary for outcomes, should screening decisions be left to the algorithm. Additionally, estimating outcomes for children screened out by humans but screened in by the algorithm in the counterfactual scenario allows for variability across a spectrum of potential reductions in child harm due to a screen-in, assuming homogeneous impacts and a baseline level of child harm. The counterfactual outcome for these children is calculated as: max(yi − R, H), where yi represents the realized outcome for child i, R denotes the hypothetical effect of a screen-in, and H signifies the lowest possible standardized child harm value (no visits across all hospitalization categories included in the harm index). Although independently developed, this method is comparable to that proposed by Ben-Michael et al. (2024), who also employ a bounding methodology. The results from this counterfactual analysis are illustrated in Figure 6. We compare child harm outcomes under an optimal algorithm-only scenario (dashed orange line) with those observed under human-only (dashed light blue line) and human-plus-algorithm settings (solid blue line with a confidence interval). The algorithm-only counterfactual overtakes the human-only scenario by design due to the assumption that children screened in by humans but screened out by the algorithm experienced no detriment from being screened out. This is visually represented by the algorithm-only line being lower than the human-only line. The horizontal axis varies the screen-in effect for children screened out by humans but potentially screened in by the algorithm, spanning hypothetical effects from zero to four standard-deviation decreases in harm. The vertical axis indicates the average child harm index across the sample for each hypothetical screen-in effect. It is anticipated that the actual screen-in treatment effect lies on the low end of the axis (< 1 SD harm reduction), considering a screen-in is not a miracle cure and that the harm disparity between the most severely maltreated children (those in foster care) and others is less than 0.5 standard deviations. Thus, under reasonable algorithm-favorable assumptions, findings indicate that child outcomes in a human-plus-algorithm scenario surpass those in a purely algorithmic scenario under realistic screen-in effects (< 1 SD) and are comparable under higher treatment impacts. This underscores the constraints of fully automating complex social decisions with algorithms and supports the idea of human-algorithm synergy. In this scenario, the algorithm used only past data for its assessments, while social workers had the advantage of both historical data and the real-time, comprehensive reports from callers detailing the reasons why a family was referred. As the algorithm was designed to support human judgment rather than replace it, a pertinent analysis is evaluating what happens when there's a slight increase in using the algorithm's score to inform decisions, instead of wholly deferring to the rules dictated by the algorithm. Such increased reliance could mean screening in additional children that the algorithm indicated were at high risk. In real-world terms, this would be akin to enforcing a mandatory screen-in policy for families that exceed a certain high-risk threshold, similar to the procedures applied in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (Lacey et al., 2024). Our findings suggest that the possible advantages of deferring more to an algorithm have already been realized by standard human oversight over algorithmic recommendations. Figure 7 illustrates the real-life harm experienced by children who were not investigated by Child Protective Services (CPS), categorized by their treatment status and the risk level predicted by the algorithm. Each plotted point denotes the average harm index for children who were screened out, based on their algorithm risk score. Among these children, a decision-maker relying solely on the algorithm would prioritize screening those with the highest risk scores, found on the right side of the graph. Notably, there's a remarkable opportunity for enhancing welfare with algorithmic decision support: prior to tool availability, children with a risk score of 20 who weren't investigated faced harm levels nearly 0.6 standard deviations above the mean (indicated by the light blue line with circles). Social workers missed a set of high-scoring children within the control group who suffered significant harm, suggesting that a mandatory screen-in protocol for these children could have substantially improved outcomes. In contrast, social worker access to algorithmic insights (shown by the dark blue line with diamonds) improved the precision of screen-in targeting and significantly reduced the potential gains from obligatory screen-ins for top risk scores, even though screen-out rates remained constant at the upper end of the score distribution. With algorithm access, the harm reduction for screened-out children on referrals scoring a 20 is statistically significant at a 10 percent level (β = −0.44, p = 0.071). For high algorithm risk scores, the average harm for screened-out children when the algorithm was used is marginally larger, 0 to 0.1 standard deviations above the control group mean. This implies that the chief opportunities for harm reduction have already been seized by social workers leveraging the algorithm independently, rendering additional benefits from a mandatory screen-in rather modest in comparison to the expenses associated with the resulting extra investigations. Instituting a mandatory screen-in for all children receiving an algorithm score of 20 would lead to a notable 20 percent (or 6 percentage point) increase in total screen-in rates.18 Figure 7 thus underscores two main insights regarding the synergy of human and algorithm contributions. Firstly, the algorithm enhanced workers’ ability to more accurately target investigations. Even though workers didn't alter their screen-in rates for children with the highest algorithm scores while using the tool (referenced in Figure 3), they did manage to screen in a group of more vulnerable children in retrospect. Secondly, workers relied on additional information not available to the algorithm to reduce harm. In instances where workers “disagreed” with the algorithm's suggestion (high algorithm score, worker chose to screen-out), the outcomes for children weren’t considerably worse than those of other screened-out children within the same sample. Consequently, partial automation of investigation decisions using only algorithm predictions is likely to offer minimal benefits in our setting. Subsequent studies with larger sample sizes might assess partial automation combined with optimal triage methods, as suggested by Raghu et al. (2019). 18Due to a temporary flaw from the implementing partner in setting probabilistic score cutoffs, slightly more than five percent of children received an algorithm score of 20 during the trial phase. This analysis is rooted in the initial counterfactual exercise described in Section 6.1. The counterfactual situation, where only the algorithm's recommendations are followed, allows us to infer screen-in disparities with minimal assumptions. We can derive these recommendations by ranking algorithm risk scores from highest to lowest, as detailed in Section 6.1, without needing to assume how these screen-ins influence child harm. Figure 8 illustrates the disparities in CPS surveillance (screen-in) among key demographic subgroups under three distinct decision regimes: decisions made solely by humans, a combination of human and algorithm inputs, and decisions guided by the algorithm alone. Our findings indicate that the use of human-plus-algorithm decision-making improved equity not just when compared to decisions made solely by human experts, but also when compared to a theoretical scenario where only algorithm recommendations were followed without human intervention. Specifically, when compared to a purely algorithm-driven decision rule, human oversight reduced discrepancies in CPS investigations across race, ethnicity, gender, and socioeconomic status. As depicted by the dark blue squares in Figure 8 (representing human with algorithm), the disparities are consistently closer to zero compared to the orange diamonds (algorithm only), though precision in some point estimates varies. Additionally, an algorithm-only system would have resulted in a markedly higher investigation rate for Hispanic children and those from low-income backgrounds compared to the current human expert paradigm (shown by the light blue triangles). This observation aligns somewhat with concerns from social workers that algorithmic tools might reinforce historical biases within CPS actions (Stapleton et al., 2022). Importantly, the increase in surveillance noted under the algorithm-only scenario does not equate to a reduction in harm for these demographics compared to the observed human-plus-algorithm strategy (as evidenced in Appendix Figure A.15), implying that certain algorithm-only disparities might lack justification. Essentially, the equitable advancements seen during the trial wouldn't have been fully achieved—and could have actually worsened for some demographics—absent human oversight in algorithmic processes. Integrating algorithmic support with human oversight yields more balanced CPS surveillance levels than using the algorithm independently. Figure 8 clearly highlights this: showing point estimates and 90 percent confidence intervals for demographic-based disparities in screen-in rates. We directly observe human-only and human-plus-algorithm disparities in the dataset, while we infer algorithm-only disparities with minimal assumptions by ranking control group observations by risk score and enforcing mandatory screen-ins beyond a certain threshold to maintain consistent overall screen-in rates. The vertical axis represents the disparity in screen-in rates. Zero disparity is marked by a horizontal dashed black line, indicating equal screen-in rates. For instance, in the "Black vs. Other" panel, if humans worked without algorithm assistance (human only, noted by the light blue triangle on the left), Black children would experience screen-in rates 20 percentage points higher than other children. Low income status is defined as families receiving SNAP benefits. Estimating child health disparities under an algorithm-only hypothetical scenario necessitates further assumptions about the uniform effects of screen-ins across subgroups, with supplementary estimates provided in Appendix Figure A.16. Human-plus-algorithm decisions seem to more effectively curb health disparities compared to the sole use of the algorithm, though the differences don't reach statistical significance. Our conclusion is that involving humans in decision-making not only enhanced efficiency and equity over a strictly human approach but also improved equity in contrast to fully relying on algorithms (Stapleton et al., 2022). In some contexts, merging algorithmic support with human expert oversight may be a powerful method to address public skepticism regarding algorithms and mitigate the persistence of disparities.   ### References In recent years, there has been a growing interest and critical examination of machine learning tools in domains such as social services and criminal justice, with a particular focus on Child Protective Services (CPS). This paper presents one of the pioneering randomized studies evaluating the interplay between humans and algorithms within this context. CPS offers a vital and broadly applicable case for assessing the effectiveness of algorithmic decision support systems. Much like numerous public agencies, CPS (i) has amassed extensive datasets over time that are suitable for predictive risk modeling and (ii) necessitates urgent, crucial decisions from staff who often have limited experience and face high turnover rates. Our trial's high-stakes environment includes a sample of children referred to CPS during the study period that can be considered reasonably representative. Additionally, the algorithm's scalability, as evidenced by its deployment in other counties across states like Colorado, Pennsylvania, and California, provides cautious optimism about the external validity of our findings (c.f., List 2020). The study reveals that the combined efforts of humans and algorithms enhance decision quality and equity more than when either operates independently. When social workers could utilize algorithmic support, hospitalizations related to child injuries dropped by 29%, and they were able to avert two-thirds of the most extreme cases of child harm (identified in the top percentile of the child harm index). The algorithm in use was intended to assist rather than replace human workers, who were acutely aware of the distinctions between the information provided by the algorithm and that available solely through their own assessments. In this setting, algorithm support enabled workers to sift through additional, complementary information regarding the families. Additionally, the algorithm helped mitigate workers' bias in investigating Black children labeled as low risk, while human judgment reduced excess CPS scrutiny that the algorithm might have imposed on Hispanic and low-income families. Thus, the synergy between human and algorithmic decision-making proves crucial not only for boosting efficiency but also for promoting equity. Our model and identified mechanisms offer a rationale for these outcomes and suggest that similar effects might be observed in other decision-making contexts where algorithms help reduce the variability in choices, by either enriching discussions around critical data or by lessening unnecessary cognitive strains. Drawing from prior studies that have underscored benefits derived from collective decision-making approaches (Galton, 1907; Simoiu et al., 2019; Chiang et al., 2023), the scenario in which the algorithm was provided to a team of workers required to formulate a consensus decision might have augmented its effectiveness. Although our paper's evaluation spans several years, it is crucial for subsequent research to ascertain the impact of algorithmic decision support over even longer durations. Algorithms may influence workers' skill levels, the future flow of decisions, and the types of professionals organizations are able to recruit or retain due to the algorithms' potential impact on turnover (Brynjolfsson et al., 2023). Emerging studies have voiced concerns regarding the potential for worker de-skilling or increased turnover as a result of algorithms supplanting professional expertise (Rinta-Kahila et al., 2018; Grennan and Michaely, 2020). Nevertheless, in a sophisticated social environment such as child protection, where the expertise of human workers is vital, long-term effects might align more closely with new research indicating that humans can develop the capacity to make improved and innovative decisions as they engage with AI over time (Shin et al., 2023). Long-term evaluations could provide additional insights into how algorithms might be statistically or dynamically adjusted to align with human cognitive biases (Kleinberg et al., 2024). Lastly, while employing predictive risk modeling is invaluable for fine-tuning worker decisions, our discussions with workers reveal the limitations of professional discretion. In our context, agencies are legally mandated to gather supporting (non-algorithmic) evidence to probe referrals alleging maltreatment, although other types of allegations warrant an investigation regardless of the perceived risk. A legally optimal policy must, therefore, scrutinize at least a portion of predicted low-risk reports, while it cannot afford the luxury of investigating all high-risk reports.   ### Appendix A Moving away from the crucial role of human oversight and accountability could potentially violate legal requirements. This highlights the essential need for those who design algorithms to take into account both the incentives and behaviors exhibited by human decision-makers. Promising avenues for research include determining the best decision points for implementing new algorithms, effectively triaging decisions into algorithm-only, human-only, or combined tracks that involve both humans and algorithms, and enhancing the clarity and presentation of predictive information.
